ECD then removes outside​(Li,s)\text{outside}(L\_{i},s) from the remaining region before processing the next halfspace [Line [1](#alg1 "In IV-A Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
After partitioning 𝒳vi\mathcal{X}\_{v\_{i}} into these new convex sets, ECD adds a vertex corresponding to each new set to 𝒢\mathcal{G} [Line [1](#alg1 "In IV-A Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
After processing all kk tuples, ECD updates the edges of 𝒢\mathcal{G} by checking intersections among new neighboring sets [Line [1](#alg1 "In IV-A Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning") shows an example for an intermediate tuple (vi,𝐱i,𝐲i)(v\_{i},\mathbf{x}\_{i},\mathbf{y}\_{i}) with 1<i<k1<i<k.

Vertex-States Sequence Construction:
Before applying ECD to reserve a piecewise linear trajectory τ\tau on a given graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we must construct a sequence of vertex-states tuples {(vi,𝐱i,𝐲i)}i=1k\{(v\_{i},\mathbf{x}\_{i},\mathbf{y}\_{i})\}\_{i=1}^{k} such that each segment 𝐱i→𝐲i\mathbf{x}\_{i}\rightarrow\mathbf{y}\_{i} lies entirely within one single 𝒳vi\mathcal{X}\_{v\_{i}}. This construction is particularly relevant in our prioritized planning frameworks (Sec. [IV-B](#S4.SS2 "IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")) and for dynamic obstacles, where ECD reserves trajectories for collision avoidance. Three cases arise: (1) If τ\tau is reconstructed from an ST-GCS solution (Φ,𝐱,𝐲)(\Phi,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) computed on the same graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, each segment 𝐱→𝐲\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{y} naturally maps to a unique convex set of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. (2) If a segment 𝐱→𝐲\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{y} intersects more than one convex set of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we subdivide it at each boundary so that each sub-segment lies in exactly one convex set. (3) If a convex set 𝒳v\mathcal{X}\_{v} contains multiple segments 𝐱→𝐲\mathbf{x}\rightarrow\mathbf{y} (non-overlapping in time), we slice 𝒳v\mathcal{X}\_{v} by the planes t=𝐱.tt=\mathbf{x}.t and t=𝐲.tt=\mathbf{y}.t, ensuring each resulting subset contains at most one segment. Note that, when our ST-GCS is used with our prioritized planning frameworks, only cases (1) and (2) occur.

### IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks

We now introduce two prioritized planning frameworks for MRMP that use ST-GCS as the single-robot planner and ECD as a subroutine for trajectory reservation.

Random-Prioritized Planning (RP):
RP (Alg. [2](#alg2 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")) explores random total priority orders (i.e., permutations of the robots). For each order, the robots plan sequentially [Line [2](#alg2 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
Each robot ii plans its trajectory τi\tau\_{i} by solving ST-GCS on the current graph 𝒢′\mathcal{G}^{\prime} [Line [2](#alg2 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")], which is then updated with the planned τi\tau\_{i} reserved via ECD [Line [2](#alg2 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
RP returns the first feasible solution once all robots successfully plan their trajectories [Line [2](#alg2 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")]. Otherwise, it attempts the next order, until a terminal condition (e.g., runtime limit) is met.

Priority-Based Search (PBS):
PBS (Alg. [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")) systematically explores priority orders to resolve collisions by searching a priority tree, where each node NN contains a unique priority set ≺N\bm{\boldsymbol{\prec}}\_{N} of ordered pairs of robots and a set N.𝒯N.\mathcal{T} of nn trajectories that respect the prioritized planning scheme specified by ≺N\bm{\boldsymbol{\prec}}\_{N}. PBS initializes the root node with an empty priority set and potentially colliding trajectories [Lines [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")-[3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
When expanding a node NN, PBS
checks N.𝒯N.\mathcal{T} for collisions [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
If none are found, then it returns N.𝒯N.\mathcal{T} as a solution [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
Otherwise, it identifies a colliding pair τi\tau\_{i} and τj\tau\_{j} [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")] and generates two child nodes N1N\_{1} and N2N\_{2}, adding the pair i≺ji\prec j (ii has a higher priority than jj) to ≺N1\bm{\boldsymbol{\prec}}\_{N\_{1}} and j≺ij\prec i to ≺N2\bm{\boldsymbol{\prec}}\_{N\_{2}} [Lines [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")-[3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
For each child node N′N^{\prime}, PBS invokes UpdateNode to replan the trajectories for a list of robots [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")] to ensure that all trajectories in N′.𝒯N^{\prime}.\mathcal{T} respect ≺N′\bm{\boldsymbol{\prec}}\_{N^{\prime}}.
With all the high-priority trajectories reserved on 𝒢\mathcal{G} via ECD [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")], each replanning calls ST-GCS for a lower-priority robot jj [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
If UpdateNode succeeds, PBS pushes the child node N′N^{\prime} to the stack top [Lines [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")-[3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].
PBS returns failure if no valid solution can be found after visiting all possible nodes in the priority tree [Line [3](#alg3 "In IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")].

ST-GCS Solving:
Solving ST-GCS to optimality can be expensive, especially after many ECD updates that enlarge the graph. Therefore, as a low-level planner for RP and PBS, we employ the convex-restriction and path-restriction heuristic approach from [[29](#bib.bib29)] rather than seeking global optimality [[3](#bib.bib3)].
In short, this approach first relaxes binary edge variables to fractional values, then heuristically reconstructs a graph path πΦ\pi\_{\Phi} by interpreting each fractional ϕe\phi\_{e} as the probability of using edge ee.
Fixing πΦ\pi\_{\Phi} yields a final convex program for ST-GCS that can be solved at a relatively low computational cost.
Re-running this procedure multiple times with different random seeds can further improve solution quality, returning the best trajectory found.

## V Experiments

This section presents our experimental results on an Apple® M4 CPU machine with 16GB RAM.
We evaluate RP+ST-GCS and PBS+ST-GCS against three baseline methods in 2D mobile robot domains.
All methods are implemented in Python, and our ST-GCS MICP is solved using the Drake [[32](#bib.bib32)] library with the Mosek44
4
<https://www.mosek.com/> solver.
All the source code and numerical results are available on GitHub55
5
<https://github.com/reso1/stgcs>.

### V-A Experiment Setup

Instances:
We use three benchmark 2D maps (Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ V-A Experiment Setup ‣ V Experiments ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")): empty, simple, and complex [[29](#bib.bib29)].
Their spatial collision-free convex sets are given; we extrude each along time t∈[0,50]t\in[0,50] to create space-time convex sets.
For simple, we additionally introduce four dynamic disk obstacles moving at constant velocities, then apply ECD to reserve their trajectories.
For each map and each n∈[1,10]n\in[1,10] of robots, we generate 12 random instances by sampling start states and goal positions within the space-time convex sets.

Baselines:
We compare against three sequential planning (SP) baselines—i.e., prioritized planning with the fixed priority order by robot index—each with a different low-level single-robot planner.
(1) (Adapted) SP+T-PRM [[16](#bib.bib16)]: We adapt T-PRM to support collision checks on roadmap edges when finding shortest paths (missed by the original implementation) and restrict its random sampling to the given spatial convex sets.
(2) (Adapted) SP+ST-RRT∗ [[18](#bib.bib18)]: We restrict the random sampling of ST-RRT∗ random sampling to the given spatial convex sets.
(3) SP+ST-GCS.

Parameters:
For empty, we set a maximum velocity limit of 0.50.5 for each space dimension; For empty and complex, we set a maximum velocity limit of 1.01.0 for each spatial dimension.
We set a runtime limit of 150 seconds for all methods. SP+T-PRM allocates 150/n150/n seconds for each robot’s PRM construction (omitting its shortest-path finding runtime), and SP+ST-RRT∗ allocates 150/n150/n seconds for each single-robot ST-RRT∗ planning.
For ST-GCS MICP solving on any graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) using the heuristic approach (see Sec. [IV-B](#S4.SS2 "IV-B Prioritized Planning Frameworks ‣ IV ST-GCS For Multi-Robot Motion Planning ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning")), we limit the number of graph paths sampled to 1​e3×log⁡|ℰ|1e^{3}\times\log|\mathcal{E}|.

### V-B Results and Analysis

Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ V-A Experiment Setup ‣ V Experiments ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning") reports four metrics: Success Rate (out of 12 random instances), Runtime (in seconds, on a log-scaled y-axis), SoC (the sum of time costs of all trajectories), and Makespan (the maximum time costs of all trajectories, on a log2-scaled y-axis).
The last three metrics are averaged only over the intersection of instances solved by each method, ensuring a fair comparison. If a method solves fewer than 3 of 12 instances for a given nn, it is excluded from that average to avoid empty intersections.

Success Rates and Runtimes:
PBS+ST-GCS solves all instances on empty and complex, with average runtimes consistently under 1 second and 10 seconds on average, respectively—often orders of magnitude faster than sampling-based methods. Adding dynamic obstacles on simple significantly enlarges the initial space-time graph (via ECD), which can slow ST-GCS solving; nevertheless, PBS+ST-GCS still achieves the highest success rates overall.
RP+ST-GCS randomly explores different priority orders until timeout generally attains higher success rates than SP+ST-GCS which uses only a fixed priority order.
Among sampling-based methods, SP+ST-RRT∗ outperforms SP+T-PRM on empty and simple, likely due to the inherent faster tree-based exploration rooted at the starts and goals. However, on complex with many spatial corridors, the more global random exploration of T-PRM yields higher success rates than ST-RRT∗.
Still, both fail when n>2n>2 on complex.
Comparing all SP-based methods, SP+ST-GCS typically runs faster than the two sampling-based methods and achieves higher success rates in settings with more spatial corridors. However, its success rates are lower for larger nn, due to the heuristic MICP solver failing more frequently, as analyzed in the ablation study below.

Solution Quality:
PBS+ST-GCS consistently yields the best solution quality across all maps. Its SoC scales almost linearly with nn, and its makespan barely increases as nn grows. Other ST-GCS variants also produce better solutions than the sampling-based methods in many cases.

Ablation—Effectiveness of PBS for ST-GCS:
Our raw data indicates that large space-time graphs (over 1000 edges) resulting from numerous dynamic obstacles can impede the heuristic MICP solver under limited path-sampling budgets. Fig. [5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ V-B Results and Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning") demonstrates that PBS mitigates this issue by reserving only conflicting trajectories deemed high-priority, controlling graph growth more effectively than SP+ST-GCS and RP+ST-GCS (which both rely on total priority orders with sequential ECD, thus expanding the graph faster as nn grows).

Ablation—Constrained Sampling:
Fig. [6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ V-B Results and Analysis ‣ V Experiments ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning") compares T-PRM and ST-RRT∗ with random sampling constrained to the spatial collision-free convex sets versus unconstrained sampling (labeled T-PRM(u) and ST-RRT∗(u)) over the entire bounding box. Constrained sampling yields modest improvements in success rates (though T-PRM still fails for higher n) and better solution quality for ST-RRT∗. This confirms that focusing sampling on collision-free regions can be beneficial, albeit insufficient to match ST-GCS performance.

### V-C Case Study

We highlight two examples of ST-GCS and PBS+ST-GCS.
Figure [7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ V-C Case Study ‣ V Experiments ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning") demonstrates ST-GCS finding a safe shortcut through dynamic obstacles, where ST-RRT∗ struggles to connect sample points to exploring trees, and T-PRM fails to find a feasible solution even after 20k samples.
Figure [8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ V-C Case Study ‣ V Experiments ‣ Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets for Multi-Robot Motion Planning") compares PBS+ST-GCS against SP+ST-RRT∗ for 8 robots on simple.
PBS+ST-GCS lets them move through the center congested region simultaneously with minimal waiting or detours, whereas SP+ST-RRT∗ schedules them one by one, creating more zig-zagging and delays.

![Refer to caption](2503.00583v1/demo_dynamic_obstacles.png)
![Refer to caption](2503.00583v1/demo_mrmp.png)

## VI Conclusions & Future Work

We presented ST-GCS, a time-optimal deterministic approach to MRMP that addresses the inherent limitations of sampling-based methods in spatiotemporal settings.
By extending the GCS formulation to a space-time domain, ST-GCS systematically covers spatiotemporal bottlenecks using collision-free convex sets. Our ECD algorithm further enables straightforward reservation of piecewise linear trajectories of dynamic obstacles for collision avoidance. We integrated ST-GCS and ECD into prioritized planning frameworks and demonstrated through extensive experiments that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art sampling-based methods in both success rates and solution quality, often with orders-of-magnitude faster runtimes, especially in challenging scenarios such as narrow corridors and crowded environments.
Future work includes investigating robust pruning strategies for managing the ST-GCS graph size when numerous trajectories are reserved via ECD, generalizing ECD to higher-dimensional spaces and more complex obstacle models, and extending ST-GCS with richer motion models with nonholonomic and dynamic constraints.

args.summary:
This paper presents Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets (ST-GCS), a novel deterministic approach to Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) that addresses limitations of sampling-based methods in spatiotemporal settings. The key contributions include: (1) extending Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) into the time dimension to formulate time-optimal trajectories in a unified convex optimization that naturally accommodates velocity bounds and flexible arrival times; (2) introducing Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) to reserve trajectories as spatiotemporal obstacles, maintaining collision-free space-time graphs for subsequent planning; and (3) integrating ST-GCS into two prioritized-planning frameworks (Random-Prioritized Planning and Priority-Based Search).

The method works by systematically covering the collision-free space-time domain with convex sets rather than relying on random sampling. ST-GCS solves a generalized shortest-path problem on a graph whose vertices are convex sets, determining which sets form the path and the state within each set, jointly optimizing a time-minimizing objective. The ECD algorithm partitions space-time convex sets to avoid conflicts with already-planned trajectories, treating higher-priority robot trajectories as dynamic obstacles.

Experimental results on 2D mobile robot scenarios demonstrate that ST-GCS consistently achieves higher success rates and better solution quality than state-of-the-art sampling-based planners (adapted T-PRM and ST-RRT*), often with orders-of-magnitude faster runtimes. PBS+ST-GCS solves all instances on empty and complex maps, with average runtimes under 1 second and 10 seconds respectively. The approach is particularly effective in narrow corridors and crowded settings where sampling-based methods struggle to capture spatiotemporal safe transit windows.

# [Tommy's Research Blog](https://blog.tommycohn.com/)

### Differing Formulations of GCS for Motion Planning

In case you haven't heard of it before, GCS stands for "Graph of Convex Sets", and it is a framework for certain mixed integer convex optimization problems, primarily used for robot motion planning. I previously wrote a blog post on my experience implementing a basic version of it, which you can find [here](https://blog.tommycohn.com/2022/09/reimplementing-gcs-shortest-paths-in.html). I'd recommend reading that blog post before looking at this one.

If you've read that previous blog post, you may recall that I described two different ways of transcribing the motion planning problem into a graph of convex sets. I implemented one version, which seems more faithful to the [original GCS paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11565). However, the other transcription, presented in the [planning-specific followup paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04422), has several benefits over the previous approach. In this blog post, I'll briefly present both methodologies, and explain their costs and benefits.

## Formulation 1: Conjugate Graph

|  |
| --- |
| [Fig. 1 of *Shortest Paths in Graphs of Convex Sets*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11565) |

The classic picture of GCS is the one shown in Figure 1 of the original paper (included above). However, it's not immediately obvious how to use this for collision free motion planning. If the sets shown are regions which we know to be collision free, that says nothing about whether the paths between the sets are also collision free.

The idea behind the conjugate graph formulation is to use the intersections of collision-free sets as the sets in the graph. We can then move between two sets if the straight line path between them is contained within a collision-free set, i.e., if the intersections share a constituent set. In effect, we have interchanged the role of the sets and edges. The corresponding graph-theoretic construction is called the [line graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_graph), but it has many other names. I find that "line graph" is a rather ambiguous term, so I always refer to it as the conjugate graph.

## Formulation 2: Overlap Graph

|  |
| --- |
| [Fig. 1 of *Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04422) |

In generalizing the motion planning framework of GCS to handle [Bézier curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9zier_curve) trajectories, the authors use a different way of encoding the collision free sets. They place several points in each free region, and use them as control points to describe a segment of the trajectory. The trajectory endpoints are then constrained to be equal to each other on the overlap between each set (if the boolean variable corresponding to that edge being traversed is true).

## Tradeoffs

In my experience with both formulations, I've found that the conjugate graph formulation is more straightforward to implement. But beyond that, there are few reasons to not go with the overlap graph formulation. The overlap graph formulation parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, enabling its use for broader optimization problems. It's also likely to be the "official" formulation going forward.

The conjugate graph does present a subtle benefit over the overlap graph, but it comes with a hidden cost. Suppose one wanted to preprocess the graph of convex sets, after a start and goal have been defined, but before formulating the optimization problem. Given a lower bound on each edge and vertex cost, and any feasible solution (which is easily obtainable via heuristic methods), it's possible to prune away many edges and sets if the cumulative best-case cost from the start or goal exceeds the incumbent solution. This could potentially dramatically reduce the size of the optimization problem.

In the conjugate graph formulation, it's easy to compute useful lower bounds. But in the overlap graph formulation, the lower bound is trivially zero, as all the points in the set could be made identical. However, there is no free lunch for the conjugate graph formulation. In scenarios where many of the convex sets overlap, the number of sets and edges in the conjugate graph can grow quite large. So the gains from the preprocessing may not outweigh the overall increase in problem size. Perhaps the conjugate graph lower bounds could be adapted to the overlap formulation, but I haven't come up with a way to to do this yet. GCS is still a young framework, and there is still a lot of room for clever heuristics, preprocessing techniques, and overall engineering effort to improve the algorithm.

Going back to the main point of this post, I think the overlap graph is the best formulation for actually using GCS in the future. (Even if it takes a little more effort to wrap your head around how it actually fits into the optimization framework.)

# Faster algorithms for growing collision-free convex polytopes in robot configuration space

[Peter Werner](#con1) <https://orcid.org/0009-0000-1599-0594> [wernerpe@mit.edu](mailto:wernerpe@mit.edu), [Thomas Cohn](#con2), […], [Rebecca H. Jiang](#con3), [Tim Seyde](#con4), [Max Simchowitz](#con5), [Russ Tedrake](#con6), and [Daniela Rus](#con7)+4-4[View all authors and affiliations](#tab-contributors)

## Abstract

We propose two novel algorithms for constructing convex probabilistically collision-free polytopes in robot configuration space. Finding these polytopes enables the application of stronger motion-planning frameworks such as trajectory optimization with Graphs of Convex Sets ([Marcucci et al., 2023](#bibr26-02783649261436917)) and is currently a major roadblock in the adoption of these approaches. In this paper, we build upon the IRIS-NP algorithm (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite & Nonlinear Programming) of [Petersen and Tedrake (2023)](#bibr35-02783649261436917) to significantly improve tunability, runtimes, and scaling to complex environments. IRIS-NP uses nonlinear programming paired with uniform random initialization to find configurations on the boundary of the free configuration space. Our key insight is that finding nearby configuration-space obstacles using sampling is inexpensive and greatly accelerates region generation. We propose two algorithms using such samples to either employ nonlinear programming more efficiently (IRIS-NP2) or circumvent it altogether using a massively parallel zero-order optimization strategy (IRIS-ZO). Both algorithms employ a novel termination condition that controls the probability of exceeding a user-specified permissible fraction-in-collision, eliminating a significant source of tuning difficulty in IRIS-NP. We further present an approach for applying both algorithms in parametrized configuration spaces. We compare the performance across eight robot environments, showing that IRIS-ZO achieves an order-of-magnitude speed advantage over IRIS-NP, which is extended roughly by an additional order of magnitude by parallelizing it with a GPU. IRIS-NP2, also significantly faster than IRIS-NP, builds larger polytopes using fewer hyperplanes which has the additional benefit of accelerating downstream motion planning. Website: <https://sites.google.com/view/fastiris>.

## 1. Introduction

A major challenge in robot motion planning is the need to simultaneously consider *task space*, the world in which the robot physically resides, and *configuration space*, , the set of all possible robot configurations. The planner must produce a trajectory in the configuration space, but many constraints are formulated in the task space. Collision avoidance is particularly challenging, because even geometrically simple obstacles in task space can have intractably complicated descriptions when transformed into configuration space through the robot’s inverse kinematics. While there is work on constructing explicit configuration-space representations of workspace obstacles ([Bajaj and Kim, 1990](#bibr3-02783649261436917); [Lozano-Pérez, 1990](#bibr24-02783649261436917); [Pan and Manocha, 2015](#bibr34-02783649261436917)), these methods are intractable for the high degree-of-freedom (dof) robotic systems being used today.

The unavailability of obstacles’ configuration-space descriptions has not prevented the development of a rich literature of motion planning algorithms. Many approaches approximate the set of collision-free configurations  without explicitly constructing the individual obstacles. Interval analysis and cell decompositions can approximate  as the union of boxes ([Jaulin, 2001](#bibr15-02783649261436917); [Latombe, 2012](#bibr18-02783649261436917), §5.6), but these methods are computationally intractable for high-dimensional configuration spaces. Perhaps the most widely used technique has been sampling-based planning, in which samples are drawn from  and connected into a graph structure.

These representations of  are popular due to their simplicity and versatility. However, they all struggle with the “curse of dimensionality”—the memory use of the representation may grow exponentially with the dimension of the configuration space. This has led the motion planning community to explore volumetric approximations of  such as the union of spheres used by [Yang and LaValle (2004)](#bibr48-02783649261436917) or the polytopes constructed by [Deits and Tedrake (2015)](#bibr11-02783649261436917). In contrast to the grid- or sampling-based approaches, the individual sets used in these approaches describe free-space regions rather than points. Although these sets are harder to construct, they often enable a more concise approximation of  and yield convex (probabilistic) collision-avoidance constraints.

Modern decomposition-based motion planning algorithms (DBMPs) leverage these representations to quickly produce high-quality, collision-free trajectories and can scale to high-dimensional robotic systems ([Chen et al., 2016](#bibr7-02783649261436917); [Chew Chia et al., 2024](#bibr8-02783649261436917); [Liu et al., 2017](#bibr21-02783649261436917); [Marcucci et al., 2023](#bibr26-02783649261436917), [2024](#bibr27-02783649261436917); [Morozov et al., 2024](#bibr29-02783649261436917), [2025](#bibr30-02783649261436917); [Natarajan et al., 2024](#bibr32-02783649261436917); [Wu et al., 2024](#bibr47-02783649261436917)). Furthermore, by nature of their use of optimization, these planners can handle a variety of costs and constraints. However, the performance of these planners is highly dependent on the properties of the convex sets. It is desirable for these sets to have large volumes in order to reduce the number of sets required to approximate , while retaining simple descriptions to make downstream planning more efficient. While creating perfectly collision-free sets is very costly, practical algorithms should provide a straightforward way to trade off between precision and runtime.

Recent results for planning on Graph of Convex Sets (GCSTrajOpt) leverage the IRIS-NP algorithm ([Cohn et al., 2024](#bibr9-02783649261436917); [Marcucci et al., 2023](#bibr26-02783649261436917); [Morozov et al., 2024](#bibr29-02783649261436917), [2025](#bibr30-02783649261436917)). IRIS-NP takes in a collision-free *seed* configuration and attempts to construct a convex, collision-free polytope containing it. IRIS-NP, however, falls short of meeting the aforementioned criteria in practice. Its runtime is substantial and trading off between runtime and correctness (how much of the region is collision-free) proves challenging. IRIS-NP only terminates after failing to solve a user-specified number of nonlinear programs in succession, a time-consuming process dependent on this user-specified parameter acting as a proxy for correctness, when the actual relationship is unclear. Furthermore, these nonlinear programs must be run separately for every object in the scene, causing IRIS-NP to scale poorly with environment complexity.

In this paper, we improve upon IRIS-NP, focusing on a key subroutine that constructs hyperplanes to separate the seed point from obstacles. Our improvements leverage the fact that we can evaluate thousands of configurations for collisions in the time it takes to solve a single nonlinear optimization problem. We employ random sampling and collision-checking to estimate the proportion of the polytope that is collision-free, providing a rigorous probabilistic certificate and enabling intuitive tradeoffs between region correctness and computation times. We further present two algorithms that utilize sampling and collision-checking to improve polytope generation: IRIS-ZO rapidly generates polytopes using a simple parallelized zero-order optimization strategy that requires no gradient computations and is easy to implement. IRIS-NP2 uses sampled collisions to seed nonlinear optimizations, increasing search success and dramatically reducing the required number of programs. We demonstrate that both algorithms outperform IRIS-NP in terms of computation time and region quality.

This paper further extends the initial conference paper ([Werner et al., 2024b](#bibr44-02783649261436917)) in several ways. We demonstrate that our algorithmic improvements accelerate downstream motion planning and lead to lower-cost plans, and show that IRIS-ZO can be further sped up by a factor of 10 by leveraging GPU-parallelism. Finally, we show how both IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2 can be used to grow regions under any smooth parametrization of configuration space. This allows us to grow regions for kinematically constrained systems (e.g., for constrained bimanual manipulation), even when the feasible set is measure-zero, as in ([Cohn et al., 2024](#bibr9-02783649261436917)). An open-source implementation of our method is made available as part of the Drake modeling and simulation framework ([Tedrake and the Drake Development Team, 2019](#bibr40-02783649261436917)).

## 2. Problem formulation

In this section, we introduce the problem formulation and discuss the required inputs and provided outputs of our proposed algorithms.

We aim to generate polytopes[1](#fn2-02783649261436917) in configuration space whose volume is large, and whose fraction in collision is less than a user-provided constant. More precisely, let *λ* denote the Lebesgue measure in the free configuration space . Given a user-specified admissible fraction in collision *ɛ* ∈ (0, 1) and confidence *δ* ∈ (0, 1), we will compute positive-volume polytopes  such that

Since obtaining a closed-form description of  is intractable for general robotic systems according to ([LaValle, 2006](#bibr20-02783649261436917), §4.3.3) and ([Latombe, 2012](#bibr18-02783649261436917), §3), our algorithms utilize a task-space description. Such descriptions are readily provided via common robot description formats such as URDFs ([http://ros.org/](http://ROS.org)[ROSorg, 2024](#bibr36-02783649261436917)) or SDFs ([Open Source Robotics Foundation, 2024](#bibr33-02783649261436917)).

We expect the robotic system to be described as *M* sets  representing collision geometries in task space. Here, *N*ts ∈ {2, 3} is the dimension of the task space, and  is the configuration. The sets  are represented in their body frame *B**i*. Using monogram notation ([Tedrake, 2023](#bibr39-02783649261436917), §3.1), each  is paired with a configuration-dependent rigid-body  that defines the forward kinematics of  in the world frame *W*. We use the shorthand  for  expressed in the world frame:

We let  be the set of all collision geometries.

For a configuration *q*, the system is *in collision* if there exists a *valid*[2](#fn3-02783649261436917) pair of collision geometries  such that . For a valid collision pair , the corresponding *configuration-space obstacle*  is implicitly defined as

We avoid explicitly describing  by using non-convex task-space constraints, as in the work of [Petersen and Tedrake (2023)](#bibr35-02783649261436917).

## 3. Related works

Algorithms for computing positive-volume subsets of  can be divided into two categories: those which require explicit descriptions of the obstacles in configuration space, and those that can use implicit descriptions. Explicit descriptions of obstacles are generally only available for robots with simple kinematics (e.g., only prismatic joints).

If descriptions of all obstacles are given as convex sets, the original IRIS algorithm can construct large collision-free polytopes about a seed points using a series of convex optimizations ([Deits and Tedrake, 2015](#bibr11-02783649261436917)). Such descriptions can be obtained from arbitrary meshes via approximate convex decomposition techniques ([Mamou and Ghorbel, 2009](#bibr25-02783649261436917)). [Wu et al. (2024)](#bibr47-02783649261436917) use a similar approach to grow polytopes around an existing trajectory, towards producing a shorter, collision-free path.

Due to the complex kinematics of robotic manipulators, obstacles in configuration space are frequently given by implicit descriptions. [Yang and LaValle (2004)](#bibr48-02783649261436917) leveraged the kinematic Jacobian to relate motion in configuration-space and task space, allowing the construction of collision-free ellipsoids. Unfortunately, large numbers of ellipsoids are required to approximate even simple, low-dimensional configuration spaces.

The original IRIS algorithm has been extended to handle such implicit descriptions in two ways. IRIS-NP ([Petersen and Tedrake, 2023](#bibr35-02783649261436917)) uses nonlinear programming to find multiple locally separating hyperplanes to each obstacle, until the program becomes infeasible—an imprecise termination condition that often leaves some obstacle volume in regions. [Jaitly and Farzan (2024)](#bibr14-02783649261436917) modified IRIS-NP to use a nonuniform sampling strategy to seed the collision search program. The other option is to use a rational parametrization of the kinematics to construct regions that are rigorously certified to be collision-free with sums-of-squares programming ([Dai et al., 2024](#bibr10-02783649261436917)). However, such optimizations are computationally expensive, and the regions are grown in a stereographic projection of configuration space, which distorts distances.

Alternatively, [Sarmientoy et al. (2005)](#bibr37-02783649261436917) directly decompose three-dimensional spaces into polytopes only using sample-based collision-checking. Unfortunately, this approach requires dense sampling of the configuration space to produce large sets which is intractable in all but the simplest cases.

## 4. Background on IRIS algorithms

In this section, we review the key algorithms our approach builds upon. The IRIS algorithm ([Deits and Tedrake, 2015](#bibr11-02783649261436917)) takes in a list of convex obstacles and produces a collision-free polytope around a seed point in the same space as these obstacles. IRIS-NP ([Petersen and Tedrake, 2023](#bibr35-02783649261436917)) generalizes IRIS to operate in configuration space using nonlinear programming.

To understand the upcoming modifications to IRIS-NP, we review the SeparatingPlanes step in detail.

This section discusses how we leverage sampling to produce a rigorous termination condition for SeparatingPlanes in robot configuration space (see sec. 4.2), and two improved approaches for solving the step, yielding the new algorithms IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2, whose parameters are given in [Table 1](#table1-02783649261436917). ### 5.1. Termination condition for the separating planes step

### 5.2. The IRIS-ZO algorithm

The IRIS-ZO algorithm uses a simple parallelized zero-order optimization strategy to directly solve SeparatingPlanes in Alg. 1 for all collision pairs simultaneously. We call this subroutine ZeroOrderSeparatingPlanes and summarize it in Alg. 2. [Figure 3](#fig3-02783649261436917) illustrates how ZeroOrderSeparatingPlanes optimizes hyperplanes.

The ZeroOrderSeparatingPlanes step constructs a probabilistically collision-free polytope  by repeating 5 steps until the statistical test passes. We take as input the domain , the current ellipsoid , the current outer iteration *i* and options that are summarized in Tab. 1. Here, we assume that the center of the current ellipsoid is collision-free. We then initialize  with the domain  (typically a polytope describing the joint limits).

The first step is to uniformly sample a batch of configurations  in  via hit-and-run sampling ([Lovász, 1999](#bibr22-02783649261436917)) with a batch size of max{*M*, *N**p*}. Then, we find all configurations  that are in collision by running a collision checker. These samples are used to check the termination condition by running the unadaptive test, returning  if it accepts. More precisely, counting the collisions  in the first *M* samples in  and accepting if .

If the probabilistic test fails, we then add hyperplanes to the polytope. We produce candidate solutions for the closest point in collision program (5) based on the first *N*p configurations *q* in . For each *q*, we use bisection search to step toward the center *c* of the ellipsoid, while ensuring that *q* is still in collision. In practice, we bisect a fixed number *N**b* of times and pick the configuration *q*⋆ that is closest to *c* and still in collision. This yields our updated batch . This strategy is guaranteed to converge to the boundary of an obstacle for each configuration *q*, but not necessarily the obstacle containing the original *q* or the one that is closest to *c*. Because this optimization procedure is gradient-free and only relies on a collision checker, it is highly parallel and its performance scales with available computational resources. Finally, we order all candidates  by ellipsoidal metric in ascending order. We then repeatedly select the closest candidate *q*⋆ inside the current polytope and add a hyperplane at that configuration tangent to the ellipsoid, until we hit *N**f* non-redundant hyperplanes or run out of candidates. We remark that this is a computationally cheap way of guaranteeing that the currently placed hyperplane is not redundant, which avoids solving any redundancy checks via linear programming but discards candidates outside of the current polytope, which would produce non-redundant hyperplanes and potentially reduce the number of iterations required.

### 5.3. The IRIS-NP2 algorithm

The IRIS-NP2 algorithm (Alg. 3) places hyperplanes more carefully than IRIS-ZO, increasing runtime in favor of larger regions with fewer hyperplanes, while still improving upon IRIS-NP runtimes. Like IRIS-NP, IRIS-NP2 uses nonlinear programming, solving (5) to find separating hyperplanes. In contrast to IRIS-NP, IRIS-NP2 always initializes NLP searches with feasible initial guesses *q*0, prioritizing initial guesses with lower ellipsoid metric . These initial guesses, along with the corresponding pair of bodies in collision,  such that , are obtained via a subroutine GetConfigInCollision, two options for which are outlined at the end of this section.

![](/cms/10.1177/02783649261436917/asset/18abc73e-bead-42d1-999f-9016e1b35cee/assets/graphic/10.1177_02783649261436917-img3.png)

This strategy of always using a feasible initial guess presents a major advantage over IRIS-NP, as IRIS-NP spends substantial time in NLP solves that return infeasible. In part, this property of IRIS-NP is due to initializing NLP searches with uniform samples *q*0, in the hopes that the nonlinear program solver can pull those *q*0 not in collision into collision to return feasible optimized solutions *q*⋆. In practice, this frequently fails even when the polytope does contain collisions. Furthermore, as discussed in Sec. 4.2, IRIS-NP *requires* that many consecutive NLP solves return infeasible in order to terminate. Assessing termination readiness via the Bernoulli trials is faster, allowing the NLP, which is slow to solve, to be used only to construct hyperplanes. Another advantage of this strategy is it scales better with environment complexity. IRIS-NP must solve a minimum number of NLPs for every valid collision pair. This quantity grows quickly with scene complexity, while many of these pairs never actually collide, resulting in infeasible NLPs and wasted computation time. IRIS-NP2 only considers pairs known to collide, and hence solves only feasible NLPs. We present two options for GetConfigInCollision, with differing costs and benefits: the greedy collision finder, which is hyperparameter-free, and the ray collision finder, which can be tuned for higher performance.

For the *Greedy Collision Finder*, all samples from the Bernoulli trial that are in collision are aggregated and sorted in ascending order of distances to the center point of the ellipsoid, w.r.t. the ellipsoidal metric. (In effect, *N**p* is dynamically set to equal the number of collision particles.) When queried, this subroutine returns the sample with the next-lowest ellipsoid metric, until all in-collision samples from the Bernoulli trial have been exhausted. If a sample is not in the polytope (due to new hyperplanes from an earlier sample), it would no longer be a feasible initial guess for Equation (5), so None is returned.

The *Ray Collision Finder* ([Figure 4](#fig4-02783649261436917)) prioritizes the quality of the constructed hyperplanes via an inexpensive line search to find configurations in collision near the ellipsoid center. The ray collision finder takes a subset of the samples drawn for the Bernoulli trial, and, for each sample, steps outward in discrete steps along the ray from the ellipsoid center through the sample. The first step in collision is returned. If a step has exited the polytope, None is returned. This discrete search serves a purpose similar to the objective of (5): to limit the hyperplanes needed, we desire to add hyperplanes at the closest (in the ellipsoid metric) points in collision. Because the discrete search is not restricted to a specific collision pair, it may find configuration-space obstacles closer than (5). In contrast to the bisection search performed by IRIS-ZO, this line search sweeps monotonically outward from the ellipsoid center in an attempt to find the closest collision; the IRIS-ZO bisection search steps inward from the sample, finding a point on a boundary of a configuration-space obstacle. (The ray may pass through several such boundaries).

## 6. Growing polytopes in parametrized configuration spaces

For collision-free motion planning, constructing convex subsets of  is tractable because  itself is positive-measure. This is not the case for systems like mechanical linkages, which physically must satisfy (nonlinear) equality constraints. Even when there are no physical constraints, satisfying such constraints may still be necessary for task completion. For example, consider a bimanual robot moving a rigid object with both hands. In this case, the two grasps define a “virtual linkage” ([Williams and Khatib, 1993](#bibr46-02783649261436917)), and the set of kinematically valid configurations  is a measure-zero subset of the full configuration space . We refer to this set as the *constraint manifold* (although it is only truly a manifold if we excise singularities).

To plan along constraint manifolds, sampling-based planners must use specialized techniques to draw samples ([Kingston et al., 2018](#bibr17-02783649261436917)). Trajectory optimizers must use similar techniques ([Bordalba et al., 2022](#bibr5-02783649261436917)) or accept slight constraint violations away from the control points of the trajectory ([Bonalli et al., 2019](#bibr4-02783649261436917)). But GCSTrajOpt, and DBMPs in general, were wholly inapplicable, as any convex subset of  would have an empty interior and relative interior.

### 6.1. Prior methods

Recent work, using analytic inverse kinematics as a parametrization of the constraint manifold, enabled trajectory optimization intrinsic to  ([Cohn et al., 2024](#bibr9-02783649261436917)). The key ingredient is a smooth mapping from some other space to , the image of which is a subset of . This mapping effectively defines (minimal) nonlinear coordinates on the constraint manifold, which are used to represent the trajectories. Costs and constraints can then be imposed both in these nonlinear coordinates as well as in  by precomposing the parametrization. Using this approach guarantees, by construction, that trajectories obey the kinematic constraints up to floating-point error.

[Cohn et al. (2024)](#bibr9-02783649261436917) propose growing convex sets in terms of the nonlinear coordinates in order to use DBMPs restricted to . To this end, they modified IRIS-NP to operate through the parametrization: given a smooth mapping  that parametrizes , the algorithm finds hyperplanes to

(1) avoid function domain violations,

(2) avoid joint limit violations, and

(3) avoid non-reachable configurations

(in that order), before finally searching across all possible collision pairs. While this approach enables planning intrinsic to  using DBMPs, users were confronted with the same challenges with IRIS-NP as discussed in Sec. 1 and 4.2, which are exacerbated due to the greater problem complexity. Ultimately, the regions had a large number of hyperplanes, and the fraction of the region in collision (or violating a constraint) was difficult to control as a user, even with careful tuning of the number of consecutive solve failures for each constraint and collision pair.

In the following, we show that we can circumvent these challenges by adapting both IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2 to operate in parametrized configuration spaces.

## 7. Experiments

### 7.1. Polytope construction benchmark

To evaluate our proposed changes to the IRIS-NP algorithm, we put forth a comprehensive benchmark. This benchmark includes eight different robotic systems, described in [Figure 6](#fig6-02783649261436917). For each benchmark, we select 10 seed configurations manually, placing the robot in a variety of configurations in its environment. Each experiment is run for a single outer iteration, to isolate performance differences in the SeparatingPlanes steps.

![](/cms/10.1177/02783649261436917/asset/472173fd-534b-452c-829c-1fd7caa000b0/assets/images/large/10.1177_02783649261436917-fig6.jpg)

Figure 6. The systems we use to benchmark our algorithms, along with the number of degrees of freedom, number of collision pairs, and the ratio of the volume of the free configuration space relative to the entire configuration space . The ratio  is estimated with 107 samples uniformly drawn from .

We compare the approaches for two different settings: a “fast” setting, where we request the region to be 90% collision-free, with 90% confidence, and a “precise” setting, where we request the region to be 99% collision-free with 95% confidence. IRIS-NP cannot take these arguments directly, so we hand-tune the required number of consecutive infeasible solves to roughly match the average collision fractions achieved by our algorithms. For IRIS-NP2, we tuned the algorithm hyperparameters of [Table 1](#table1-02783649261436917) on a per-experiment basis.

To mitigate the effects of randomness of the algorithms in our comparisons, we construct regions around each seed point 10 times. This yields 100 trials per robot environment, or 800 total, for each algorithm. For the parallelized components of the algorithms, an Intel Core i9-10850K (10 cores, 20 threads) is used. All convex programs are solved using MOSEK ([MOSEK ApS, 2025](#bibr31-02783649261436917)) and the nonlinear programs are solved using SNOPT ([Gill et al., 2005](#bibr12-02783649261436917)). The volume of the maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid is used as a proxy for polytope volume, as actual volume is intractable to compute in higher dimensions. We report these volumes normalized by the averaged IRIS-NP results.

Compared to the conference version of this paper ([Werner et al., 2024b](#bibr44-02783649261436917)), we have rerun these benchmarks using the publicly available implementations of IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2 in Drake ([Tedrake and the Drake Development Team, 2019](#bibr40-02783649261436917)).

For each algorithm and robotic system, we include the runtime, number of hyperplanes, volume, and proportion of the region in collision, averaged over all trials on all seed points in [Table 2](#table2-02783649261436917). Region volume and number of hyperplanes are both dependent on the seed configuration—if the robot is in a narrow passage in , the region may be small, and if it is near non-convex obstacles, many hyperplanes may be required. In [Figure 7](#fig7-02783649261436917), we visualize the runtime and hyperplane data across the 10 trials for the 8 corresponding seed configurations shown in [Figure 6](#fig6-02783649261436917). Our algorithms show significant improvements relative to IRIS-NP in runtime and number of hyperplanes. In particular, IRIS-ZO gains approximately an order-of-magnitude time advantage with a comparable number of hyperplanes. While IRIS-NP2 is slower than IRIS-ZO, it generally remains faster than IRIS-NP and uses significantly fewer hyperplanes.

args.summary: This paper proposes two novel algorithms (IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2) for constructing convex, probabilistically collision-free polytopes in robot configuration space, building upon the IRIS-NP algorithm. The key insight is that sampling to find nearby configuration-space obstacles is inexpensive and greatly accelerates region generation. IRIS-ZO uses a parallelized zero-order optimization strategy requiring no gradient computations, achieving roughly an order-of-magnitude speed advantage over IRIS-NP (extendable by another order of magnitude via GPU parallelization). IRIS-NP2 uses sampled collisions to seed nonlinear optimizations, building larger polytopes with fewer hyperplanes, which accelerates downstream motion planning. Both algorithms introduce a novel termination condition based on a Chernoff bound that allows users to specify an admissible fraction-in-collision (ε) and confidence (δ), eliminating a major tuning difficulty in IRIS-NP. The methods are also extended to work in parametrized configuration spaces (e.g., for constrained bimanual manipulation). Experiments across eight robot environments show: for "Fast" settings, IRIS-ZO was 11.9x faster than IRIS-NP with 1.4x fewer hyperplanes; IRIS-NP2 (greedy) was 6.55x faster with 2.1x fewer hyperplanes. For "Precise" settings, IRIS-ZO was 13.4x faster; IRIS-NP2 (greedy) was 33.9x faster with 2.4x fewer hyperplanes. An open-source implementation is available in the Drake framework.

# Growing Convex Collision-Free Regions in Configuration Space using Nonlinear Programming

![](https://static.alphaxiv.org/images/organizations/harvard.png)
![](https://static.alphaxiv.org/images/organizations/mit.jpg)
![Russ Tedrake](https://proxy.assets.alphaxiv.org/aHR0cHM6Ly9zY2hvbGFyLmdvb2dsZXVzZXJjb250ZW50LmNvbS9jaXRhdGlvbnM_dmlld19vcD12aWV3X3Bob3RvJnVzZXI9bnhOa0VpWUFBQUFKJmNpdHBpZD0y)

## Abstract

One of the most difficult parts of motion planning in configuration space is
ensuring a trajectory does not collide with task-space obstacles in the
environment. Generating regions that are convex and collision free in
configuration space can separate the computational burden of collision checking
from motion planning. To that end, we propose an extension to IRIS (Iterative
Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) [5] that allows it to operate
in configuration space. Our algorithm, IRIS-NP (Iterative Regional Inflation by
Semidefinite & Nonlinear Programming), uses nonlinear optimization to add the
separating hyperplanes, enabling support for more general nonlinear
constraints. Developed in parallel to Amice et al. [1], IRIS-NP trades rigorous
certification that regions are collision free for probabilistic certification
and the benefit of faster region generation in the configuration-space
coordinates. IRIS-NP also provides a solid initialization to C-IRIS to reduce
the number of iterations required for certification. We demonstrate that
IRIS-NP can scale to a dual-arm manipulator and can handle additional nonlinear
constraints using the same machinery. Finally, we show ablations of elements of
our implementation to demonstrate their importance.

Save

## AI Overview

## Introduction

Robot motion planning in complex environments remains a fundamental challenge in robotics. For robots to navigate safely, they must avoid collisions with obstacles while efficiently reaching their goals. This is particularly challenging for robots with many degrees of freedom (DoF) operating in cluttered environments.

![Robot reaching into shelf with collision-free motion](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-0.jpeg "Robot reaching into shelf with collision-free motion")
*Figure 1: A robot arm reaching into a shelf with convex, collision-free regions visualized. The transparent orange shapes represent safe regions in which the robot can move without collision.*

![Robot reaching into shelf with collision-free motion](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-0.jpeg "Robot reaching into shelf with collision-free motion")

The paper "Growing Convex Collision-Free Regions in Configuration Space using Nonlinear Programming" by Mark Petersen (Harvard University) and Russ Tedrake (MIT) presents IRIS-NP, a novel algorithm that efficiently generates convex, collision-free regions in a robot's configuration space (C-space). These regions serve as "safe zones" for motion planning, allowing robots to move confidently without the computational expense of continuous collision checking.

IRIS-NP extends the original IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) algorithm to handle the complex, nonlinear mappings between a robot's configuration space and the physical workspace. It achieves this through nonlinear programming techniques, offering a scalable approach for high-dimensional robotic systems.

## Background and Challenges

Motion planning algorithms must work within the robot's configuration space (C-space), where each point represents a complete specification of the robot's position. While obstacles may be simple (convex) in the physical world, they become complex (non-convex) when mapped to C-space through the robot's forward kinematics.

![C-space to task space mapping](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-1.jpeg "C-space to task space mapping")
*Figure 2: Illustration of the mapping between configuration space (Q) and task space (X) via forward kinematics (FK). The ellipse ε in C-space maps to complex shapes in task space, while obstacles (red) in task space create complex non-convex regions in C-space.*

![C-space to task space mapping](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-1.jpeg "C-space to task space mapping")

This presents two major challenges:

Explicitly computing obstacle representations in C-space is computationally expensive or sometimes intractable, especially for robots with many degrees of freedom.

The non-convexity of these obstacles makes optimization-based planning difficult, as most efficient optimization methods require convex constraints.

Prior approaches to this problem include:

IRIS-NP addresses these limitations by avoiding explicit C-space obstacle mapping while still providing practical collision-free regions with probabilistic guarantees.

## IRIS-NP Algorithm

The IRIS-NP algorithm generates convex, collision-free regions in C-space through an iterative process that alternates between two steps:

The algorithm starts with an initial seed configuration (known to be collision-free) and an initial polytope defined by the robot's joint limits. It then iteratively refines this polytope by:

![Hyperplane addition for collision avoidance](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-2.jpeg "Hyperplane addition for collision avoidance")
*Figure 3: Addition of hyperplanes to separate collision-free regions. The red area represents obstacles, the blue line represents a separating hyperplane, and δ represents a safety margin. The green star indicates the seed point.*

![Hyperplane addition for collision avoidance](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-2.jpeg "Hyperplane addition for collision avoidance")

The counterexample search is formulated as a nonlinear optimization problem:

`minimize ||q - c||²
subject to q ∈ P (current polytope constraints)
p₁ ∈ B₁ (point in body 1)
p₂ ∈ B₂ (point in body 2)
FK₁(q, p₁) = FK₂(q, p₂) (collision constraint)`

where:

The algorithm computes the largest inscribed ellipsoid within the updated polytope to serve as a metric for the next iteration, aiming to maximize the volume of the collision-free region.

## Probabilistic Certification

IRIS-NP trades rigorous guarantees for computational efficiency by using a probabilistic approach to certify collision-free regions. The key insight is that while the algorithm cannot guarantee that the entire region is collision-free (due to the non-convexity of obstacles in C-space), it can reduce the probability of missing collisions through repeated counterexample searches.

![Probabilistic certification effectiveness](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-3.jpeg "Probabilistic certification effectiveness")
*Figure 4: Effect of increasing the number of consecutive infeasible counterexample searches on the percentage of the region volume that is in collision. More infeasible samples lead to higher confidence in collision-free certification.*

![Probabilistic certification effectiveness](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-3.jpeg "Probabilistic certification effectiveness")

The approach uses a Markov chain Monte Carlo strategy to sample different initial guesses for the counterexample search. The search terminates when a specified number of consecutive optimization attempts fail to find a collision. As shown in Figure 4, increasing this threshold significantly reduces the percentage of the region that might still be in collision.

This probabilistic certification makes IRIS-NP practical for real-world applications, offering a favorable trade-off between computational speed and safety guarantees.

## Implementation Details

Several implementation details significantly impact the performance of IRIS-NP:

**Collision pair ordering**: Ordering collision pairs by their task-space distance improves both speed and quality of the resulting polytopes. Prioritizing potentially colliding bodies that are close in task space helps identify relevant constraints earlier.

**Configuration-space margin**: Adding a margin to the separating hyperplanes accounts for the non-convexity of obstacles in C-space and increases the safety of the resulting regions.

**Optimization formulation**: The counterexample search is formulated as a distance minimization problem to improve numerical stability and convergence.

**Ellipsoid calculation**: The largest inscribed ellipsoid is computed efficiently using semidefinite programming, providing a good metric for region growth and guiding counterexample searches.

The algorithm is implemented using standard nonlinear programming solvers like SNOPT or IPOPT, making it accessible to robotics researchers with standard optimization tools.

## Experimental Results

IRIS-NP was evaluated on several challenging scenarios, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability:

**Single-arm manipulation**: The algorithm successfully generated collision-free regions for a 7-DoF robot arm reaching into a shelf (Figure 1).

**Narrow passage navigation**: IRIS-NP created useful regions even in challenging environments with narrow passages, as shown with a robot arm navigating between vertical obstacles.

![Robot navigating through narrow passages](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-4.jpeg "Robot navigating through narrow passages")
*Figure 5: Robot arm navigating through narrow passages with collision-free regions generated by IRIS-NP. The regions adapt to the complex environment.*

![Robot navigating through narrow passages](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-4.jpeg "Robot navigating through narrow passages")

![Dual-arm manipulation setup](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-5.jpeg "Dual-arm manipulation setup")
*Figure 6: Dual-arm robot setup (14 DoF) where IRIS-NP successfully generated collision-free regions.*

![Dual-arm manipulation setup](https://paper-assets.alphaxiv.org/figures/2303.14737/img-5.jpeg "Dual-arm manipulation setup")

The experimental results showed that IRIS-NP can generate reasonably sized collision-free regions in about one minute, making it practical for offline planning and potentially suitable for online replanning in some applications.

## Comparison with Other Approaches

IRIS-NP offers several advantages over existing approaches:

**Compared to mesh-based methods**: IRIS-NP avoids the need for explicit C-space obstacle representation, which is often intractable for high-DoF robots.

**Compared to original IRIS**: The new algorithm handles nonlinear kinematics mappings, enabling it to work directly with task-space obstacle definitions.

**Compared to C-IRIS**: While C-IRIS provides rigorous guarantees through sum-of-squares programming, IRIS-NP trades these guarantees for faster computation times and the ability to handle more general nonlinear constraints.

**Compared to sampling-based planners**: The convex regions generated by IRIS-NP can improve the performance of sampling-based planners by reducing the need for frequent collision checks.

IRIS-NP can also serve as an initialization method for C-IRIS, potentially accelerating the certificate computation process while maintaining rigorous guarantees.

## Applications and Significance

The convex, collision-free regions generated by IRIS-NP have several important applications in robotics:

**Motion planning**: These regions can be used directly in optimization-based motion planners, enabling fast trajectory generation within safe zones.

**Collision avoidance**: The regions provide a compact representation of safe configurations, reducing the need for expensive online collision checking.

**Handling nonlinear constraints**: IRIS-NP can incorporate additional nonlinear constraints on the robot's configuration, such as orientation constraints, making it applicable to a wider range of robotic tasks.

**High-dimensional systems**: The algorithm's scalability to high-DoF systems makes it suitable for complex manipulation tasks involving multi-arm systems or humanoid robots.

**Real-time applications**: The relatively fast region generation times make IRIS-NP potentially suitable for real-time applications where the environment changes moderately.

## Limitations and Future Work

Despite its advantages, IRIS-NP has several limitations that suggest directions for future work:

**Probabilistic guarantees**: Unlike methods with rigorous certificates, IRIS-NP provides only probabilistic guarantees of collision avoidance. While practical, this may not be sufficient for safety-critical applications.

**Optimization challenges**: The nonlinear optimization at the core of the algorithm can sometimes struggle with convergence or get stuck in local minima, particularly in complex environments.

**Computational complexity**: While faster than methods with rigorous guarantees, IRIS-NP still requires significant computation time for complex scenarios, limiting its use in highly dynamic environments.

Future work could address these limitations by:

## Conclusion

IRIS-NP represents a significant contribution to robot motion planning by providing an efficient and scalable algorithm for generating convex, collision-free regions in configuration space. By using nonlinear programming techniques and probabilistic certification, it offers a practical solution to the challenge of planning safe motions in complex environments.

The algorithm's ability to handle high-dimensional configuration spaces and additional nonlinear constraints makes it applicable to a wide range of robotic tasks. While it trades rigorous guarantees for computational efficiency, the probabilistic nature of its certification provides a reasonable assurance of safety for many practical applications.

As robots continue to work in increasingly complex and unstructured environments, approaches like IRIS-NP that efficiently identify safe regions will play a crucial role in enabling robust and reliable robot motion planning.

<webpage_content>
### Search This Blog

# [Tommy's Research Blog](https://blog.tommycohn.com/)

Ideas, paper summaries, and general ruminations on robotics research

### IRIS on a Torus: Growing Convex Sets on Manifolds

* Get link
* Facebook
* X
* Pinterest
* Email
* Other Apps

My current research focus at MIT is motion planning along manifolds, which we're primarily exploring through the lens of the *graph of convex sets* framework, abbreviated as GCS. (Refer to a [previous blog post](https://blog.tommycohn.com/2022/09/reimplementing-gcs-shortest-paths-in.html) for more details, or check out the papers of Marcucci et. al. [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.11565) and [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04422).) Convexity is a property that is examined through the lens of Euclidean geometry, but it is possible to consider it in the broader context of smooth manifolds. This is reliant on the idea of a geodesic: a shortest path on a manifold.

Replacing Euclidean spaces with manifolds and lines with geodesics allows us to consider a graph of *geodesically* convex sets (GGCS). We've begun laying the groundwork for planning over manifolds with such a tool, and you can read about it in our paper *Non-Euclidean Motion Planning with Graphs of Geodesically-Convex Sets*, to appear at RSS 2023. (You can read the [preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.06341) today on arXiv!)

While GGCS assumes the geodesically convex sets are given, computing such sets is an important part of the framework. GCS is best friends with the IRIS algorithm, which can produce collision-free convex sets. (I discussed IRIS in [another previous blog post](https://blog.tommycohn.com/2022/09/reimplementing-iris-computing-large.html), and you can read the original paper [here](https://groups.csail.mit.edu/robotics-center/public_papers/Deits14.pdf).) It turns out that just as convexity can be easily generalized to manifolds, so too can IRIS. In particular, we use [IRIS-NP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.14737), which can handle the nontrivial kinematic mappings between configuration space (where we plan) and task space (where the obstacles live).

Before I can describe how we modified IRIS-NP to work on manifolds, I'll provide some brief theoretical background. A manifold is a locally Euclidean space, generalizing the idea of smooth curves and surfaces to arbitrary dimensions. A *Riemannian metric* is an additional piece of structure we can put on a manifold that, among other myriad things, allows us to measure the length of a path. A curve is called a *geodesic* if any small enough segment of it is length minimizing. For example, geodesics in Euclidean space are lines, and geodesics on the sphere are great circles.  

Geodesics allow us to generalize convexity to manifolds. A set S is *geodesically convex* (henceforth abbreviated g-convex) if for every pair of points x and y in S, there is a unique length-minimizing geodesic connecting them, and it is entirely contained in S. This definition is somewhat more verbose than the definition of ordinary convexity, due to the non-uniqueness of geodesics. For example, for any two points on the sphere, the great circle connecting them describes two possible geodesics. And there are infinitely many shortest paths between the north and south pole of a sphere.

With the preliminaries out of the way, we can now discuss the modifications to IRIS-NP. Given a seed point on the manifold, we consider a maximal coordinate chart containing it. (In particular, we consider the [Riemannian normal coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_coordinates), up to the [cut locus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cut_locus).) We then try to grow the region under the image of this chart, in effect, growing the polytope in a full dimensional space. The inverse of the chart mapping is simply precomposed with the forward kinematics function when checking collisions. In other words, to check if a point in the image of the chart is collision free, we lift it to the manifold, and then apply forward kinematics.

Because IRIS-NP is leveraging nonlinear programming, this doesn't lead to many programmatic changes. However, there is a more subtle problem: the minimizing geodesic can go "the wrong way around" the manifold. This means that sets which look convex in the coordinate chart may not be g-convex when lifted to the manifold! In the case of the sphere, the northern hemisphere (up to, but not including the equator) is g-convex. But if the set is extended to include any of the southern hemisphere, then g-convexity is lost, even though the set still looks convex in the chart's coordinate system.

For any point on a Riemannian manifold, there is a strictly positive "radius of convexity" about that point. For any ball with radius less than this quantity, the ball is g-convex. If the manifold is compact, we can consider the minimum convexity radius -- so any ball on the manifold with radius smaller than that quantity will be g-convex. This enables us to grow g-convex sets on a chart, while capping its size in such a way as to guarantee the minimizing geodesics can't go the wrong way around. (The details for why this is true can be found in our paper.)

As an illustrative example, consider the torus manifold. (The torus may seem like a contrived example, but it's actually precisely the configuration space of a robot with two continuous revolute joints.) Instead of the classic "donut" picture, we can realize it as a square, with the opposite edges identified:

args.summary: This blog post by Tommy Cohn (MIT) describes extending the IRIS algorithm to work on Riemannian manifolds, enabling the growth of geodesically convex (g-convex) collision-free sets. The work builds on the Graph of Geodesically Convex Sets (GGCS) framework, which generalizes the Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) motion planning approach to non-Euclidean spaces, and uses IRIS-NP to handle nontrivial kinematic mappings. The post explains key theoretical background: manifolds are locally Euclidean spaces, Riemannian metrics allow measuring path lengths, and geodesics (e.g., lines in Euclidean space, great circles on a sphere) generalize lines to manifolds. A set is g-convex if every pair of points is connected by a unique minimizing geodesic contained entirely within the set. The modified IRIS-NP algorithm grows regions in a maximal coordinate chart (Riemannian normal coordinates up to the cut locus) around a seed point. To guarantee g-convexity, growth is capped by the radius of convexity, preventing geodesics from going 'the wrong way around' the manifold. An example on the torus (which models a robot with two revolute joints) is provided, with code available on GitHub. The paper *Non-Euclidean Motion Planning with Graphs of Geodesically-Convex Sets* is to appear at RSS 2023.
