# Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs

###### Abstract

Many computations in robotics can be dramatically accelerated if the robot configuration space is described as a collection of simple sets. For example, recently developed motion planners rely on a convex decomposition of the free space to design collision-free trajectories using fast convex optimization.
In this work, we present an efficient method for approximately covering complex configuration spaces with a small number of polytopes.
The approach constructs a visibility graph using sampling and generates a clique cover of this graph to find clusters of samples that have mutual line of sight.
These clusters are then inflated into large, full-dimensional, polytopes. We evaluate our method on a variety of robotic systems and show that it consistently covers larger portions of free configuration space, with fewer polytopes, and in a fraction of the time compared to previous methods.

## I Introduction

Approximating complex sets as a union of simpler sets is a common pre-processing method for accelerating downstream computations.
Familiar examples include clustering methods for high-dimensional data in machine learning [[1](#bib.bib1), §2.5.2], approximating complex shapes via triangular meshes to facilitate graphics rendering [[2](#bib.bib2)], and describing geometries as unions of convex sets for efficient collision checking [[3](#bib.bib3)].
Similarly, recently developed methods for robot motion planning rely on (conservative) decompositions of the environment into convex sets to design smooth trajectories around obstacles using efficient convex optimization [[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8)].
These motion planners have demonstrated great potential, and performance frequently superior to widely used sampling-based methods [[5](#bib.bib5)].
However, the required decomposition of the environment is a daunting task, often demanding a substantial degree of human supervision. This is largely due to the fact that the collision-free subset of a robot’s configuration space (𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}) is intractable to describe analytically [[9](#bib.bib9), §3], even if the robot’s task space is relatively simple (e.g. see Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs")).

In [[10](#bib.bib10)], the authors proposed an algorithm called IRIS to quickly compute large convex subsets of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.
This method takes as input a “seed” configuration and inflates a large polytopic region around this seed point using convex optimization. While originally limited to the case of convex obstacles, the IRIS algorithm has been recently extended to handle nonconvex obstacles and the complicated configuration spaces of multi-link robot manipulators [[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)].
The polytopes generated with these algorithms have been used with great success for motion planning in high dimensions [[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)].
Nevertheless, seeding collections of these regions so that they cover diverse areas of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} remains a challenge: manual seeding is tedious, and naively growing regions around randomly chosen configurations leads to very inefficient decompositions.

![Refer to caption](2310.02875v2/title_3dof_decomp_v3.png)

In this paper, we propose an efficient method for the approximate decomposition of robot configuration spaces into few large convex sets, without any human supervision. A guiding illustration is shown in Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs").

Similar to some motion-planning algorithms [[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)], our method constructs a visibility graph by sampling points in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.
The vertices of this graph are collision-free samples, and the edges connect pairs of points with mutual line of sight.
The visibility graph contains rich information about the geometry of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.
In particular, our key observation is that, as the number of samples grows, fully connected subgraphs of this visibility graph (so-called “cliques”) tend to represent better and better approximations of collision-free convex sets in the underlying configuration space.
Our approach is to decompose the visibility graph into a small collection of large cliques.
We then circumscribe the points in each clique with an ellipsoid by solving a convex-optimization problem.
The center and the principal directions of these ellipsoids are subsequently used to initialize an inflation algorithm analogous to IRIS.

Through a large variety of experiments, we show that our algorithm outperforms previous approaches for seeding and inflating convex regions; both in terms of runtimes and number of regions used to cover the space.
As an example, for a robot arm with seven degrees of freedom, and many task-space obstacles, our method requires approximately 4646 regions and one hour of computations to cover 70%70\% of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}, whereas the approach outlined in [[12](#bib.bib12)] requires ten times more regions and is ten times slower.

## II Related Works

Finding the minimum convex cover of a set is a hard problem; even in the case of two-dimensional polygons, the problem is hard to solve exactly and approximately.11
1
More formally, the problem is ∃ℝ\exists\mathbb{R}-complete [[16](#bib.bib16)], and therefore NP-hard, as well as APX-hard [[17](#bib.bib17)].
Nonetheless, finding low-cardinality convex covers of high-dimensional nonconvex spaces (both polygonal and non-polygonal) remains a problem of practical importance, for which a variety of approximate algorithms have been devised.
In the following, we group these algorithms into two categories: ones that require explicit (e.g., analytic) descriptions of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}, and ones that only use implicit descriptions of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} (and are hence suitable for most complex configuration spaces). In this literature review, we particularly focus on IRIS algorithms, due to their efficient scaling to high dimensions.

### II-A Algorithms Requiring Explicit Obstacle Descriptions

The recent work [[18](#bib.bib18)] constructs low-cardinality convex covers of two-dimensional polygons by first decomposing them into small convex pieces (for example triangles), and then by joining the pieces based on a small clique cover of an approximated set-to-set visibility graph. Similarly, the visibility graph of polygons is directly used to construct convex covers in [[19](#bib.bib19)].
In three dimensions the approach in [[20](#bib.bib20)] can be used to decompose 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} into sets that are approximately convex, provided that a triangle mesh description is available.
Finally, if the configuration-space obstacles are explicitly described as convex sets, the original IRIS algorithm from [[10](#bib.bib10)] can be used to inflate a large polytope in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} around a specified seed point in arbitrary dimensions.

### II-B Algorithms Allowing Implicit Obstacle Descriptions

Most commonly, the explicit descriptions of the obstacles are only available in task space; while the collision-free configuration space 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} is defined implicitly through the robot’s inverse kinematics, and is intractable to describe analytically [[9](#bib.bib9), §3].
Some works have focused on approximately describing the configuration space obstacles, rather than 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} [[21](#bib.bib21), [22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23)].
Conversely, multiple works have studied directly obtaining convex decompositions of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.
In [[24](#bib.bib24)] visibility graphs and kernels are used to compute convex decompositions of three-dimensional spaces via sample-based collision checking.
However, their method represents the convex sets through their vertices, and is inefficient in higher dimensions.
In the family of IRIS algorithms, two methods can deal with implicit descriptions of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}: IRIS-NP [[12](#bib.bib12)] and C-IRIS [[11](#bib.bib11), [13](#bib.bib13)].
The former extends the original IRIS method [[10](#bib.bib10)] to arbitrary configuration spaces using nonlinear programming and inflates polytopes that are collision-free with high probability.
The latter grows polytopes that are rigorously *certified* to be collision-free using a rational reparametrization of the configuration space and sums-of-squares programming.

## III Convex Covers, Visibility, and Cliques

In this section, we formally define our main problem: approximating the free configuration space 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} with a low-cardinality collection of convex sets. We also briefly review the main technical tools that we will use in the development of our algorithm, namely, visibility graphs and clique covers.

### III-A Problem Statement

Let 𝒞free⊆ℝn\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be the collision-free subset of an nn-dimensional configuration space, which we assume to have a well-defined finite volume.
Let also α\alpha be a constant in the interval (0,1](0,1].

###### Definition 1

An *α\alpha-approximate convex cover* of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} is a collection of potentially overlapping convex sets ℛ1,…,ℛN⊆𝒞free\mathcal{R}\_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{R}\_{N}\subseteq\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} whose union covers at least an α\alpha-fraction of the volume of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}:

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | 𝐯𝐨𝐥(⋃i=1Nℛi)≥α​𝐯𝐨𝐥(𝒞free).\mathop{\bf vol}\left(\bigcup\_{i=1}^{N}\mathcal{R}\_{i}\right)\geq\alpha\mathop{\bf vol}\left(\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}\right). |  |

Our problem is to find an α\alpha-approximate convex cover of minimum cardinality NN.

In practice, we are interested in solving this problem for values of α\alpha that are sufficiently high to accomplish a task of interest, such as collision-free motion planning, but not so large that the cardinality NN grows unreasonably. Indeed, when α=1\alpha=1, Min α\alpha-ApproxConvexCover might not even have a finite solution.22
2
For α<1\alpha<1 a finite solution is guaranteed to exist. This can be seen by computing the volume of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} with a lower Darboux integral over finite hyperrectangle partitions.

### III-B Visibility Graphs and Clique Covers

Our algorithm is based on the idea that clusters of points that see each other can approximate convex subsets of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}. Here, we formally define the notion of visibility as well as introduce some formal tools from graph theory to guide the development of our algorithm.

We begin by defining visibility in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.

###### Definition 2

Two points q,q′∈𝒞freeq,q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} are said to *see each other* if the entire line connecting them is collision-free: t​q+(1−t)​q′∈𝒞freetq+(1-t)q^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} for all t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1].
Notice that this definition is symmetric in qq and q′q^{\prime}.

We are now ready to define the visibility graph of a set of collision-free configurations.

###### Definition 3

The *visibility graph* of a set of points q1,…,qK∈𝒞freeq\_{1},\dots,q\_{K}\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} is an undirected graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) with vertices 𝒱={1,…,K}\mathcal{V}=\{1,\ldots,K\}, and with an edge {i,j}∈ℰ\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E} for every pair of distinct points qiq\_{i} and qjq\_{j} that see each other.

We show an example of a visibility graph in Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs"). We note that clusters of points that can all see each other form a clique in the visibility graph.

###### Definition 4

Let 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) be an undirected graph. A *clique* 𝒦\mathcal{K} is a subset of 𝒱\mathcal{V} where every pair of vertices is connected by an edge.

Note that if a cluster of configurations can be placed in the same convex set, then these configurations must form a clique in the visibility graph. The second panel in Figure [2](#S1.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ I Introduction ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs") highlights a collection of five cliques in the visibility graph that have this property. These five cliques form what is called a clique cover; which resembles a discrete analog of a convex cover.

###### Definition 5

A collection 𝒯\mathcal{T} of cliques 𝒦1,…,𝒦N\mathcal{K}\_{1},\dots,\mathcal{K}\_{N} is a *clique cover* of a graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} if every vertex in the graph is contained in at least one clique.

A natural discrete counterpart of the minimum convex cover is the MinCliqueCover problem, where we look for the minimum number of cliques NN required to cover a graph. Our observation is that, as the number of samples in the visibility graph increases, a minimum clique cover typically does an increasingly better job of approximating a minimum convex cover.
Limitations of this analogy are discussed in §[VI](#S6 "VI Limitations of Approximating Convex Sets with Cliques ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs").

MinCliqueCover is NP-complete [[25](#bib.bib25)].
There exist heuristics, such as [[26](#bib.bib26)], that attempt to solve MinCliqueCover directly.
Alternatively, one can greedily construct a clique cover by repeatedly eliminating the largest clique. The problem of finding the largest clique in a graph is called MaxClique. Even though this problem is also NP-complete [[25](#bib.bib25)], it is often substantially faster to solve in practice.
We found the latter approach with exact solutions of MaxClique to perform particularly well on our problem instances.

## IV Algorithm

We now present our Visibility Clique Cover (VCC) algorithm, which consists of four main steps.
First, we randomly sample a collection of points in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} and construct their visibility graph.
Second, we compute an approximate clique cover of the graph.
Third, we summarize the geometric information of each clique using an ellipsoid.
Fourth, we use these ellipsoids to initialize a polytope-inflation algorithm analogous to IRIS.
This process is repeated until the generated set of polytopes ℛ\mathcal{R} covers a given fraction α\alpha of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.
This procedure is summarized in Algorithm [1](#alg1 "In IV Algorithm ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs"), and the remainder of this section details the individual steps.

### IV-A Sampling the Visibility Graph

At the beginning of every iteration of VCC, the subroutine SampleVisibilityGraph
samples KK configurations uniformly at random from the portion of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} that is not already covered by the polytopes in ℛ\mathcal{R}.
Then, it constructs the visibility graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}), by checking for collisions along the line segments connecting each pair of sampled configurations.
Currently, this is performed using sampling-based collision checkers.
Exact visibility checking is possible using methods such as [[27](#bib.bib27)], [[28](#bib.bib28), §5.3.4], or [[29](#bib.bib29)].

### IV-B Truncated Clique Cover

In the subroutine TruncatedCliqueCover we approximately cover the visibility graph with a collection of cliques, each of which contain at least smins\_{\min} vertices.
We construct this approximate cover 𝒯\mathcal{T} greedily, by solving a sequence of MaxClique problems.
Each instance of MaxClique is formulated as an integer linear program

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | | | | | | |
|  | maximize\displaystyle\mathop{\text{maximize}}\quad | ∑i=1Kbi\displaystyle\sum\_{i=1}^{K}b\_{i} |  | | | (1a) |
|  | subject to\displaystyle\mathop{\text{subject to}}\quad | bi+bj≤1,\displaystyle b\_{i}+b\_{j}\leq 1, |  | ∀{i,j}∈¯​ℰ,\displaystyle\forall\{i,j\}\in\bar{}\mathcal{E}, |  | (1b) |
|  |  | bi∈{0,1},\displaystyle b\_{i}\in\{0,1\}, |  | ∀i=1,…,K.\displaystyle\forall i=1,\ldots,K. |  | (1c) |

A binary decision variable bib\_{i} is added for each vertex. The role of this variable is to take unit value if and only if vertex ii is included in the clique.
The set ¯​ℰ\bar{}\mathcal{E} contains all the pairs of vertices {i,j}\{i,j\} such that i≠ji\neq j and {i,j}∉ℰ\{i,j\}\notin\mathcal{E}.
Therefore the first constraint ensures that two vertices are selected only if they share an edge.

After solving the integer program ([1](#S4.E1 "In IV-B Truncated Clique Cover ‣ IV Algorithm ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs")), the clique found is removed from the graph and added to the clique cover.
Since small cliques are not informative, we stop this iterative process when the largest clique left in the graph is smaller than a given threshold
smins\_{\min}.
For this reason, our clique covers will be truncated, i.e., generally, not all vertices will be contained in one of the cliques.

### IV-C Summarizing Cliques with Ellipsoids

In the subroutine MinVolumeEllipsoids, we solve a semidefinite program to enclose each clique with an ellipsoid of minimum volume [[30](#bib.bib30), §8.4.1].
This collection ℬ\mathcal{B} of ellipsoids allows us to summarize the geometry of each clique with a point and a set of principal directions, which are then used to initialize the region-inflation algorithm.
For the upcoming computations, it is necessary that the center of each ellipsoid is not in collision; if this is not the case, we recenter the ellipsoid around the vertex in the clique that is closest to its center.

### IV-D Inflating Polytopes

![Refer to caption](2310.02875v2/figures/side.png)
![Refer to caption](2310.02875v2/figures/vert.png)

In the last step of VCC, the subroutine InflatePolytopes inflates a large, collision-free polytope around the center of each ellipsoid induced by a clique.

Let us initially assume that the obstacles are convex.
Consider a single ellipsoid;
using convex optimization, we compute the point in each obstacle that is closest to the center of the ellipsoid, according to the distance metric induced by the ellipsoid.
These points anchor separating hyperplanes between the ellipsoid center and the obstacles, which form a polytope of obstacle-free space. These steps are repeated for each ellipsoid (i.e., for each clique) to obtain a collection of collision-free polytopes that we add to the set ℛ\mathcal{R}.

These computations correspond to a single iteration of the IRIS algorithm [[10](#bib.bib10)], and ensure that the largest uniformly-scaled, collision-free version of the ellipsoid is contained in the resulting polytope. Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV-D Inflating Polytopes ‣ IV Algorithm ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs") illustrates how the initial metric is fundamental in guiding the shape of the regions generated by IRIS.
Traditionally, the IRIS algorithm was initialized with an uninformed ellipsoidal metric and needed to run for multiple (expensive) iterations in order to expand and cover a larger volume of space; in VCC we require only a single IRIS iteration.

When the obstacles are not convex, we run one iteration of the nonlinear programming variant IRIS-NP [[12](#bib.bib12)] instead.
Alternatively, C-IRIS [[11](#bib.bib11), [13](#bib.bib13)] could be employed to obtain certifiably collision-free regions.

### IV-E Convergence Check

The subroutine CheckCoverage estimates the fraction of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} covered by the regions in ℛ\mathcal{R}, and terminates our algorithm if this value exceeds the threshold α\alpha.
Computing this fraction exactly is impractical, and so we resort to randomized methods.
The coverage is estimated by drawing a large number of MM samples in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}, and computing the ratio of samples that land in at least one of the regions in ℛ\mathcal{R}.
More sophisticated checks, such as one-sided Bernoulli hypothesis testing, are possible.

### IV-F Completeness

Analogous to [[31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32)], VCC is probabilistically complete under mild assumptions. This means as the number of iterations goes to infinity, the probability of completely covering 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} goes to one.

## V Experiments

As there are no direct baseline methods, we compare our VCC algorithm against an extension of the method in [[12](#bib.bib12), §III.D]. The natural extension of this approach is to iteratively grow polytopes around uniformly sampled points from the uncovered free space using IRIS, while treating previously computed regions as obstacles. This process is repeated until the desired coverage is met. We call this approach Iterative Obstacle Seeding (IOS).

In the following, all experiments are implemented in [Drake](https://drake.mit.edu/) [[33](#bib.bib33)], and all computations are performed on a single desktop computer with an Intel Core i9-10850K CPU and 32 Gb of RAM. We solve all MaxClique instances to global optimality using Gurobi [[34](#bib.bib34)].

We evaluate VCC and IOS on four environments: Village, 3DOF Flipper, 5DOF UR3, and 7DOF IIWA.
The dimension nn of these environments ranges from 33 to 77.
For each environment, we run the two algorithms ten times and report their performance in Table [I](#S4.T1 "TABLE I ‣ IV-D Inflating Polytopes ‣ IV Algorithm ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs").
The Village environment from [[8](#bib.bib8)] contains only convex obstacles and is compatible with the original IRIS [[10](#bib.bib10)]. All other examples involve the configuration spaces of robotic manipulators and therefore IRIS-NP [[12](#bib.bib12)] is employed.
The number of samples used in the convergence check in Algorithm [1](#alg1 "In IV Algorithm ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs") is M=5000M=5000.

VCC meets the required coverage threshold with significantly fewer regions and in a substantially shorter amount of time. Notably, in the most challenging benchmark, 7DOF IIWA, VCC requires 10 times fewer regions and meets the required coverage of 70%70\% around 16 times faster.
This substantial speedup can be attributed to two key factors.
First, the region inflation in VCC is parallelized.
Second, IRIS is the most computationally expensive step. While VCC only requires a single iteration of IRIS per region, IOS can requires around five IRIS iterations per region, due to the initialization with a potentially uninformative spherical metric.

## VI Limitations of Approximating Convex Sets with Cliques

Despite the strong performance of our algorithm, the hardness of solving Min α\alpha-ApproxConvexCover makes it possible to construct simple examples that highlight pitfalls of our heuristic approach.
In this section, we discuss holes in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} which leads to one such pitfall that is particularly insightful.

While every convex set in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} naturally corresponds to a clique in the visibility graph, a clique in the visibility graph does not necessarily correspond to a convex set in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}. The convex hull of a clique can enclose holes.
This problem persists even if we sample arbitrarily dense visibility graphs, and if we restrict the analysis to maximum cliques.
A visual proof is shown in Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ VI Limitations of Approximating Convex Sets with Cliques ‣ Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs"), which illustrates a triangular configuration space with a triangular hole of size ε\varepsilon.
As ε\varepsilon goes to zero, the largest convex subset of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} is the green trapezoid, whose area approaches 5/95/9 of the total area of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}.
On the other hand, a larger subset of mutually visible points is given by the union of the three red parallelograms, whose area approaches 6/96/9 of the total area.
Therefore, if configurations are sampled uniformly at random, an optimum solution of MaxClique will almost surely enclose a hole as the number of samples goes to infinity.
A similar construction can be used to show an analogous discrepancy between the minimum convex cover of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} and MinCliqueCover.

In principle, this problem can be addressed by solving a modified version of MaxClique that better captures the notion of a convex set.
In short, we require that every vertex of the visibility graph that is contained in the convex hull of the maximum clique must be a member of the clique.
For an infinitely dense visibility graph, this ensures that the maximum clique cannot enclose holes.

We enforce the contrapositive of the latter condition through linear constraints that separate all non-clique members qiq\_{i}, with i∈{1,…,K}i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, from the points in the clique with a hyperplane ℋi={q∣ciT​q+di=0}\mathcal{H}\_{i}=\{q\mid c\_{i}^{T}q+d\_{i}=0\}, parameterized by the decision variables (ci,di)∈ℝn+1(c\_{i},d\_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}.

## VII Conclusions

We have proposed an algorithm for approximately decomposing complex configuration spaces into small collections of polytopes.
Our algorithm uses clique covers of visibility graphs as an effective heuristic for obtaining local information about 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}}, and for seeding a region-inflation algorithm.
The parallels between convex sets in 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} and cliques in visibility graphs have also been discussed.
Our experiments demonstrate that VCC reliably finds approximate convex covers of 𝒞free\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{free}} with fewer regions and in less time than previous approaches.

args.summary:
This paper presents an efficient method called Visibility Clique Cover (VCC) for approximately decomposing complex robot configuration spaces (𝒞^free) into a small number of convex polytopes, without human supervision. The approach works by: (1) randomly sampling points in 𝒞^free and constructing a visibility graph where edges connect points with mutual line of sight; (2) computing an approximate clique cover of this graph by solving MaxClique integer programs; (3) summarizing each clique with a minimum-volume ellipsoid; and (4) inflating these ellipsoids into large collision-free polytopes using a single iteration of IRIS/IRIS-NP. The process repeats until a target coverage fraction α is achieved.

The method is evaluated against Iterative Obstacle Seeding (IOS) on four environments: Village (2D), 3DOF Flipper, 5DOF UR3, and 7DOF IIWA robot arms. Results show VCC consistently requires fewer regions and less time to achieve target coverage. Most notably, for the 7DOF IIWA at 70% coverage, VCC uses 46.3 regions in ~5,700 seconds versus IOS using 482.6 regions in ~89,000 seconds—approximately 10x fewer regions and 16x faster.

The paper also discusses theoretical limitations: cliques in visibility graphs can enclose holes in 𝒞^free, meaning not all cliques correspond to convex sets. A modified MaxClique formulation with separation constraints is proposed to address this, though it is computationally expensive for practical use. The authors note that in practice, only ~0.1% of vertices in the first MaxClique problem were excluded from the clique that could not be separated by a hyperplane.

# Russ Tedrake: Motion Planning Around Obstacles with Convex Optimization

## Overview
This is a talk given by Russ Tedrake (Toyota Professor at MIT, VP of Robotics Research at Toyota Research Institute) at the TAU CG Seminar on January 18, 2023. The talk presents new work on motion planning using convex optimization, captured in two papers: a general optimization framework for "shortest path in graphs of convex sets" and a specific application to motion planning.

## Key Problem
Traditional trajectory optimization suffers from local minima (e.g., a point robot going around a box obstacle gets stuck in one direction and cannot flip to the shorter path). Sample-based planners like RRT* converge slowly and handle dynamic constraints poorly. The goal is to combine the global optimality properties of sample-based planning with the efficiency of trajectory optimization for dynamically feasible motions.

## Three Key Ingredients
1. **Linear programming formulation of shortest path on discrete graphs** – leveraging the well-known property that the LP relaxation is tight (binary feasible).
2. **Convex formulations for continuous motion planning** – when obstacles are not present or a decision about which way to go has been made.
3. **Approximate convex decompositions of configuration space** – breaking free space into convex regions.

## Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)
The core innovation generalizes the shortest path problem: each vertex in the graph is associated with a convex set, and edge costs are convex functions of continuous variables within those sets. This is formulated as a mixed-integer convex program with a *tight convex relaxation* — meaning the convex relaxation alone often solves the global optimization problem.

Key advances:
- **Strengthening constraints** (spatial conservation of flow) added to make the convex relaxation tight, without changing the binary-feasible solution.
- The convex relaxation recovers the global optimal solution in many practical instances.
- Orders of magnitude faster than previous mixed-integer formulations for motion planning.

## Results and Applications
- **Quadrotor flight**: Solving global optimal paths through obstacle fields with dynamic constraints, minimizing time or effort.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14D configuration space)**: Two KUKA robots navigating complex configuration space obstacles, solving "Twister"-like mug rearrangement problems.
- **Footstep planning for humanoid robots**: Orders of magnitude faster than prior mixed-integer methods.
- **Maze navigation**: Continuous path optimization solved to global optimality via convex relaxation.

## Convex Decomposition of Configuration Space
The approach uses fast approximate decompositions:
- Alternating between quadratic programs and semi-definite programs to find separating hyperplanes and grow largest contained ellipsoids.
- For configuration space obstacles, uses sums-of-squares polynomial optimization to certify collision-free regions.
- Achieves surprisingly tight bounds (e.g., 7.33mm gap between two bimanual manipulators).

## Statistical Performance
In procedurally generated quadrotor environments:
- The convex optimization **often achieves true minimal cost**.
- In worst cases, the solution is guaranteed to be **within 20% of optimal**.
- The convex relaxation can certify optimality without additional branch-and-bound work in many instances.

## Open Problems
- What defines an optimal convex decomposition for this planner?
- Connections to maximum vertex hidden set problems and visibility graphs.
- Extending to non-Euclidean geometry (mobile manipulators, wrap-around effects).
- Task and motion planning integration.

## Implementation
All code is available in the open-source software **Drake** (MIT's robotics simulator and optimization library).

Research Topic 1: Technical Feasibility of PRM + Convex Decomposition Pipeline for Generating GCS Safety Regions

Background: The Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) algorithm (from Tobia Marcucci, et al., MIT) is a motion planning and trajectory optimization framework that solves a shortest path problem over a graph where each vertex is associated with a convex set. Currently, the convex sets (safety regions) in GCS are typically generated through a combination of manual seeding and automated tools like IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) or IRIS-NP, which are run offline with human guidance.

Query: Investigate the technical feasibility of the following pipeline:
1. Use a Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm (or improved variants like PRM*, SPARS, SPARTA, or lazy PRM) to generate a static connectivity graph of the free space in a robotics/planning environment.
2. Apply convex decomposition and optimization algorithms (such as IRIS, IRIS-NP, CIDR (Convex Iterative Decomposition of Regions), or other convex region growing methods) on the nodes and/or edges of the PRM graph to automatically construct convex safety regions.
3. Feed these automatically generated convex sets into the GCS algorithm for path solving.

Specific questions to answer:
- What are the theoretical connections between PRM sampling/connectivity and convex region decomposition? Is there existing literature combining sampling-based planners with convex optimization?
- How can PRM milestones (nodes) serve as seeds for convex region growing algorithms like IRIS? What are the geometric properties that make a PRM node a good or bad seed?
- How should the PRM graph's edges inform convex decomposition? E.g., should convex sets be grown along edges, around nodes, or between connected nodes?
- What are the key challenges: overlapping convex sets, coverage completeness, computational complexity of the decomposition, and handling narrow passages in the environment?
- What PRM variants are best suited for this pipeline (e.g., PRM* for asymptotic optimality, SPARS for sparsity, or bridge-test PRM for narrow passages)?
- How does the quality (size, number, overlap) of the generated convex sets affect GCS solver performance?

Provide a thorough technical analysis of feasibility, including reference to relevant algorithms and their properties.

URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375669203_Motion_planning_around_obstacles_with_convex_optimization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), a motion planning framework that enables convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan collision-free trajectories around obstacles. The key insight is using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets to design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem, which is typically very tight. A cheap postprocessing of the relaxation solution is almost always sufficient to identify a globally optimal collision-free trajectory.

The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity. It reduces the planning problem to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. The method is sound (trajectories satisfy all constraints) and complete up to the conservatism of space decomposition.

Key results include:
- **Maze planning (2,500 cells)**: GCS finds optimal trajectories with 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10^7 required by existing mixed-integer planners. Solved in 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP).
- **Quadrotor flying through buildings (100 random environments)**: 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, worst case 2.9%. Average runtime 2.65 seconds.
- **7-DOF robot arm comparison with PRM**: GCS finds shorter trajectories faster online than both standard PRM and PRM with shortcutting. All trajectories are optimal (δopt=0) within the space decomposition.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF)**: GCS plans coordinated motions including arm crossing, near-self-collision configurations, and handoffs. Largest optimality gap 13.9%, runtimes 21-185 seconds.

GCS uses Bèzier curves for trajectory parameterization, guaranteeing safety at all times with no discretization error. The free space is decomposed into convex safe regions Q_i, and an intersection graph encodes connectivity. The method scales polynomially with the number of regions and curve degree.

The paper argues GCS generalizes PRM by extending collision-free samples to convex regions inflated as much as obstacles allow, reducing combinatorial complexity. It handles differential costs and constraints, exploits combinatorial structure, and has low runtimes. The implementation is available in the open-source software Drake.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) Optimization ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/graphs-of-convex-sets-gcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) is a mixed discrete-continuous optimization framework that integrates graph search with convex optimization, primarily used for path planning and control in robotics. In GCS, graph structure represents combinatorial choices, and each selected vertex or edge carries a convex optimization problem. The framework generalizes classical problems like shortest path, TSP, spanning tree, and assignment by coupling discrete decisions with continuous convex program solvers.

**Foundational Model:** A general GCS problem selects an admissible subgraph along with continuous variables on selected vertices. Edge costs need not be static and can encode distances, control-theoretic stage costs, or continuity constraints. The shortest-path problem in GCS is NP-hard.

**Exact Formulations:** The standard exact formulation uses mixed-integer convex programs (MICP) via perspective/homogenization operators. Convex relaxations (dropping integrality) are often very tight but not exact in general. Tools like GCSOPT automatically transform ILP models into MICPs.

**Search Algorithms:** Several efficient algorithms have been developed: A*-GCS (uses heuristics on representative points, provable lower bounds), GCS* (forward heuristic search, complete and cost-optimal), IxG/IxG* (interleaves graph search with convex optimization), and multi-query SPP (offline SDP for lower bounds, online in milliseconds).

**Temporal Logic Integration:** GCS has been integrated with LTL and STL for symbolic task planning with continuous motion. For LTL, product graphs combine transition systems with finite automata; for STL, timed automata are used. Reported benchmarks include a 30-DoF humanoid solved in ~7.72 seconds and a 5-key/5-door problem in 5.82 seconds.

**Space-Time Planning:** ST-GCS adds time as an optimization dimension, enabling multi-robot planning in dynamic environments. Applications include autonomous driving (with Bézier curves and polynomial time-scaling) and game-theoretic highway driving scenarios.

**Limitations:** GCS problems remain NP-hard in general. Relaxation quality is problem-dependent. Model fidelity may be traded for convexity (e.g., small-slip assumptions in driving). Augmented formulations for TSP remain exponential. Software ecosystem includes GCSOPT, Drake, MOSEK, CVXPY, and CLARABEL.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Tommy Cohn's blog post provides a detailed analysis of the Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm for sampling-based motion planning. The post first describes the PRM algorithm, introduced by Lydia Kavraki in 1996: it randomly samples collision-free configurations, uses a local planner to connect nearby configurations (via k-nearest neighbors or radius-based approaches), and constructs a graph that can be searched with Dijkstra's or A* for multi-query planning.

The main focus is on the theoretical analysis of PRM, specifically the 2004 paper by Ladd and Kavraki. The analysis is based on the concept of **path clearance** (ε-clear paths), where a path maintains at least distance ε from obstacles. The key result is a bound on the expected number of samples needed to find a path: it is proportional to (2L/ε) * H(2L/ε) * (μ(X) / μ(B)), where L is path length, ε is clearance, μ(X) is the volume of free space, and μ(B) is the volume of a ball of radius ε/2. This bound grows logarithmically in L/ε but is highly sensitive to the curse of dimensionality through the volume ratio term.

# Superfast Configuration-Space Convex Set Computation on GPUs for Online Motion Planning

This paper presents a GPU-accelerated approach for constructing probabilistically collision-free convex sets in robot configuration space for online motion planning in changing environments.

<summary>
This is a scientific article (Mathematics, 2025) presenting exact and heuristic algorithms for convex polygon decomposition. The problem involves partitioning a non-convex polygon into the smallest possible number of convex subpolygons, which is a key preprocessing step in applications such as robotic motion planning, 2D packing, pattern recognition, and manufacturing.

**Authors:** Johana Milena Martínez Contreras, Germán Fernando Pantoja Benavides, Astrid Xiomara Rodríguez, John Willmer Escobar, and David Álvarez-Martínez (affiliations: Universidad de Los Andes, Colombia; Tecnologico de Monterrey, Mexico; Universidad del Valle, Colombia).

**Key Contributions:**
1. An exact convex decomposition method inspired by Keil's dynamic-programming approach (Algorithm 1), which recursively subdivides the polygon into triangles and subpolygons, evaluating candidate merges to obtain minimal convex components (complexity O(n³)).
2. A heuristic algorithm that approximates decomposition by identifying and linking notches (concave vertices), selecting vertices with high visible neighbors, and exploring three-vertex configurations.
3. A visibility-preserving bridge transformation that converts polygons with holes into equivalent simple instances, enabling decomposition of more complex topologies.
4. A convex-union post-processing phase applied to both exact and heuristic outputs to further reduce the number of convex pieces.
5. A new publicly available dataset of polygons with holes, addressing the lack of standardized benchmark instances in the literature.
6. The exact model produces optimal decompositions for small and medium instances, while the heuristic achieves near-optimal solutions with significantly reduced computation times.

**Literature Review:** The paper reviews convex decomposition applications in topographic modeling, pattern recognition, packing/nesting problems, machine learning, and multi-robot terrain coverage. Key prior methods discussed include Keil's exact dynamic programming approach, Fernández et al.'s vector-dependency procedure, and Lien and Amato's approximate convex decomposition framework for polygons with holes.

**Methodology Details:**
- Visibility is defined as the ability to connect two points with a straight segment entirely inside the polygon without intersecting edges.
- Reference vertices include all concave (reflex) vertices plus the initial and final vertices of the polygon's boundary traversal.
- The exact algorithm uses dynamic programming, solving small subproblems once and storing information to avoid repetitive iterations.
- The heuristic processes vertices in counterclockwise order (simplifying implementation), drawing partially on Fernández et al.'s method.
- For polygons with holes, a bridge construction converts holed polygons into equivalent simple polygons while preserving structural relations.

**Algorithm 1 (Exact Convex Decomposition):** Input is vertex coordinates; output is coordinates of convex parts. Steps include computing angles, determining notches (concave vertices), finding visibility of vertices, ordering subpolygons, determining base triangles, and using dynamic programming to find minimum convex decomposition.

**Algorithm 2 (Visibility Between Points):** Determines which points are mutually visible using the v1v2 function, which evaluates the position of one point with respect to lines formed by another point, considering collinearity and intersection checks.

--- SOURCE 2: Analysis of Sampling-Based Planners: PRMs ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn (a PhD student at MIT's Robot Locomotion Group) provides a theoretical analysis of the Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm, the first in a series on sampling-based planners. The PRM algorithm, introduced by Lydia Kavraki in 1996, is a multi-query motion planning algorithm that involves: (1) randomly sampling collision-free configurations via rejection sampling, (2) connecting nearby configurations using a local planner (e.g., straight-line paths checked for collisions) to build a graph, and (3) in the online phase, linking start and goal points into the roadmap and solving via graph search (Dijkstra's or A*).

The key analysis focuses on results from Ladd and Kavraki (2004) which proved a bound on the expected number of samples required to find a path. This bound is based on **path clearance** (ϵ-clear path: a path that maintains at least distance ϵ from obstacles). The analysis shows that an ϵ-clear path can be covered by balls of radius ϵ/2. By the Coupon Collector's Problem, the expected number of samples needed is bounded by N × H(N) (where N is the number of balls and H(N) is the harmonic number). For a path of length L, 2L/ϵ balls are needed. The bound demonstrates that the expected sample count is logarithmic in the ratio of path length to clearance. However, the volume ratio of free space to ball volume increases rapidly with dimension, revealing the curse of dimensionality's effect on PRMs.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents research on "Graphs of Convex Sets" (GCS), a framework for solving motion planning and optimization problems that combine discrete graph structures with continuous convex optimization. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (submitted March 26, 2023) by Mark Petersen (Harvard University) and Russ Tedrake (MIT) presents IRIS-NP (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite & Nonlinear Programming), an algorithm that generates convex, collision-free regions in a robot's configuration space (C-space) for motion planning.

**Algorithm:** IRIS-NP works iteratively by alternating between two steps: (1) finding counterexamples (collisions) within the current polytope using nonlinear optimization, and (2) adding separating hyperplanes to remove those colliding configurations. It computes the largest inscribed ellipsoid within the updated polytope to guide region growth.

The search terminates after a specified number of consecutive optimization attempts fail to find a collision, offering a favorable trade-off between computational speed and safety.

**Inverse Kinematics (IK):** The author frames IK as a constrained optimization problem rather than simply inverting the forward kinematics function. **IK vs Differential IK:** Differential IK works well for incremental motions; IK solves more global problems but isn't guaranteed to succeed. IK can switch between distinct solutions (e.g., going around an obstacle on either side), while differential IK cannot make such leaps.

**Global IK:** Drake's GlobalInverseKinematics uses mixed-integer convex optimization (Dai17) with solution times on the order of seconds.

**Kinematic Trajectory Optimization:** Extends the optimization perspective to solve for a sequence of joint angles simultaneously. Uses B-spline trajectory parameterization, which has useful properties: derivatives remain B-splines, the convex hull property allows constraints on positions and derivatives for all time using linear constraints. The default Drake implementation combines a path r(s) with time-scaling: q(t) = r(t/T).

**Collision Avoidance:** Minimum-distance constraints can only be enforced at discrete samples along the path, not for all time. The author suggests adding constraints at modest sampling during optimization, then checking more densely before execution.

**Sampling-Based Motion Planning:** The author notes these methods provide probabilistic completeness but struggle with derivative constraints and high dimensions. References LaValle06 and the Open Motion Planning Library.

**Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS):** A framework bridging trajectory optimization and sampling-based planning. GCS generalizes shortest-path problems on graphs by allowing each vertex to have an associated convex set from which a point is selected. The motion planning application uses convex decompositions of collision-free space. The resulting mixed-integer convex programs have strong convex relaxations, often solving to optimality without needing the full MICP. GCS can encode minimum-time, minimum-path-length, and minimum-energy objectives, with constraints on velocities, continuity, and region membership guaranteed for all time. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This tutorial explains how to use the point cloud region growing segmentation algorithm implemented in PCL (Point Cloud Library)'s `pcl::RegionGrowing` class. The algorithm merges points that are close in terms of smoothness constraint, producing clusters where each cluster represents points belonging to the same smooth surface. It works by comparing angles between point normals.

**Algorithm Overview:**
1. Points are sorted by curvature value; growth starts from the point with minimum curvature (located in flattest area) to reduce total segments.
2. For each seed point, neighboring points are found. If the angle between the neighbor's normal and the seed's normal is below a threshold, the neighbor is added to the current region. If the neighbor's curvature is below a threshold, it becomes a new seed.
3. When seeds are empty, the region is complete and the process repeats for remaining unlabeled points.

**Key Parameters:**
- Smoothness threshold: maximum allowable angle deviation between normals (set to 3.0 degrees in example)
- Curvature threshold: maximum curvature difference for continuing growth (set to 1.0)
- Minimum/maximum cluster size: clusters outside this range are discarded (min=50, max=1,000,000 in example)
- Number of neighbors for K-nearest search (30 in example)

**Code Implementation Steps:**
- Load point cloud from PCD file
- Compute normals using `pcl::NormalEstimation` with KdTree search (k=50)
- Remove NaN points from cloud
- Instantiate `pcl::RegionGrowing<PointXYZ, Normal>` and set parameters
- Call `extract()` to perform segmentation, returning clusters as `pcl::PointIndices`
- Visualize results using colored cloud from `getColoredCloud()` method

**Output:** The algorithm produces clusters where each cluster has its own color. Points shown in red are those rejected due to cluster size constraints.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Autonomy Talks - Tobia Marcucci: A Tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS)

## Overview
Prof. Tobia Marcucci (UCSB, ECE and Mechanical Engineering) presented a tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), an optimization framework developed during his PhD at MIT and refined at Amazon. The talk was delivered on November 18, 2025, as part of the Autonomy Talks series.

## Core Problem
Many robotics problems require simultaneous optimization of high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous control. Examples include:
- Atlas robot parkour (sequence of obstacles + continuous trajectories)
- Robot manipulation (making/breaking contacts + object positions)
- UAV trajectory optimization with obstacles (left/right decisions + continuous trajectories)
- Warehouse pick-and-place (object sorting + trajectory optimization)

## What is a Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)?
A GCS is a graph where:
- **Vertices** are paired with convex optimization problems (continuous variable Xv, convex constraint set, objective function)
- **Edges** couple vertex optimization problems through additional convex costs and constraints
- Unlike ordinary weighted graphs, weights are not fixed scalars but functions of underlying continuous variables

## Key Advantages
1. **Unified framework** bridging discrete and continuous optimization
2. **Leverages existing tools**: combines graph search/optimization (scalable) with convex optimization (mature continuous optimization technology)
3. **Accessible**: users define the graph structure, variables, and constraints; the framework handles the optimization automatically

## Problem Classes
Classical graph problems naturally generalize to GCS:
- Shortest Path in GCS
- Traveling Salesman Problem in GCS
- Minimum Spanning Tree in GCS
- Facility location, bipartite matching, etc.

## Solution Approach
Most GCS problems are NP-hard. The framework formulates them as Mixed Integer Convex Programs (MICP) by:
1. Encoding the graph structure using incidence vectors (binary variables for vertices/edges)
2. Translating GCS constraints using binary variables to activate/deactivate relevant parts
3. Convexifying bilinear constraints exactly (leveraging binary variable structure)
4. Efficiency depends on the tightness of the convex relaxation

## Applications Demonstrated
- **Solar-powered helicopter path planning**: shortest path through islands with recharging, solved in 24 seconds (convex relaxation gives 99%+ accuracy in fraction of a second)
- **School bus routing with mobile passengers**: Traveling Salesman variant where children can move to meet the bus
- **Camera surveillance placement**: Minimum Spanning Tree variant ensuring camera visibility
- **Motion planning and collision avoidance**: Shortest path through obstacles

## Software Tool
**GCSOPT**: Open-source Python library for solving real-world GCS problems in just a few lines of code. Handles the mathematical complexity automatically behind the scenes.

## Key Quote
The research addresses "the observation that at the core of many robotics problems is the need to simultaneously optimize high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous decisions."

**Inverse Kinematics (IK):** The author frames IK as a constrained optimization problem rather than simply inverting the forward kinematics function. This allows for rich costs and constraints (joint limits, collision avoidance, position/orientation constraints). Drake provides an InverseKinematics class for assembling these constraints into a MathematicalProgram. The author recommends keeping costs simple (e.g., joint-centering quadratic cost) and using minimal constraints.

**IK vs Differential IK:** Differential IK works well for incremental motions; IK solves more global problems but isn't guaranteed to succeed. IK can switch between distinct solutions (e.g., going around an obstacle on either side), while differential IK cannot make such leaps.

**Global IK:** Drake's GlobalInverseKinematics uses mixed-integer convex optimization (Dai17) with solution times on the order of seconds.

**Kinematic Trajectory Optimization:** Extends the optimization perspective to solve for a sequence of joint angles simultaneously. Uses B-spline trajectory parameterization, which has useful properties: derivatives remain B-splines, the convex hull property allows constraints on positions and derivatives for all time using linear constraints. The default Drake implementation combines a path r(s) with time-scaling: q(t) = r(t/T).

**Collision Avoidance:** Minimum-distance constraints can only be enforced at discrete samples along the path, not for all time. The author suggests adding constraints at modest sampling during optimization, then checking more densely before execution.

**Sampling-Based Motion Planning:** The author notes these methods provide probabilistic completeness but struggle with derivative constraints and high dimensions. References LaValle06 and the Open Motion Planning Library.

**Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS):** A framework bridging trajectory optimization and sampling-based planning. GCS generalizes shortest-path problems on graphs by allowing each vertex to have an associated convex set from which a point is selected. The motion planning application uses convex decompositions of collision-free space. The resulting mixed-integer convex programs have strong convex relaxations, often solving to optimality without needing the full MICP. GCS can encode minimum-time, minimum-path-length, and minimum-energy objectives, with constraints on velocities, continuity, and region membership guaranteed for all time. --- SOURCE 1: Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.08909v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets (INSATxGCS or IxG and IxG*) as a superior alternative to the existing GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets) method for smooth, collision-free motion planning in robotics. 

The key insight is that the GCS approach solves a massive joint optimization problem (Mixed Integer Convex Program) whose size is invariant to the planning query, making it slow even for trivial queries. The authors propose interleaving graph search with trajectory optimization, only optimizing over the fraction of the graph explored by the search.

**Main contributions:**
- **IxG**: Combines implicit graph search (INSAT) with GCS representation, using a Lower Bound Graph (LBG) for admissible heuristics and a weighted A* search that optimizes trajectories only over partial paths from the search.
- **IxG***: An optimal/bounded-suboptimal version that allows re-expansion of convex regions (tree search) with pruning based on LBG cost-to-go estimates.
- **Stronger guarantees**: IxG* provides stronger completeness (handles challenging initial conditions requiring revisiting convex sets) and stronger optimality (prespecify suboptimality bound) compared to GCS.
- **Theoretical properties**: IxG* provides optimality, bounded suboptimality, and completeness guarantees.

**Technical approach:**
- Decomposes planning space into convex sets represented as a graph
- Uses LBG (offline-constructed surrogate graph) to provide provable underestimates for heuristics and pruning
- Decouples the MICP into graph search (exploring convex regions) and convex optimization over prespecified sequences
- Warm-starts trajectory optimizations using dynamic programming

**Results**: Numerical comparisons show IxG finds lower-cost solutions orders of magnitude faster than GCS across multiple applications, including an 18-degree-of-freedom multi-arm assembly scenario.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Differing Formulations of GCS for Motion Planning ---
URL: https://blog.tommycohn.com/2023/03/differing-formulations-of-gcs-for.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn compares two formulations of Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) for robot motion planning. The first formulation, the "Conjugate Graph," uses intersections of collision-free sets as graph nodes, with edges representing paths between sets that share a constituent set. The second, the "Overlap Graph," places control points in each free region for Bézier curve trajectories and constrains endpoints to be equal on overlaps between sets. The author concludes that while the conjugate graph is more straightforward to implement and allows for preprocessing to compute lower bounds, the overlap graph is superior for future use because it parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, supports broader optimization problems, and is likely to be the "official" formulation going forward. The conjugate graph's advantage in preprocessing (pruning edges/sets using lower bounds) comes with a hidden cost: when many convex sets overlap, the conjugate graph's size grows significantly, potentially negating preprocessing gains.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The idea behind the conjugate graph formulation is to use the intersections of collision-free sets as the sets in the graph.", "In my experience with both formulations, I've found that the conjugate graph formulation is more straightforward to implement. But beyond that, there are few reasons to not go with the overlap graph formulation.", "The overlap graph formulation parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, enabling its use for broader optimization problems.", "In the conjugate graph formulation, it's easy to compute useful lower bounds. But in the overlap graph formulation, the lower bound is trivially zero, as all the points in the set could be made identical.", "GCS is still a young framework, and there is still a lot of room for clever heuristics, preprocessing techniques, and overall engineering effort to improve the algorithm."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The paper presents GCS*, a forward heuristic search algorithm that generalizes A* to Shortest Path Problems on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS). GCS addresses mixed discrete-continuous planning problems (e.g., motion planning, task and motion planning) where continuous decisions at graph vertices are coupled by constraints across edges. Unlike discrete graphs, GCS lacks the optimal substructure property, making naive A* application impossible. The key insight is that while optimal substructure fails at the path level, it holds at the trajectory level. GCS* uses two domination checks: ReachesCheaper (for cost-optimality) and ReachesNew (for completeness/satisficing). These checks are implemented via polyhedral-containment (exact, complete, optimal) or sampling-based (probabilistically complete, asymptotically optimal) methods. The algorithm is demonstrated on planar pushing tasks (AROUND, SQUEEZE, STACK) with graphs up to ~1.3e9 vertices and ~8.5e17 edges. On the STACK task, sampling-based GCS* finds a solution in 21.9 seconds, while prior methods requiring explicit graph construction are intractable. GCS* compares favorably to baselines IxG and IxG*, particularly for large implicit graphs where preprocessing heuristic computation becomes prohibitive.

Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) is a mathematical framework that associates graph vertices with convex sets to integrate combinatorial properties and convex optimization. It encodes structural constraints through convex graph invariants and invariant convex sets, enabling efficient relaxations such as spectral and semidefinite programming (SDP) methods. The framework unifies problems like graph deconvolution, hypothesis testing, and graph generation by leveraging robust optimization and permutation symmetry.

**Foundations:** Convex graph invariants are real-valued functions f defined on adjacency matrices that are convex and invariant under vertex relabelings. Examples include sum of edge weights, maximum node degree, MAXCUT value (via SDP relaxation), and spectral invariants like sum of the k largest eigenvalues. These invariants can be enforced via convex constraints to form invariant convex sets.

**Representation:** Every convex graph invariant can be expressed as a supremum over elementary convex graph invariants. Direct computation is NP-hard (equivalent to Quadratic Assignment Problem), but tractable spectral relaxations (replacing permutations with orthogonal group) and SDP relaxations provide efficient approximations.

**Applications:**
- Graph deconvolution posed as convex optimization over convex hulls
- Hypothesis testing between graph families via linear functional optimization
- Graph generation by constructing matrices in intersections of invariant convex sets

**Key insight:** The convex hull of a graph under node permutation actions serves as the minimal invariant convex set, analogous to uncertainty sets in robust optimization. This bridges the discrete/continuous divide and allows application of convex analysis tools to combinatorial domains.

**Limitations:** Information loss from convex relaxations (aggregate vs. pointwise properties), computational challenges for large graphs, and ongoing research into tighter relaxation guarantees.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Autonomy Talks - Tobia Marcucci: A Tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS)

## Overview
Prof. Tobia Marcucci (UCSB, ECE and Mechanical Engineering) presented a tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), an optimization framework developed during his PhD at MIT and refined at Amazon. The talk was delivered on November 18, 2025, as part of the Autonomy Talks series.

## Core Problem
Many robotics problems require simultaneous optimization of high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous control. Examples include:
- Atlas robot parkour (sequence of obstacles + continuous trajectories)
- Robot manipulation (making/breaking contacts + object positions)
- UAV trajectory optimization with obstacles (left/right decisions + continuous trajectories)
- Warehouse pick-and-place (object sorting + trajectory optimization)

## What is a Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)?
A GCS is a graph where:
- **Vertices** are paired with convex optimization problems (continuous variable Xv, convex constraint set, objective function)
- **Edges** couple vertex optimization problems through additional convex costs and constraints
- Unlike ordinary weighted graphs, weights are not fixed scalars but functions of underlying continuous variables

## Key Advantages
1. **Unified framework** bridging discrete and continuous optimization
2. **Leverages existing tools**: combines graph search/optimization (scalable) with convex optimization (mature continuous optimization technology)
3. **Accessible**: users define the graph structure, variables, and constraints; the framework handles the optimization automatically

## Problem Classes
Classical graph problems naturally generalize to GCS:
- Shortest Path in GCS
- Traveling Salesman Problem in GCS
- Minimum Spanning Tree in GCS
- Facility location, bipartite matching, etc.

## Solution Approach
Most GCS problems are NP-hard. The framework formulates them as Mixed Integer Convex Programs (MICP) by:
1. Encoding the graph structure using incidence vectors (binary variables for vertices/edges)
2. Translating GCS constraints using binary variables to activate/deactivate relevant parts
3. Convexifying bilinear constraints exactly (leveraging binary variable structure)
4. Efficiency depends on the tightness of the convex relaxation

## Applications Demonstrated
- **Solar-powered helicopter path planning**: shortest path through islands with recharging, solved in 24 seconds (convex relaxation gives 99%+ accuracy in fraction of a second)
- **School bus routing with mobile passengers**: Traveling Salesman variant where children can move to meet the bus
- **Camera surveillance placement**: Minimum Spanning Tree variant ensuring camera visibility
- **Motion planning and collision avoidance**: Shortest path through obstacles

## Software Tool
**GCSOPT**: Open-source Python library for solving real-world GCS problems in just a few lines of code. Handles the mathematical complexity automatically behind the scenes.

## Key Quote
The research addresses "the observation that at the core of many robotics problems is the need to simultaneously optimize high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous decisions."
</summary>

This paper presents Space-Time Graphs of Convex Sets (ST-GCS), a novel deterministic approach to Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) that addresses limitations of sampling-based methods in spatiotemporal settings. The key contributions include: (1) extending Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) into the time dimension to formulate time-optimal trajectories in a unified convex optimization that naturally accommodates velocity bounds and flexible arrival times; (2) introducing Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) to reserve trajectories as spatiotemporal obstacles, maintaining collision-free space-time graphs for subsequent planning; and (3) integrating ST-GCS into two prioritized-planning frameworks (Random-Prioritized Planning and Priority-Based Search).

The method works by systematically covering the collision-free space-time domain with convex sets rather than relying on random sampling. ST-GCS solves a generalized shortest-path problem on a graph whose vertices are convex sets, determining which sets form the path and the state within each set, jointly optimizing a time-minimizing objective. The ECD algorithm partitions space-time convex sets to avoid conflicts with already-planned trajectories, treating higher-priority robot trajectories as dynamic obstacles.

Experimental results on 2D mobile robot scenarios demonstrate that ST-GCS consistently achieves higher success rates and better solution quality than state-of-the-art sampling-based planners (adapted T-PRM and ST-RRT*), often with orders-of-magnitude faster runtimes. PBS+ST-GCS solves all instances on empty and complex maps, with average runtimes under 1 second and 10 seconds respectively. The approach is particularly effective in narrow corridors and crowded settings where sampling-based methods struggle to capture spatiotemporal safe transit windows.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn compares two formulations of Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) for robot motion planning. The first formulation, the "Conjugate Graph," uses intersections of collision-free sets as graph nodes, with edges representing paths between sets that share a constituent set. The second, the "Overlap Graph," places control points in each free region for Bézier curve trajectories and constrains endpoints to be equal on overlaps between sets. The author concludes that while the conjugate graph is more straightforward to implement and allows for preprocessing to compute lower bounds, the overlap graph is superior for future use because it parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, supports broader optimization problems, and is likely to be the "official" formulation going forward. The conjugate graph's advantage in preprocessing (pruning edges/sets using lower bounds) comes with a hidden cost: when many convex sets overlap, the conjugate graph's size grows significantly, potentially negating preprocessing gains.

This paper presents IRIS-NP (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite & Nonlinear Programming), an algorithm for generating convex, collision-free regions in a robot's configuration space (C-space) for motion planning. Authored by Mark Petersen (Harvard University) and Russ Tedrake (MIT) and submitted on March 26, 2023, IRIS-NP extends the original IRIS algorithm to handle the complex, nonlinear mappings between a robot's configuration space and physical workspace using nonlinear programming.

**Key Methodology:**
- The algorithm iteratively alternates between finding counterexample collisions (via nonlinear optimization that minimizes distance from a seed point subject to collision constraints) and adding separating hyperplanes to carve away collision zones.
- It computes the largest inscribed ellipsoid within the updated polytope to guide safe region growth.

**Probabilistic Certification:**
- Unlike rigorous methods like C-IRIS, IRIS-NP provides probabilistic rather than guaranteed certification of collision-free regions.
- Uses Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to search for counterexamples; the search terminates after a specified number of consecutive failed optimization attempts.
- Increasing the number of consecutive infeasible searches significantly reduces the probability of undetected collisions.

**Experimental Results:**
- Successfully demonstrated on a 7-DoF single-arm robot and a 14-DoF dual-arm manipulator.
- Generates reasonably sized collision-free regions in about one minute.
- Handles narrow passages and cluttered environments.

**Key Advantages:**
- Avoids explicit C-space obstacle mapping (often intractable for high-DoF robots).
- Handles nonlinear kinematics and additional nonlinear constraints (e.g., orientation constraints).
- Can serve as initialization for C-IRIS to accelerate rigorous certification.
- Scalable to high-dimensional systems.

**Limitations:**
- Probabilistic (not rigorous) guarantees may not suffice for safety-critical applications.
- Nonlinear optimization can struggle with convergence or local minima in complex environments.
- Still requires significant computation for highly dynamic environments.

**Implementation details:** Uses SNOPT or IPOPT solvers, orders collision pairs by task-space distance, and applies a configuration-space margin to separating hyperplanes for added safety.

--- SOURCE 13: Motion planning around obstacles with convex optimization ---
URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375669203_Motion_planning_around_obstacles_with_convex_optimization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), a motion planning framework that uses convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan collision-free trajectories around obstacles. The key innovation is that it reformulates the nonconvex motion planning problem as a convex relaxation that is typically very tight, allowing global optimality to be achieved through a cheap post-processing step (randomized rounding) rather than expensive branch-and-bound mixed-integer programming.

The algorithm works by decomposing the free space into convex regions (safe sets), constructing an intersection graph of these regions, and using B-spline curves to parameterize trajectories. The resulting optimization is a Shortest Path Problem in GCS, whose convex relaxation is a Linear Program or Second-Order Cone Program that can be solved efficiently.

Key results demonstrated:
- Maze (2,500 cells): GCS finds optimal trajectories in 0.98-9.1 seconds, solving mixed-integer programs with ~5,000 binary variables
- Quadrotor through buildings (100 random environments): 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, average runtime 2.65 seconds
- Robot arm (7 DOF) vs PRM: GCS produces shorter trajectories in less online time across all 5 tasks, with optimality gap δopt = 0%
- Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF): GCS plans coordinated motions across 3 tasks, with runtimes of 21-185 seconds

GCS is sound (guarantees collision-free trajectories at all times) and complete (guaranteed to find a feasible trajectory if one exists, given no hard time limits and sufficient trajectory parameterization). The authors provide an open-source implementation in Drake and compare favorably against PRM and PRM with shortcutting, both in terms of trajectory quality and computational efficiency.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: Invited talk: Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization by Tobia Marcucci, MIT ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a recording of an invited talk by Tobia Marcucci, a PhD candidate at MIT, presented on September 17, 2022, as part of the Artificial and Mechanical Intelligence seminar series. The talk introduces a novel framework for motion planning around obstacles using convex optimization.

**Key Points:**

- **Problem:** Motion planning around obstacles (e.g., for quadrotors, robot arms) is traditionally nonconvex and difficult to solve, especially in high-dimensional cluttered environments. Sampling-based planners (like PRM) don't scale well to high dimensions and struggle with continuous differential constraints.

- **Proposed Solution:** A framework for finding shortest paths in "graphs of convex sets." The free space is decomposed into convex regions, and an adjacency graph is constructed. The problem becomes a mixed-integer program with a very tight convex relaxation.

- **Methodology:** 
  - Decompose free space into convex regions.
  - Build an adjacency graph from the decomposition.
  - Formulate a shortest path problem where vertex positions are continuous variables within convex sets and edge costs are convex functions.
  - Solve a convex relaxation (typically a linear or second-order cone program) and then use randomized rounding (e.g., randomized depth-first search) to obtain a discrete path.
  - The relaxation is so tight that in most practical cases, a single convex optimization—followed by cheap rounding—yields the globally optimal trajectory.

- **Advantages:**
  - Solves problems in high-dimensional spaces (demonstrated in 7D, 14D, and up to 180 dimensions).
  - Provides certifiable optimality bounds (lower bound from relaxation, upper bound from rounding).
  - Outperforms sampling-based planners like PRM in both trajectory quality and computation time.
  - Does not require expensive mixed-integer solver software; can use standard convex optimization solvers.

- **Results:**
  - In 95% of 100 random 3D building environments, a single convex optimization found the global minimum.
  - In the worst case, the solution was only 3% worse than the global optimum.
  - The method is orders of magnitude faster than previous mixed-integer approaches (e.g., seconds vs. tens of minutes for footstep planning).
  - Computation time grows linearly with problem complexity (number of regions and dimensions), unlike exponential growth for sampling-based methods.

- **Applications:** UAV navigation, robot arm manipulation in warehouses (collaboration with Amazon, Toyota, and XI), footstep planning for humanoids, and multi-robot coordination.

- **Ongoing Work:** Extending to acceleration constraints, vision-based constraints, GPU-accelerated custom solvers, and online/exploration scenarios where the full graph is not known in advance.

- **Implementation:** Available in the Drake robotics software library (C++).
</summary>

<summary>
This paper presents a novel method for convex geometric motion planning on Lie groups using moment relaxation (Lasserre's hierarchy). The key contribution is that by formulating robot dynamics models on matrix Lie groups, the kinodynamic motion planning problem can be expressed as exact polynomial optimization problems (POPs) that are relaxed as semidefinite programs (SDPs). The approach demonstrates that bridging geometric robotics formulations with Lasserre's hierarchy enables certifiably optimal solutions for motion planning using full dynamics models. The main limitations include numerical challenges with SDP solvers for hard cases and high memory/time costs for real-time applications.

--- SOURCE 1: Accelerating Mixed Discrete-Continuous Motion Planning ... ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2608.15440v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (arXiv:2608.15440) introduces Neural GCS, a data-driven pipeline designed to accelerate Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) motion planning for mixed discrete-continuous problems. GCS jointly optimizes discrete decisions (e.g., which obstacle-free region to traverse) with continuous trajectories. While powerful, the convex relaxation step in nominal GCS is computationally expensive, taking seconds to minutes for practical tasks.

The authors propose replacing the costly convex relaxation with a single forward pass through a Graph Attention Network (GAT) that predicts candidate paths through the graph. A lightweight ranking network orders these candidates by estimated trajectory cost, enabling early termination after evaluating only the top-ranked paths while maintaining near-optimal solutions.

The method is validated across three robotic domains: (1) collision-free 3D quadrotor navigation, (2) multi-step pick-and-place with a 7-DoF manipulator, and (3) planning through contact for planar pushing. Across both convex and non-convex cost/constraint settings, Neural GCS achieves up to two orders of magnitude speedup over nominal GCS while maintaining 100% success rate. For example, planning a quadrotor trajectory drops from 28.8 seconds to 0.027 seconds (convex) and from 8.2 to 0.164 seconds (non-convex). For the T-shaped object pushing problem, total time drops from 118.25 seconds to 0.611 seconds.

Training requires offline generation of 500 GCS instances per domain (~25 hours total), but inference runs on CPU with no GPU needed. The approach generalizes to graph sizes not seen during training. A limitation is that the SDP for contact-rich tasks can be too large to fit in memory for objects with more than eight faces, preventing offline dataset generation.
</summary>
