--- SOURCE 3: Motion planning around obstacles with convex optimization ---
URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375669203_Motion_planning_around_obstacles_with_convex_optimization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), a motion planning framework that enables convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan collision-free trajectories around obstacles. The key insight is using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets to design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem, which is typically very tight. A cheap postprocessing of the relaxation solution is almost always sufficient to identify a globally optimal collision-free trajectory.

The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity. It reduces the planning problem to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. The method is sound (trajectories satisfy all constraints) and complete up to the conservatism of space decomposition.

Key results include:
- **Maze planning (2,500 cells)**: GCS finds optimal trajectories with 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10^7 required by existing mixed-integer planners. Solved in 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP).
- **Quadrotor flying through buildings (100 random environments)**: 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, worst case 2.9%. Average runtime 2.65 seconds.
- **7-DOF robot arm comparison with PRM**: GCS finds shorter trajectories faster online than both standard PRM and PRM with shortcutting. All trajectories are optimal (δopt=0) within the space decomposition.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF)**: GCS plans coordinated motions including arm crossing, near-self-collision configurations, and handoffs. Largest optimality gap 13.9%, runtimes 21-185 seconds.

GCS uses Bèzier curves for trajectory parameterization, guaranteeing safety at all times with no discretization error. The free space is decomposed into convex safe regions Q_i, and an intersection graph encodes connectivity. The method scales polynomially with the number of regions and curve degree.

The paper argues GCS generalizes PRM by extending collision-free samples to convex regions inflated as much as obstacles allow, reducing combinatorial complexity. It handles differential costs and constraints, exploits combinatorial structure, and has low runtimes. The implementation is available in the open-source software Drake.
</summary>

**What is Motion Planning?**

--- SOURCE 6: [PDF] CS164: Collision Detection, Motion Planning ---
URL: http://graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs164-10-spring/Protected/10cs164-05-26.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage contains lecture slides from CS164 (Collision Detection, Motion Planning) at Stanford University, taught by Leonidas Guibas. The content covers two major topics:

**Collision Detection - GJK Algorithm:**
- The Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi (GJK) algorithm maintains the closest pair of points between two moving convex objects.
- GJK computes distance d and can return the closest pair of points PA, PB for two convex polyhedra.
- The algorithm works with a support mapping function and iteratively constructs a simplex to find the minimum norm point.
- A simplified version handles one object as a point at the origin; generalization to two bodies uses Minkowski difference (A-B contains origin iff A and B intersect).
- Support mapping is separable: SC-A-B(d) = SA(d) - SB(-d).
- For moving bodies, the problem can be transformed into moving vs. stationary, using point duplication or modified support mapping.
- Distance subalgorithm approaches: algebraic (Johnson's, original 1988) or geometric (using ClosestPointOnEdgeToPoint, ClosestPointOnTriangleToPoint, etc.).

**Motion Planning:**
- Basic problem: Given a movable object and environment, find a sequence of collision-avoiding configurations from start to goal.
- Configuration space maps the robot to a point; C-obstacle = O ⊕ (-R) (Minkowski sum).
- Minkowski sum properties: sum of two convex polygons yields convex polygon with m+n vertices; computational efficiency O(n+m) for convex polygons.
- 3D Minkowski sum: convex case O(nm); non-convex case O(n³m³) and computationally challenging.
- Path planning approaches:
  1. Roadmap methods: Visibility graphs (shortest paths, O(n²) optimal), Voronoi diagrams (maximize clearance, O(n log n)), Silhouette method, Probabilistic RoadMaps (PRM).
  2. Cell decomposition: Exact (trapezoidal, O(n log n)) and approximate (quadtree/octree).
  3. Potential field methods: Attractive and repulsive forces; local minima issues addressed via best-first search, random walks, or navigation functions.
- PRM construction: sample free configurations, connect nearby nodes via local paths, query connects start/goal to roadmap.
- Completeness: Complete (visibility graph, Voronoi, exact cell decomposition), resolution-complete, probabilistically complete.
- The course also covered 2D/3D transformations, shape representation, registration (ICP), PCA, shape matching, Voronoi/Delaunay, surface reconstruction, and topology/homology.
</summary>

Classic result by Lozano-Perez and Wesley 1979", "Computing the shortest collision-free path in a polyhedral space is NP-hard"

--- SOURCE 7: GitHub - bmaxdk/path-planning: Path Planning · GitHub ---
URL: https://github.com/bmaxdk/path-planning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This GitHub repository (bmaxdk/path-planning) is a comprehensive educational resource on robot path planning, covering three main approaches:

**1. Discrete (Combinatorial) Path Planning:** Discretizes the robot's workspace into a connected graph and applies graph-search algorithms. It involves:
- **Continuous Representation:** Using configuration space (C-space) where obstacles are inflated by the robot's radius.
- **Minkowski Sum:** A mathematical method to compute C-space from obstacle and robot geometry.
- **Roadmap Methods:** Visibility Graph (shortest path hugging obstacles), Voronoi Diagram (maximizes clearance), and Cell Decomposition (Exact and Approximate, including quadtree/octree decomposition).
- **Potential Field Method:** Combines attractive (toward goal) and repulsive (away from obstacles) potential functions.
- **Graph Search Algorithms:** BFS (complete, optimal for equal costs), DFS (neither complete nor optimal), Uniform Cost Search (optimal for varying costs), A* Search (informed, uses heuristic; optimal if heuristic is admissible and consistent), and Bidirectional Search (improves efficiency).

**2. Sample-Based Planning:** Probes workspace incrementally to construct a graph, suitable for high-dimensional problems. Includes:
- **Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM):** Multi-query planner that builds a graph by random sampling; probabilistically complete.
- **Rapidly Exploring Random Tree (RRT):** Single-query planner that builds a tree from start toward goal; supports non-holonomic systems.
- **Path Smoothing:** Post-processing to optimize paths via shortcutting.

**3. Probabilistic Path Planning:** Uses Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) to account for uncertainty in robot motion. Defined by states, actions, transition model, and rewards. Unlike reinforcement learning, in path planning the robot is fully aware of all MDP components.

The repository includes a Lab_Path_Planning folder, minkowski_sum.cpp implementation, and a README with detailed explanations and image references.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This video, part of a mobile robotics course series at Universitat Politècnica de València, introduces motion planning using cell decomposition techniques. The presenter covers three main approaches:

1. **Exact Cell Decomposition**: Uses trapezoidal cells with polygonal obstacles. A connectivity graph is built based on adjacency between cells, and optimal paths are computed using algorithms like A-star.

2. **Approximate Cell Decomposition (Regular Cells)**: Divides configuration space into regular cells. Semi-occupied cells are marked as occupied. Memory-intensive, suitable for low-dimensional (2D) spaces, but impractical beyond 3D.

3. **Tree-Based Decomposition (Irregular Cells)**: Uses quadtrees (2D) and octrees (3D) to reduce memory usage by varying cell size based on resolution needs. Only leaf nodes are used for path planning, with adjacency checked between neighbors.

In all approaches, a connectivity graph is built from cells, and standard path optimization (e.g., A-star) is applied to find a collision-free route from start to goal configuration.

This paper presents a novel algorithm for generating an optimal convex cover (Safe Flight Corridor or SFC) of collision-free space to enable efficient trajectory generation for autonomous robots like quadrotors. The approach addresses a key limitation of existing methods: the greedy selection of convex polytopes (or ellipsoids) that does not account for the downstream trajectory optimization, leading to suboptimal paths.

The key components of the method are:
- **Problem Formulation**: The authors formulate SFC generation as a joint optimization problem involving ellipsoids, polytopes, and intermediate waypoints. The goal is to find a sequence of overlapping convex sets (polytopes) with maximum volume that cover a given geometric path, while also optimizing for trajectory cost.
- **Algorithm**: The authors propose an iterative algorithm inspired by the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) with partially distributed variables. The proposed method consistently achieves lower worst-case trajectory cost with similar computational time.
- **Results**: Ellipsoid and polytope volumes grow consistently with each iteration, reaching more than 90% of maximum volumes within 5-10 iterations. The method demonstrates improved performance in complex environments (e.g., narrow mazes) and over longer start-to-end distances.

--- SOURCE 15: Graph of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/graph-of-convex-sets-gcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) is a mathematical framework that associates graph vertices with convex sets to integrate combinatorial properties and convex optimization. It encodes structural constraints through convex graph invariants and invariant convex sets, enabling efficient relaxations such as spectral and semidefinite programming (SDP) methods. The framework unifies problems like graph deconvolution, hypothesis testing, and graph generation by leveraging robust optimization and permutation symmetry.

**Foundations:** Convex graph invariants are real-valued functions f defined on adjacency matrices that are convex and invariant under vertex relabelings. Examples include sum of edge weights, maximum node degree, MAXCUT value (via SDP relaxation), and spectral invariants like sum of the k largest eigenvalues. These invariants can be enforced via convex constraints to form invariant convex sets.

**Representation:** Every convex graph invariant can be expressed as a supremum over elementary convex graph invariants. Direct computation is NP-hard (equivalent to Quadratic Assignment Problem), but tractable spectral relaxations (replacing permutations with orthogonal group) and SDP relaxations provide efficient approximations.

**Applications:**
- Graph deconvolution posed as convex optimization over convex hulls
- Hypothesis testing between graph families via linear functional optimization
- Graph generation by constructing matrices in intersections of invariant convex sets

**Key insight:** The convex hull of a graph under node permutation actions serves as the minimal invariant convex set, analogous to uncertainty sets in robust optimization. This bridges the discrete/continuous divide and allows application of convex analysis tools to combinatorial domains.

**Limitations:** Information loss from convex relaxations (aggregate vs. pointwise properties), computational challenges for large graphs, and ongoing research into tighter relaxation guarantees.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Autonomy Talks - Tobia Marcucci: A Tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS)

## Overview
Prof. Tobia Marcucci (UCSB, ECE and Mechanical Engineering) presented a tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), an optimization framework developed during his PhD at MIT and refined at Amazon. The talk was delivered on November 18, 2025, as part of the Autonomy Talks series.

## Core Problem
Many robotics problems require simultaneous optimization of high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous control. Examples include:
- Atlas robot parkour (sequence of obstacles + continuous trajectories)
- Robot manipulation (making/breaking contacts + object positions)
- UAV trajectory optimization with obstacles (left/right decisions + continuous trajectories)
- Warehouse pick-and-place (object sorting + trajectory optimization)

## What is a Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)?
A GCS is a graph where:
- **Vertices** are paired with convex optimization problems (continuous variable Xv, convex constraint set, objective function)
- **Edges** couple vertex optimization problems through additional convex costs and constraints
- Unlike ordinary weighted graphs, weights are not fixed scalars but functions of underlying continuous variables

## Key Advantages
1. **Unified framework** bridging discrete and continuous optimization
2. **Leverages existing tools**: combines graph search/optimization (scalable) with convex optimization (mature continuous optimization technology)
3. **Accessible**: users define the graph structure, variables, and constraints; the framework handles the optimization automatically

## Problem Classes
Classical graph problems naturally generalize to GCS:
- Shortest Path in GCS
- Traveling Salesman Problem in GCS
- Minimum Spanning Tree in GCS
- Facility location, bipartite matching, etc.

## Solution Approach
Most GCS problems are NP-hard. The framework formulates them as Mixed Integer Convex Programs (MICP) by:
1. Encoding the graph structure using incidence vectors (binary variables for vertices/edges)
2. Translating GCS constraints using binary variables to activate/deactivate relevant parts
3. Convexifying bilinear constraints exactly (leveraging binary variable structure)
4. Efficiency depends on the tightness of the convex relaxation

## Applications Demonstrated
- **Solar-powered helicopter path planning**: shortest path through islands with recharging, solved in 24 seconds (convex relaxation gives 99%+ accuracy in fraction of a second)
- **School bus routing with mobile passengers**: Traveling Salesman variant where children can move to meet the bus
- **Camera surveillance placement**: Minimum Spanning Tree variant ensuring camera visibility
- **Motion planning and collision avoidance**: Shortest path through obstacles

## Software Tool
**GCSOPT**: Open-source Python library for solving real-world GCS problems in just a few lines of code. Handles the mathematical complexity automatically behind the scenes.

## Key Quote
The research addresses "the observation that at the core of many robotics problems is the need to simultaneously optimize high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous decisions."
</summary>

This is a PhD dissertation by João Luiz Dihl Comba, presented to Stanford University's Department of Computer Science in September 2000, supervised by Leonidas J. Guibas. The thesis introduces the Kinetic Vertical Decomposition Tree (KVD-tree), a novel data structure for dynamically maintaining visibility information for moving objects in 3D space.

The KVD-tree is a specialized type of Binary Space Partition (BSP) tree that represents a vertical decomposition of space. Key features include: (1) dynamic maintenance of visibility, (2) representation of a vertical space decomposition, (3) collision detection among moving objects, and (4) kinetic maintenance using the kinetic data structures framework.

The work addresses the challenge of computing visibility for moving objects - a computationally expensive problem important for graphics rendering, animation, and motion planning. The KVD-tree uses additional cuts from edges and vertices to form a vertical decomposition induced by the polygonal model. Certificates are created that indicate when object movement causes changes in the decomposition, allowing local updates to the tree structure.

The dissertation covers: BSP concepts and operations, kinetic data structures framework, KVD representation and construction, events and certificates for detecting combinatorial changes, update algorithms for structural modifications, and implementation results showing KVD-tree statistics for construction, certificates, and simulations. The structure supports occlusion culling, shadow computation, and collision detection, with applications in dynamic visibility problems for computer graphics.

# BSP Tree FAQ Summary

This document is the **Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) Tree Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)**, originally maintained by Bretton Wade at Silicon Graphics, Inc. (SGI). As of 2001-09-20, it appears to be no longer maintained, with the latest copy on ftp.sgi.com.

## What is a BSP Tree?
A Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) tree is a standard binary tree data structure that represents a recursive, hierarchical subdivision of n-dimensional space into convex subspaces. Each node stores a "hyperplane" (a plane in 3D, a line in 2D) that divides the space into two halves, with child nodes representing each half. BSP trees are used for hidden surface removal, ray tracing, solid modeling, collision detection, and robot motion planning. They are closely related to Quadtrees and Octrees.

## Key Applications

1. **Hidden Surface Removal (Painter's Algorithm)**: BSP trees sort polygons via a depth-first tree walk. By drawing polygons far from the eye first, then those closer, hidden surfaces are overwritten. Runtime is O(n) expected case, but worst-case O(n²) for autopartitions.

2. **Ray Tracing Acceleration**: Uses a forward tree walk. Unlike other applications, ray tracing does not require splitting primitives, so hyperplanes should be chosen for tree balance.

3. **Boolean Operations on Polytopes**: Supports union, intersection, and difference operations by inserting polytopes incrementally into the tree and classifying segments as inside/outside.

4. **Collision Detection**: Treats motion segments as rays to intersect with the BSP tree, or uses recursive midpoint subdivision for speed.

5. **Dynamic Scenes**: Static objects are pre-built into the tree; dynamic objects are inserted as points each frame, then expanded during traversal.

6. **Robot Motion Planning**: Builds an "exact cell decomposition" of free space, creating a planning graph for A* style search.

## Building a BSP Tree
The algorithm is simple: (1) Select a partition plane, (2) Partition the set of polygons with the plane, (3) Recurse with each of the two new sets. Partition planes are often chosen from the input polygon set (autopartition). The choice involves trade-offs between tree balance and polygon splitting.

## Efficiency
- **Space complexity**: Worst-case O(n²) for autopartitions, but expected O(n)
- **Time complexity**: Same as space complexity for rendering
- Construction of an optimal tree is NP-complete
- Balancing is important for spatial classification (ray tracing, solid modeling) but less critical for hidden surface removal

SUMMARY:

Binary space partitioning (BSP) is a computer science method for recursively subdividing a Euclidean space into two convex sets using hyperplanes, producing a tree data structure known as a BSP tree. Developed in the context of 3D computer graphics in 1969, BSP trees are useful for rendering because they efficiently provide spatial information about objects in a scene, enabling front-to-back or back-to-front ordering relative to a viewer. Key applications include: performing geometrical operations with shapes (constructive solid geometry) in CAD, collision detection in robotics and 3D video games, ray tracing, and virtual landscape simulation.

**History (key milestones):**
- 1969: Schumacker et al. first described using positioned planes to accelerate polygon ordering in flight simulators (manual scene design).
- 1980: Fuchs et al. automated the process using planes coincident with polygons to recursively partition 3D space, creating the BSP Tree algorithm.
- 1987: Thibault and Naylor described representing arbitrary polyhedra using BSP trees, enabling constructive solid geometry (CSG) — the forerunner of BSP level design using "brushes" in Quake and Unreal editors.
- 1990: Naylor, Amanatides, and Thibault provided an algorithm for merging two BSP trees, enabling combining moving objects with static environments, efficient CSG operations, and exact collision detection.
- 1991: Gordon and Chen described efficient front-to-back rendering from a BSP tree, used by John Carmack in Doom.
- 1993: Naylor characterized what makes a good BSP tree using expected case models.

**Generation:** The canonical BSP tree is constructed from an unsorted list of polygons. The recursive algorithm: (1) Choose a polygon P, (2) Make a node N and add P to it, (3) For each other polygon, classify it as in front of P, behind P, intersected by P (split into two), or coplanar with P, (4) Apply the algorithm recursively to the front and back lists. The choice of partitioning plane is important for efficiency and balance.

**Traversal:** A BSP tree is traversed in linear time. For the painter's algorithm, the traversal order ensures all polygons behind a plane are drawn first, then the plane's polygons, then those in front. The algorithm checks the viewer's location relative to each node to determine traversal order.

**Applications:** BSP trees are widely used by 3D video games, particularly first-person shooters with indoor environments (Doom, Quake, GoldSrc, Source engines). They are often used together with a Z-buffer to correctly merge movable objects onto the background scene. BSP trees have also been applied to image compression.

This tutorial from the Apache Commons Geometry project (version 1.0, last published August 20, 2021) provides a comprehensive introduction to Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) trees and their use in the Commons Geometry library.

### Key Concepts
- BSP trees recursively partition space using hyperplanes (lines in 2D, planes in 3D, etc.)
- Each node has a "cut" hyperplane that splits the node's space into two child nodes
- Leaf nodes are marked as "inside" or "outside" the represented region
- The full region consists of the union of all "inside" leaf nodes

1. Creating a Precision.DoubleEquivalence instance for floating-point comparisons

**Top-Down Construction (Preferred):** Inserting hyperplane convex subsets (segments, rays, etc.) into the top of the tree. Boundaries propagate down through the tree, being split at each internal node until reaching a leaf node. This approach requires less code.

- Convex regions produce unbalanced, linked-list-like trees that degrade performance with many sides

**IK vs Differential IK:** Differential IK works well for incremental motions; IK solves more global problems but isn't guaranteed to succeed. IK can switch between distinct solutions (e.g., going around an obstacle on either side), while differential IK cannot make such leaps.

**Collision Avoidance:** Minimum-distance constraints can only be enforced at discrete samples along the path, not for all time. The author suggests adding constraints at modest sampling during optimization, then checking more densely before execution.

**Sampling-Based Motion Planning:** The author notes these methods provide probabilistic completeness but struggle with derivative constraints and high dimensions. References LaValle06 and the Open Motion Planning Library.

**Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS):** A framework bridging trajectory optimization and sampling-based planning. GCS generalizes shortest-path problems on graphs by allowing each vertex to have an associated convex set from which a point is selected. The motion planning application uses convex decompositions of collision-free space. The resulting mixed-integer convex programs have strong convex relaxations, often solving to optimality without needing the full MICP. SUMMARY:

This tutorial explains how to use the point cloud region growing segmentation algorithm implemented in PCL (Point Cloud Library)'s `pcl::RegionGrowing` class. The algorithm merges points that are close in terms of smoothness constraint, producing clusters where each cluster represents points belonging to the same smooth surface. It works by comparing angles between point normals.

**Algorithm Overview:**
1. Points are sorted by curvature value; growth starts from the point with minimum curvature (located in flattest area) to reduce total segments.
2. For each seed point, neighboring points are found. If the angle between the neighbor's normal and the seed's normal is below a threshold, the neighbor is added to the current region. If the neighbor's curvature is below a threshold, it becomes a new seed.
3. When seeds are empty, the region is complete and the process repeats for remaining unlabeled points.

**Key Parameters:**
- Smoothness threshold: maximum allowable angle deviation between normals (set to 3.0 degrees in example)
- Curvature threshold: maximum curvature difference for continuing growth (set to 1.0)
- Minimum/maximum cluster size: clusters outside this range are discarded (min=50, max=1,000,000 in example)

URL: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8220/19/19/4165

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in the journal Sensors (2019) proposing a new convex decomposition method for coverage path planning (CPP) for autonomous vehicles, particularly UAVs.

**Context:** Coverage path planning is essential for autonomous vehicles to systematically cover an area of interest. While simple convex polygons can be easily covered using a back-and-forth (boustrophedon) method, concave polygons and areas with obstacles require decomposition into convex sub-polygons.

**Proposed Method (Interior Extension of Edges):** The method is based on the idea that convex decomposition mainly occurs at points where the interior angle between two edges exceeds 180 degrees. The algorithm:
1. Extends edges at concave vertices (interior angle > 180°) until they hit the polygon boundary or an obstacle
2. Generates initial convex sub-polygons from these extensions
3. Merges adjacent sub-polygons when the result remains convex, solving a set partitioning problem (Integer Programming model) to minimize the total width of sub-polygons
4. Uses an approximation scheme (Algorithm 1) to reduce computational complexity when many initial sub-polygons exist

**Key Results:**
- Compared against existing methods (sweep line, dynamic programming, greedy heuristics) using illustrative polygons
- For Polygon A: The proposed method matched the best solution (from Huang's dynamic programming method) with fewer initial sub-polygons
- For Polygon B: Performance was competitive with the sweep line method (marginal gap) and outperformed the greedy heuristic
- Tested on a complicated real-world polygon (Antwerp port layout): Generated 238 initial sub-polygons in 12 seconds, found merge options in ~3 minutes, solved the IP model in 3 seconds
- The approximation scheme had a 4.3% performance gap while dramatically saving computation time

**Multi-Unit Extension:** The paper also discusses how the method can be extended to multi-UAV scenarios by reformulating the IP model as a sub-polygon assignment model for multiple vehicles, with workload balancing constraints.

**Conclusions:** The proposed method is simple, fast, applicable to any polygon shape (including rectilinear shapes), and provides competitive decomposition solutions compared to existing methods. The output is directly implementable in any flight execution system using geographic coordinates.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 23: Approximating Robot Configuration Spaces with few Convex Sets using Clique Covers of Visibility Graphs ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2310.02875v2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents an efficient method called Visibility Clique Cover (VCC) for approximately decomposing complex robot configuration spaces (𝒞^free) into a small number of convex polytopes, without human supervision. The approach works by: (1) randomly sampling points in 𝒞^free and constructing a visibility graph where edges connect points with mutual line of sight; (2) computing an approximate clique cover of this graph by solving MaxClique integer programs; (3) summarizing each clique with a minimum-volume ellipsoid; and (4) inflating these ellipsoids into large collision-free polytopes using a single iteration of IRIS/IRIS-NP. The process repeats until a target coverage fraction α is achieved.

The method is evaluated against Iterative Obstacle Seeding (IOS) on four environments: Village (2D), 3DOF Flipper, 5DOF UR3, and 7DOF IIWA robot arms. Results show VCC consistently requires fewer regions and less time to achieve target coverage. Most notably, for the 7DOF IIWA at 70% coverage, VCC uses 46.3 regions in ~5,700 seconds versus IOS using 482.6 regions in ~89,000 seconds—approximately 10x fewer regions and 16x faster.

The paper also discusses theoretical limitations: cliques in visibility graphs can enclose holes in 𝒞^free, meaning not all cliques correspond to convex sets. A modified MaxClique formulation with separation constraints is proposed to address this, though it is computationally expensive for practical use. The authors note that in practice, only ~0.1% of vertices in the first MaxClique problem were excluded from the clique that could not be separated by a hyperplane.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article (Mathematics, 2025) presenting exact and heuristic algorithms for convex polygon decomposition. The problem involves partitioning a non-convex polygon into the smallest possible number of convex subpolygons, which is a key preprocessing step in applications such as robotic motion planning, 2D packing, pattern recognition, and manufacturing.

**Authors:** Johana Milena Martínez Contreras, Germán Fernando Pantoja Benavides, Astrid Xiomara Rodríguez, John Willmer Escobar, and David Álvarez-Martínez (affiliations: Universidad de Los Andes, Colombia; Tecnologico de Monterrey, Mexico; Universidad del Valle, Colombia).

**Key Contributions:**
1. An exact convex decomposition method inspired by Keil's dynamic-programming approach (Algorithm 1), which recursively subdivides the polygon into triangles and subpolygons, evaluating candidate merges to obtain minimal convex components (complexity O(n³)).
2. A heuristic algorithm that approximates decomposition by identifying and linking notches (concave vertices), selecting vertices with high visible neighbors, and exploring three-vertex configurations.
3. A visibility-preserving bridge transformation that converts polygons with holes into equivalent simple instances, enabling decomposition of more complex topologies.
4. A convex-union post-processing phase applied to both exact and heuristic outputs to further reduce the number of convex pieces.
5. A new publicly available dataset of polygons with holes, addressing the lack of standardized benchmark instances in the literature.
6. The exact model produces optimal decompositions for small and medium instances, while the heuristic achieves near-optimal solutions with significantly reduced computation times.

**Literature Review:** The paper reviews convex decomposition applications in topographic modeling, pattern recognition, packing/nesting problems, machine learning, and multi-robot terrain coverage. Key prior methods discussed include Keil's exact dynamic programming approach, Fernández et al.'s vector-dependency procedure, and Lien and Amato's approximate convex decomposition framework for polygons with holes.

**Methodology Details:**
- Visibility is defined as the ability to connect two points with a straight segment entirely inside the polygon without intersecting edges.
- Reference vertices include all concave (reflex) vertices plus the initial and final vertices of the polygon's boundary traversal.
- The exact algorithm uses dynamic programming, solving small subproblems once and storing information to avoid repetitive iterations.
- The heuristic processes vertices in counterclockwise order (simplifying implementation), drawing partially on Fernández et al.'s method.
- For polygons with holes, a bridge construction converts holed polygons into equivalent simple polygons while preserving structural relations.

**Algorithm 1 (Exact Convex Decomposition):** Input is vertex coordinates; output is coordinates of convex parts. Steps include computing angles, determining notches (concave vertices), finding visibility of vertices, ordering subpolygons, determining base triangles, and using dynamic programming to find minimum convex decomposition.

**Algorithm 2 (Visibility Between Points):** Determines which points are mutually visible using the v1v2 function, which evaluates the position of one point with respect to lines formed by another point, considering collinearity and intersection checks.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Russ Tedrake: Motion Planning Around Obstacles with Convex Optimization

## Overview
This is a talk given by Russ Tedrake (Toyota Professor at MIT, VP of Robotics Research at Toyota Research Institute) at the TAU CG Seminar on January 18, 2023. The talk presents new work on motion planning using convex optimization, captured in two papers: a general optimization framework for "shortest path in graphs of convex sets" and a specific application to motion planning.

## Key Problem
Traditional trajectory optimization suffers from local minima (e.g., a point robot going around a box obstacle gets stuck in one direction and cannot flip to the shorter path). Sample-based planners like RRT* converge slowly and handle dynamic constraints poorly. The goal is to combine the global optimality properties of sample-based planning with the efficiency of trajectory optimization for dynamically feasible motions.

## Three Key Ingredients
1. **Linear programming formulation of shortest path on discrete graphs** – leveraging the well-known property that the LP relaxation is tight (binary feasible).
2. **Convex formulations for continuous motion planning** – when obstacles are not present or a decision about which way to go has been made.
3. **Approximate convex decompositions of configuration space** – breaking free space into convex regions.

## Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)
The core innovation generalizes the shortest path problem: each vertex in the graph is associated with a convex set, and edge costs are convex functions of continuous variables within those sets. This is formulated as a mixed-integer convex program with a *tight convex relaxation* — meaning the convex relaxation alone often solves the global optimization problem.

Key advances:
- **Strengthening constraints** (spatial conservation of flow) added to make the convex relaxation tight, without changing the binary-feasible solution.
- The convex relaxation recovers the global optimal solution in many practical instances.
- Orders of magnitude faster than previous mixed-integer formulations for motion planning.

## Results and Applications
- **Quadrotor flight**: Solving global optimal paths through obstacle fields with dynamic constraints, minimizing time or effort.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14D configuration space)**: Two KUKA robots navigating complex configuration space obstacles, solving "Twister"-like mug rearrangement problems.
- **Footstep planning for humanoid robots**: Orders of magnitude faster than prior mixed-integer methods.
- **Maze navigation**: Continuous path optimization solved to global optimality via convex relaxation.

## Convex Decomposition of Configuration Space
The approach uses fast approximate decompositions:
- Alternating between quadratic programs and semi-definite programs to find separating hyperplanes and grow largest contained ellipsoids.
- For configuration space obstacles, uses sums-of-squares polynomial optimization to certify collision-free regions.
- Achieves surprisingly tight bounds (e.g., 7.33mm gap between two bimanual manipulators).

## Statistical Performance
In procedurally generated quadrotor environments:
- The convex optimization **often achieves true minimal cost**.
- In worst cases, the solution is guaranteed to be **within 20% of optimal**.
- The convex relaxation can certify optimality without additional branch-and-bound work in many instances.

## Open Problems
- What defines an optimal convex decomposition for this planner?
- Connections to maximum vertex hidden set problems and visibility graphs.
- Extending to non-Euclidean geometry (mobile manipulators, wrap-around effects).
- Task and motion planning integration.

## Implementation
All code is available in the open-source software **Drake** (MIT's robotics simulator and optimization library).
</summary>

This work focuses on practical solutions that preprocess a C-space through sampling to (a) build small roadmaps that can quickly return solutions, and (b) provide theoretical guarantees regarding path quality. Spanners are subgraphs where the shortest path between two nodes in the spanner is no longer than t times the shortest path in the original graph, where t is the stretch factor of the spanner. Spanners, however, only remove edges, and these methods have no obvious stopping criterion. The SPARS algorithm [5] provides asymptotic near-optimality and ensures the probability of adding new nodes to the roadmap converges to 0. This gives rise to a natural stopping criterion inspired by Visibility PRM [6]. SPARS builds in parallel an asymptotically optimal roadmap using PRM∗that includes all C-space samples, incurring high memory costs, and limiting practicality.

An implicit, exhaustive graph G(V,E) over Cfree can be deﬁned by taking all the elements of Cfree as nodes and collision free paths between them as edges. Then, a “roadmap spanner” is a subgraph GS(VS ⊂V,ES ⊂E) of G with the following properties: i) All GS nodes are connected in Cfree with a node on G.
ii) GS has the same number of connected components as G (connectivity).
iii) All shortest paths on GS are no longer than t times the corresponding shortest paths in G.
The above properties guarantee that if a query has a solution, then GS will provide asymptotically near-optimal paths for them. The shortest path between two conﬁgurations computed on GS is denoted as πS. Speciﬁcally, the following variant of asymptotic near-optimality is provided: Deﬁnition 3 (Asympt. Near-Optimality w. Additive Cost): An algorithm is asymptotically near-optimal with additive cost if, for a path planning problem (Cfree, qinit, qgoal) and cost function c : Π →R≥0 with a cl-robust optimal path of ﬁnite cost c∗, the probability it will ﬁnd a path with cost c ≤t · c∗+ ε, for a stretch factor t ≥1 and additive error ε ≥0, converges to 1 as the iterations approach inﬁnity.
IV. A PRACTICAL SPARSE ROADMAP SPANNER The proposed SPARS2 method (Algorithm 1) generates samples ρ ∈Cfree and decides if they must be added to the graph GS. If M consecutive samples are not added, where M is an input parameter, the algorithm returns GS.
The “coverage” criterion checks whether ρ is in a part of Cfree not covered by nodes VS ∈GS (Algorithm 1 lines 4-5).
SPARS2 adds ρ to GS as a new “guard” (see Figure 2a), if there are no nodes v ∈VS within a “visibility” distance, ∆, so that L(ρ,v) ∈Cfree. The “connectivity” criterion is tested in lines 8-12. Among the set N of spanner nodes which can connect to ρ, the algorithm identiﬁes those in different connected components. If there are disconnected nodes, ρ is useful as a “bridge” and is added together with the edges to the disconnected nodes.

An interface i(v1,v2) between two spanner nodes v1 and v2 is the shared boundary of their visibility regions (see Figure 2 (bottom left)). These samples must be included so that shortest paths π∗ cl ∈Cfree will be “covered”, illustrated in Figure 3. This is necessary to argue about the lengths of paths π∗ cl(ρ0,ρm) and πS(ρ0,ρm). The algorithm employs Close Interface, which attempts to directly add the edge L(v1,v2) and if this is not possible, then the sample ρ is added together with the edges L(ρ,v1) and L(ρ,v2).
Lines 18-26 of the algorithm serve to uphold the spanner property for GS. In relation to Figure 3, SPARS2 has to make sure that for each shortest path π∗ cl(ρi,ρi+1) between points on the interfaces, the corresponding “midpoint” path Mi satisﬁes the spanner property. The algorithm reasons over shortest paths between samples supporting interfaces.

For reasons detailed in Section V (Lemma 3 - case two), it is necessary to consider all paths between midpoints m(v,r) and m(v,r′′), where r′′ is a neighbor of v not connected to r but connected to r′. Among all such paths, ΠS, the longest, πS, is tested if it violates the spanner property relative to d(ρ,ρ′) (line 11).
If so, the spanner is extended. If a shortcut from r to r′ exists in Cfree (line 12), then only this edge needs to be added to GS. Otherwise, the algorithm employs a smoothing operation over a path from the sample σ along interface i(v,r) to ρ, then to v, ρ′ and eventually σ′ along interface i(v,r′) (lines 14-17).
V. PROPERTIES OF SPARS2 SPARS2 and SPARS are equivalent to Visibility PRM in terms of coverage and connectivity; thus, it is possible to argue [5], [6] that SPARS2 is probabilistically complete: Theorem 1 (Probabilistic Completeness): For all ρ ∈Cfree : ∃v ∈VS so that L(ρ,v) ∈Cfree, and For all v,v′ ∈VS with a collision-free path in Cfree, ∃πS(v,v′) which connects them on GS with probability 1 as M goes to inﬁnity in SPARS2.
The method also makes two assumptions: Assumption 1: For v,v′ ∈Cfree, if the set of conﬁgurations q for which L(q,v) ∈Cfree, L(q,v′) ∈Cfree, d(q,v) < ∆and d(q,v′) < ∆is non-empty, then it has non-zero measure.
Assumption 2: No sample ρ is within distance cl from obstacles. No v ∈VS is within cl-distance from obstacles.
SPARS and SPARS2 deviate on (a) how they detect pairs of nodes that share an interface (for criterion 3) and (b) estimating shortest paths in Cfree between interfaces (for criterion 4). Note that interfaces often have complex shape due to obstacles and are hard to explicitly represent.
SPARS2 ensures every two spanner nodes that share an interface also eventually share an edge in lines 14-16: Theorem 2 (Connected Interfaces): For all v1,v2 ∈VS which share an interface, then L(v1,v2) ∈ES with probability 1 as M goes to inﬁnity in SPARS2.
The above theorem is straightforward to prove, and the core of this proof relies on the fact that there is a non-zero measure set of conﬁgurations for any pair of vertices, v1,v2, which share an interface, such that all points in this set have v1 and v2 as their closest guards and are also visible. This implies samples will eventually be generated in this set, and the algorithm will bridge the interface.
SPARS2 relies on sampling rather than the dense graph to pinpoint interfaces, necessary for the last criterion. This increases computation time for construction, which will be exacerbated in high-dimensional spaces, though not main-taining the dense graph helps balance this cost. The following lemmas argue that optimal paths in Cfree will be represented by GS, which satisﬁes the spanner property.
Lemma 1 (Coverage of Optimal Paths by GS): For opti-mal path π∗ cl(ρ0,ρm), the probability of having a sequence of nodes, Vπ = (v1,v2,...,vn) ∈GS with the following properties goes to 1 as M goes to inﬁnity: • ∀ρ ∈π∗ cl(ρ0,ρm), ∃v ∈Vπ : L(ρ,v) ∈Cfree • L(ρ0,v1) ∈Cfree and L(ρm,vn) ∈Cfree • ∀vi,vi+1 ∈Vπ,L(vi,vi+1) ∈ES.
The above lemma follows from Theorems 1 and 2. Con-sider a decomposition of path πS(ρ0,ρm) in GS through Vπ into sub-paths {M0,M1,...,Mm−1} (Figure 3(right)), where Mi is the path between m(vi,vi+1) and m(vi+1,vi+2). M0 con-nects ρ0 to v1, and m(v1,v2) and Mm−1 is the corresponding last segment. The following can be easily shown: Lemma 2 (Additive Connection Cost): The length of paths M0 and Mm−1 for a path through GS connecting ρ0 to ρm is upper bounded by 4·∆.
The important property, however, of segments Mi is: Lemma 3 (Spanner Property of GS over Cfree): All Mi have length bounded by t · |π∗ cl(ρi−1,ρi)|, where ρi lies at the intersection of π∗ cl(ρ0,ρm) with interface i(vi,vi+1).
Proof Figures 4 and 5 support this proof. Given Lemma 1, the edges L(vi−1,vi) and L(vi,vi+1) are in ES, at least as M goes to inﬁnity. Assuming π∗ cl travels through the region of node vi ∈Vπ, there are three possible cases: (a) Fig. 4.
(left) The path from i(vi−1,vi) to i(vi,vi+1) via GS must satisfy the spanner property for path π∗ γ . (right) If there is a path between vi’s neighbors, then the paths πa = π(m(vi−2,vi−1),v,m(vi−1,vi+1)) and πb = π(m(vi+2,vi+1),v,m(vi+1,vi−1)) must be checked against π∗ α and π∗ β .
L(vi−1,vi+1) / ∈ES (Figure 4(left)), (b) L(vi−1,vi+1) ∈ES (Figure 4(right)), and (c) L(vi−1,vi+1) ∈ES and L(vi−2,vi) ∈ ES or L(vi,vi+2) ∈ES (Figure 5).
For case one, SPARS2 checks |Mi| against |π∗ cl(ρi−1,ρi)|.
SPARS asymptotically approximates the optimal path π∗ cl(ρi−1,ρi) via the dense graph; however, SPARS2 ap-plies a conservative approximation by checking the distance d(ρi−1,ρi) (Algorithm 4 lines 4-11) utilizing the information stored in P v(r,r′). If |Mi| > t ·d(ρi−1,ρi), Algorithm 4 adds a shortcut path: either L(vi−1,vi+1) leading to proof case two, or a path including σ and σ′, which would change the representative sequence Vπ.

In the case that vi depends on its neighbors for checking the spanner property which in turn rely on vi, it must be that |πe| < |πb|.
The second case ad-dresses the issue that |π∗ cl(ρi−1,ρi)| could be arbitrarily close to 0.
In lines 8-9 of Algo-rithm 4, the method com-pares d(ρi−1,ρi) not only with the segment Mi, but also considers all spanner paths from i(vi−1,vi) to the interfaces of all neigh-bors of vi, which are not connected to vi−1 but share an interface with vi+1. If they do, then it does not matter if segment Mi−1 satisﬁes the spanner property for path π∗ γ , because πa and πb cover all three consecutive subpaths of the optimum path.
The last case, illustrated in Figure 5, has two subcases: the solution returned from vi−2 to vi+2 does so through path πa,b,c or through path πd,e, f . Return path πa,b,c is handled by case two of this proof. For path πd,e, f , it is necessary to show that |πe| ≤t · (|π∗ α| + |π∗ β| + |π∗ γ |). An important goal of SPARS2 is to create a sparse data structure, which is supported by the following theorem: Theorem 4 (Cessation of Node Addition): As the number of iterations of SPARS2 increases, the probability of adding a node to GS goes to 0.
There are four methods for adding nodes to GS; thus, all must be shown to have no reason to add nodes to GS.
Nodes for coverage and connectivity will stop being added for reasons identical to SPARS. Theorem 2 argues that SPARS2 stops adding nodes for bridging interfaces. Nodes for ensuring path quality will stop being added due to a check in Algorithm 4, line 12.
VI. SIMULATIONS Simulations were run in the Open Motion Planning Li-brary (OMPL) [7], using the “2D Maze” (SE2) and “Bug-trap”(SE3) environments, over parameters δ = 0.5, ∆= 15, and t=(2,3,5,9), recording the maximum consecutive failures, M. Data points were taken at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 minutes and compared with PRM∗.

Figure 6 compares path quality of SPARS and SPARS2 relative to the best PRM∗ solution computed after 32 minutes.
Path quality improves over construction time, as expected, but moreover, SPARS2 produces very high-quality paths early on, even for large stretch factors.
Furthermore, paths produced by SPARS2 have lower cost than SPARS. Figure 7 (left) measures memory requirements of the ﬁnal roadmap spanner.
SPARS2 results in slightly larger spanners than SPARS, but are orders of magnitude smaller than PRM∗.
It also shows the average path degradation is signiﬁcantly smaller than the theoretical guarantees.
The maximum consecutive failures to add nodes through time is shown in Figure 7 (right). This value increases, which is critical for the stopping criterion. Figure 8 details memory requirements for SPARS2 in comparison to SPARS Fig. 7.

For online query resolution, the algorithms need only the ﬁnal planning structure to answer queries, with memory requirements shown in Figure 8 (right).
Figure 9 reports path quality and query resolution times for different construction times in SE(3). Overall, path quality for both SPARS and SPARS2 are shown to improve over time, though SPARS2 returns paths of higher quality than SPARS. The query times for the algorithms correlate to the size of the graph, giving both spanner methods a signiﬁcant advantage.
VII. DISCUSSION SPARS2 is presented as an approach for solving path planning problems in continuous conﬁguration spaces, which provides asymptotic near-optimality and greatly reduces memory requirements upon construction versus previous methods while maintaining theoretical guarantees on the rate of node addition. It removes a dependence on a dense graph representation of the space, instead relying on properties of visibility utilized by localized sampling and smoothing pro-cesseses. The resulting graph spanner provides high quality paths, which are better than theoretical bounds suggest, even early during its execution.
Open questions in this line of work include: (i) Extend-ing the given properties to graphs with directed edges; a necessary requirement for motion-constrained systems. The current work relies on a BVP solver, which is often unavail-able for interesting systems. (ii) Showing GS converges to a ﬁnite structure, as the given properties cannot guarantee this. (iii) It would be exciting to compute a conﬁdence value of attaining near-optimal paths in ﬁnite time. (iv) It is relevant to know whether the method ﬁnds important homotopic classes compared to other methods which focus Fig. 9.
Path quality at various times during execution(left) and query resolution times (right) in SE(3) for commonly solved queries.
on this issue [15]. (v) The selection of t and ∆to tune results still requires investigation, as the dependence on these parameters as well as δ is still unclear. (vi) Overall optimization of the method to reduce collision-checking calls and other expensive operations will speed up the method.

args.summary: This paper by Dobson and Bekris (Rutgers University) presents SPARS2, an extension of the SPARS algorithm for building sparse roadmap spanners in motion planning. SPARS2 provides probabilistic completeness and asymptotic near-optimality while dramatically reducing memory requirements during construction compared to prior methods. The key innovation is that SPARS2 does not require building a dense underlying roadmap (PRM∗) in parallel with the spanner, unlike its predecessor SPARS. Instead, it uses localized sampling and auxiliary information to determine when to add nodes for coverage, connectivity, interfaces, or shortcuts. The algorithm maintains the property that the probability of adding new nodes converges to zero as iterations increase, enabling a natural stopping criterion. The paper provides theoretical analysis proving probabilistic completeness, connected interfaces, and asymptotic near-optimality with additive cost. Experimental results in SE(2) and SE(3) environments (using OMPL's "2D Maze" and "Bugtrap") show SPARS2 uses approximately two orders of magnitude less memory during offline construction than SPARS or PRM∗, while returning competitive quality paths that often exceed theoretical guarantees. SPARS2 produces slightly denser final spanners than SPARS but still orders of magnitude smaller than PRM∗, leading to very efficient online query resolution. Key parameters include stretch factor t, visibility distance ∆, and sampling parameters δ and k.

<webpage_content>
Sparse Roadmap Spanners for Asymptotically Near-Optimal Motion Planning Andrew Dobson, Kostas E. Bekris Abstract Asymptotically optimal planners, such as PRM∗, guarantee that solutions approach optimal as the number of iterations increases. Roadmaps with this property, however, may grow too large for storing on resource-constrained robots and for achieving efﬁcient online query resolution. By relaxing optimality, asymptotically near-optimal planners produce sparser graphs by not including all edges. The idea stems from graph spanners, which produce sparse subgraphs that guarantee near-optimality. Existing asymptotically optimal and near-optimal planners, however, include all sampled conﬁgurations as roadmap nodes, meaning only inﬁnite-size graphs have the desired properties. To address this limitation, this work describes SPARS, an algorithm that returns a sparse roadmap spanner. The method provides the following properties: (a) probabilistic completeness, (b) asymptotic near-optimality and (c) the probability of adding nodes to the spanner converges to zero as iterations increase. The last point suggests that ﬁnite-size data structures with asymptotic near-optimality in continuous spaces may indeed exist. The approach builds simultaneously a dense graph similar to PRM∗and its roadmap spanner, meaning that upon construction an inﬁnite-size graph is still needed asymptotically. An extension of SPARS is also presented, termed SPARS2, which removes the dependency on building a dense graph for constructing the sparse roadmap spanner and for which it is shown that the same desirable properties hold. Simulations for rigid body motion planning show that algorithms for constructing sparse roadmap spanners indeed provide small data structures and result in faster query resolution. The rate of node addition is shown to decrease over time and practically the quality of solutions is considerably better than the theoretical bounds. Upon construction, the memory requirements of SPARS2 are signiﬁcantly smaller but there is a small sacriﬁce in the size of the ﬁnal spanner relative to SPARS.
Keywords sampling-based motion planning, asymptotic optimality, near-optimality, roadmap spanners 1 Introduction An important motion planning challenge is the iden-tiﬁcation of compact graphical representations for an-swering shortest-path queries in conﬁguration spaces (C-spaces) of moving systems (Latombe, 1991; Agarwal, 2011). There is a broad range of applications, which can beneﬁt from compact data structures that provide high-quality paths. One example is cloud-enabled, resource-constrained robots, where preprocessing can be per-formed ofﬂine on a computing cloud and the ﬁnal plan-ning structure is communicated wirelessly to individual robots (Kuffner, 2010).
The resulting structure should be small so as to minimize strain on the communication network and the robot. Planning among dynamic obsta-cles can also utilize such planning structures to quickly recompute paths once old ones have been invalidated by a moving obstacle (Kallman and Mataric, 2004). Another application is in the game industry, where small compu-tational budgets are given to path planning, necessitat-ing a structure which is queried quickly and returns high-quality paths (Geraerts and Overmars, 2006). This work describes how to generate such compact data-structures, which return high-quality paths. The objective is to show that these structures are practical and can be constructed in a time and memory efﬁcient manner, while it is also possible to prove desirable theoretical guarantees.
Sampling-based motion planners (Choset et al., 2005; LaValle, 2006), and especially roadmap methods, such as the Probabilistic Roadmap Method (PRM) (Kavraki et al., 1996), are particularly appropriate in this context. These methods build during a preprocessing phase a discrete Computer Science Department, Rutgers University, NJ, USA.
Corresponding author: Kostas Bekris, Computer Science, Rutgers University, 110 Frelinghuy-sen Road, Piscataway, NJ, 08854, USA.
Email: kostas.bekris at cs.rutgers.edu 1 Figure 1: A roadmap spanner in the SE(3) “Beam Site” environment, loaded in the OMPL software package (S ¸ucan et al., 2012). Conﬁgurations for a table moving along a solution path are highlighted.
representation of a C-space, in the form of a roadmap, that can then be used to answer motion planning queries.
To achieve online efﬁciency, they should return a small, sparse roadmap that can be queried quickly, and returns paths which are close to optimal. In general continuous spaces, however, only asymptotic optimality can be pro-vided, where the solution converges to the optimum as more preprocessing time is provided. A recent result de-scribes the conditions under which sampling-based plan-ners, such as PRM∗(Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011), con-verge to asymptotically optimal solutions. While these methods provide very desirable properties regarding path quality, the resulting graph is not compact and can get very large to store on a resource-constrained robot or to efﬁciently query on the ﬂy. Moreover, it is not clear when to stop the sampling process.
Recent efforts have attempted to address this issue by relaxing optimality requirements (Marble and Bekris, 2011a) and drawing inspiration from work on graph span-ners (Peleg and Sch¨ affer, 1989). Spanners are subgraphs where the shortest path between two nodes is no longer than t times the shortest path on the original graph.
The parameter t is called the stretch factor of the span-ner. An incremental integration of asymptotically optimal roadmaps with graph spanners results in efﬁcient roadmap spanners that provide asymptotic near-optimality (Mar-ble and Bekris, 2011b). Spanners, however, only remove edges, and the resulting roadmaps, similar to asymptot-ically optimal solutions, still need to include every C-space sample as a node to achieve this property.
The current contribution extends this line of work and develops practical methods for computing sparse roadmap spanners with asymptotic near-optimality guar-antees through a C-space sampling process. The result-ing structure is sparse, in the sense that it does not include the vast majority of C-space points as nodes and also in-cludes a small number of edges relative to asymptotically optimal roadmaps. Note that the notion of sparsity in this work deviates from its standard use in graph theory (lin-ear number of edges as a function of the number of nodes).
The proposed planners identify appropriate criteria for se-lecting which samples are needed in the sparse roadmap spanner while upholding theoretical guarantees regarding path quality. The asymptotic near-optimality guarantees are appropriately adapted relative to previous contribu-tions to include an additive term in order to achieve the desired sparsity in the size of the data structure. In partic-ular, the planners for constructing sparse roadmap span-ners presented in this work have the following properties: (i) probabilistic completeness, (ii) asymptotic near-optimality with additive cost, i.e., the resulting roadmap can answer any path planning query in the C-space with paths of length: t · c∗+ 4 · ∆, (1) where t and ∆are input parameters to the algorithm, c∗ is the cost of the optimum path, if one exists, between the query points in Cfree with clearance at least cl and (iii) asymptotic sparsity, i.e., the probability of adding new nodes and edges converges to 0 as the number of it-erations increases.
This framework is a candidate solution to the prob-lem of ﬁnding a compact representation for answer-ing shortest-path queries in continuous spaces.
To the best of the author’s knowledge, no previous line of work argues about the existence of ﬁnite data structures with some form of near-optimality guarantee for con-tinuous path planning.
This work provides an indica-tion that such data structures can be created.
Further-more, an important advantage of this framework is that it gives rise to a natural stopping criterion inspired by the Visibility −based PRM approach (Simeon et al., 2000). The criterion relates to a probabilistic measure of how close the roadmap is to a solution that provides the desired properties.
This paper ﬁrst describes the overall framework for 2 Figure 2: The four types of samples ρ ∈C-space that sparse roadmap spanners are considering for addition. Nodes may be added for coverage (guards), connectivity (bridges), or to connect nodes which share an “interface” (interface nodes), or to satisfy near-optimality constraints when efﬁcient C-space paths (ρ to ρ′) are found (shortcuts).
building sparse roadmap spanners. Figure 2 shows the conditions under which conﬁgurations are included in the spanner. It has to be they are useful for coverage or con-nectivity or that they improve the quality of paths on the sparse roadmap spanner relative to optimum paths in the obstacle-free C-space. Given this framework, the paper then introduces a concrete implementation, called SPARS, that constructs in parallel to the spanner an asymptotically optimal dense graph using PRM∗that includes all C-space samples. The overall approach deviates from a straight-forward integration of PRM∗with graph spanners. Instead it follows a novel methodology that is based on the identi-ﬁcation of boundaries of “visibility” regions for the span-ner nodes by utilizing their connectivity with dense graph nodes.
It eventually guarantees that all shortest paths between boundaries of “visibility” regions on the dense graph can be represented by paths on the spanner that are at most t times longer, which leads to Eq. 1. The parame-ters t and ∆control the sparsity of the spanner.
SPARS lends itself to an analysis that shows that it provides the desirable theoretical properties. Neverthe-less, the use of the dense graph is a signiﬁcant limita-tion.
So, while the method returns a sparse roadmap spanner with the desirable properties, its computational requirements are still signiﬁcant during construction, es-pecially in terms of memory.
For this reason, a sec-ond approach, SPARS2, is also presented that extends the previous one and is shown to provide the same theoret-ical guarantees without explicitly maintaining the dense graph. In SPARS2, the process for adding samples to the sparse roadmap spanner for coverage or connectivity is the same as it does not depend on the dense graph. On the other hand, “shortcut” nodes do require C-space shortest path information. This work shows that it is possible to re-lax the requirements for adding such nodes, i.e., add more nodes than needed for the desired near-optimality guaran-tees, so that the dense graph is not needed. The method introduces some conservative approximations of shortest paths in the C-space, computed through a local sampling process and bookkeeping information. The space require-ments of this bookkeeping is a ﬁnite function of the num-ber of spanner nodes. Since the probability of adding new nodes converges to zero, the probability of increasing the bookkeeping data also goes to zero.
Simulations were performed on the Open Motion Plan-ning Library (OMPL) (S ¸ucan et al., 2012) to evaluate the proposed framework and its two instantiations, SPARS and SPARS2, against the asymptotically optimal PRM∗. The experiments indicate that, during construction, SPARS2 is using a signiﬁcantly smaller amount of memory. The re-turned spanner has similar sparsity characteristics as the one returned by SPARS, alas with a small sacriﬁce in size (i.e., SPARS returns a smaller sparse roadmap spanner than SPARS2, since it has access to the dense graph and doesn’t follow as conservative approximations for shortest paths in the C-space). For both algorithms, the resulting graph is orders of magnitude smaller than the asymptotically op-timal roadmap for the same construction time. Interest-ingly, paths returned by the spanners are very competi-tive to those computed by PRM∗for the same amount of construction time and signiﬁcantly better than the theoret-ical guarantees. Online query resolution times are very efﬁcient on sparse roadmap spanners and are signiﬁcantly shorter than query resolution on the output of PRM∗for competitive path quality. Furthermore, the rate of nodes added to the spanner does decrease over time.
The next section relates this work to the state-of-the-art and is followed by a presentation of the problem state-ment and a helpful set of formal deﬁnitions and notation.
Then, the paper presents the framework for constructing sparse roadmap spanners and its theoretical analysis. The experimental results validate the properties and show the practicality of the framework and especially of SPARS2.
The paper concludes with a discussion of the methods and future research directions.
3 2 Background Piano Mover’s Problem The general mover’s problem is posed for a collection of polyhedral rigid bodies in a polyhedral workspace and is PSPACE −HARD (Reif, 1979).
A PSPACE algorithm introduced the roadmap, a 1-D subspace of C-space that captures its connectiv-ity (Canny, 1988). The algorithm, however, is imprac-tical, similarly to C-space approximations (Brooks and Lozano-P´ erez, 1983; Lozano-P´ erez, 1983; Kambhampati and Davis, 1986). A paradigm based on potential ﬁelds was developed (Khatib, 1986; Hwang and Ahuja, 1992), but complete versions of this methodology (Koditschek, 1989; Rimon and Koditschek, 1992) are difﬁcult to ap-ply in general conﬁguration spaces. A similar technique that solved difﬁcult problems took a stochastic approach to avoid local minima and motivated the development of sampling-based planners (Barraquand and Latombe, 1991; Lamiraux and Laumond, 1996).
Probabilistic Roadmaps: The ﬁrst popular method for employing a sampling strategy in order to construct a roadmap in the C-space was the Probabilistic Roadmap Method (PRM) (Kavraki et al., 1996). The algorithm sam-ples a conﬁguration in Cfree, the collision-free C-space, and adds it as a node to the roadmap. It then tries to con-nect it with a local path to its k-closest neighbors among the existing nodes (k-PRM) or those within a δ-ball (δ-PRM). If this local path, typically a straight line in the C-space, is in Cfree, an edge is added to the roadmap.
The advantages of the method lie on its simplicity, ele-gance and generality. While path non-existence cannot be proved with the PRM, probabilistic completeness can be provided instead: if a path exists, it will be found eventu-ally. This was originally proven for k-dimensional man-ifolds (Kavraki et al., 1998; Hsu et al., 1998), for non-holonomic robots (ˇ Svestka, 1997) and later for a broad class of problems (Ladd and Kavraki, 2004).
Variations of PRM: The efﬁciency of probabilistic roadmaps is dominated by the presence of “narrow pas-sages”, which require sampling from a very small set to solve them.
This motivated the development of varia-tions that appropriately sampled conﬁgurations to speed up the construction of sufﬁciently connected roadmaps (Amato et al., 1998; Hsu et al., 1998; Boor et al., 1999; Wilmarth et al., 1999; Guibas et al., 1999; Bohlin and Kavraki, 2000; Foskey et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2003; Leven and Hutchinson, 2003; Plaku et al., 2005). A num-ber of quasi-random alternatives to random sampling have also been proposed (Branicky et al., 2001) and there has been a comparative study on the subject (Geraerts and Overmars, 2003). Furthermore, the PRM framework has been adapted so as to solve a variety of different chal-lenges beyond the basic piano mover’s problem involv-ing multiple robots (S´ anchez and Latombe, 2002), ma-nipulation planning (Nielsen and Kavraki, 2000), assem-bly planning (Sundaram et al., 2001), planning for ﬂexible objects (Lamiraux and Kavraki, 2001) and bioinformatics applications (Apaydin et al., 2003).
Visibility-based PRM: A variation of PRM closely re-lated to the current work is the Visibility −based PRM (Simeon et al., 2000).
This method focuses on reject-ing speciﬁc samples while adding only those required for coverage and connectivity purposes. The combina-tion of these two properties is sufﬁcient for probabilis-tic completeness. The resulting roadmaps are small-size tree structures, because two nodes are not connected if they belong to the same connected component. Further-more, the technique provides an automatic stopping crite-rion: when M consecutive samples fail to be added to the roadmap, then a probabilistic estimation of the percentage of free space not covered by the nodes of the data structure is 1 M .
Variations Focusing on Path Quality An issue with PRM variants that employed the connected component heuristic to speed up roadmap construction is that the paths returned can often be of low quality.
This led to work that aimed to identify “useful cycles”, which adds edges between roadmap nodes if the existing path connecting the nodes is sufﬁciently lengthy (Nieuwen-huisen and Overmars, 2004). The resulting structure is no longer a tree, but remains sparse and improves path quality. The “useful cycles” criterion has been combined with the Reachability Roadmap variant of PRM to return high clearance paths in 2D and 3D C-spaces (Geraerts and Overmars, 2006). One way to improve path quality is through a post-processing, smoothing phase.
Meth-ods that reason about path homotopy provide solutions that can be smoothed to optimal ones (Jaillet and Simeon, 2006; Schmitzberger et al., 2002). Hybridization graphs can be seen as a smoothing process that combines mul-tiple solutions into a single, better quality one (Raveh et al., 2011). While such smoothing-based approaches are valid alternatives in certain cases, they construct relatively dense roadmaps and increase the online query resolution time.
Tree Sampling-based Planners: Alternatives to roadmap-based methods explore the C-space using a tree data structure by incrementally propagating paths from existing conﬁgurations, such as the popular Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) approach (LaValle and Kuffner, 2001). They tend to be more efﬁcient in quickly answering individual queries and they can be easily ap-plied to problems involving dynamics because they do not 4 algorithm edges optimal?
