## References

Supplementary Material

This document supplements the main paper *Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields*. In particular, we provide additional implementation details (Sec. [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields")), baseline comparison details (Sec. [B](#A2 "Appendix B Baseline Comparisons Details ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields")), runtime comparison with baselines (Sec. [C](#A3 "Appendix C Run time comparison with baseline methods ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields")), an alternative training objective ablation (Sec. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Ablation with Alternative Training Objectives ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields")) and more qualitative results on our proposed method (Sec. [E](#A5 "Appendix E More Results ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields")).

## Appendix A Implementation Details

### A.1 Triplet Sampling

Positives and negatives for our contrastive loss are sampled on the fly during training. For each shape, we first run marching cubes on a precomputed 2563256^{3} signed distance function grid to obtain a watertight mesh. We then uniformly sample 1024 surface points as anchor points. For each anchor point, we cast 64 random rays into the hemisphere opposite the surface normal to obtain 64 positive candidate pairs. Negative candidates are generated via rejection sampling over the surface points of the entire shape until we obtain 1024 valid negative samples for each anchor.
Triplets are then constructed by pairing positives and negatives that share the same anchor point. Specifically, for each anchor point we sample one positive pair (x,p) uniformly from the 64 positive candidates. Each positive pair is then matched with 512 negatives (x,{n})(x,\{n\}): 256 sampled uniformly and 256 selected via hard-negative mining from the pool of 1024 negative candidates. This produces triplets
(x,p,{n})(x,p,\{n\}), and the contrastive loss is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ℒ=−12[\displaystyle\mathcal{L}=-\frac{1}{2}\Bigg[ | log⁡(sim⁡(f⁡(x),f⁡(p))sim⁡(f⁡(x),f⁡(p))+∑nsim⁡(f⁡(x),f⁡(n)))\displaystyle\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{sim}\!\big(f(x),f(p)\big)}{\operatorname{sim}\!\big(f(x),f(p)\big)+\sum\_{n}\operatorname{sim}\!\big(f(x),f(n)\big)}\right) |  | (7) |
|  | +\displaystyle+ | log(sim⁡(f⁡(p),f⁡(x))sim⁡(f⁡(p),f⁡(x))+∑nsim⁡(f⁡(p),f⁡(n)))]\displaystyle\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{sim}\!\big(f(p),f(x)\big)}{\operatorname{sim}\!\big(f(p),f(x)\big)+\sum\_{n}\operatorname{sim}\!\big(f(p),f(n)\big)}\right)\Bigg] |  |

We utilize Embree [55](#bib.bib59) via pyembree to accelerate ray–mesh intersection.

### A.2 Input Preprocessing and Clustering

For all experiments except those using 3D Gaussian splats as input, we preprocess each shape into a manifold, watertight mesh following the protocol of [56](#bib.bib26). Clustering is then performed using agglomerative clustering from SciPy [54](#bib.bib58). For experiments that use 3D Gaussian splats as input, we instead operate directly on point features using K-means clustering.

### A.3 Metric Definitions

For easy comparison, we adopt the definition of the concavity metric from [58](#bib.bib9) as:

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Concavity⁡(S)=max⁡(H⁡(∂S,∂hull⁡(S)),H⁡(Vol⁡(S),Vol⁡(hull⁡(S))))\mathrm{Concavity}(S)=\max\big(H(\partial S,\,\partial\,\mathrm{hull}(S)),\;H(\mathrm{Vol}(S),\,\mathrm{Vol}(\mathrm{hull}(S)))\big) |  | (8) |

Concavity⁡(S)=max⁡(H⁡(∂S,∂hull⁡(S)),H⁡(Vol⁡(S),Vol⁡(hull⁡(S))))\mathrm{Concavity}(S)=\max\big(H(\partial S,\,\partial\,\mathrm{hull}(S)),\;H(\mathrm{Vol}(S),\,\mathrm{Vol}(\mathrm{hull}(S)))\big)

where H⁡(⋅)H(\cdot) denotes the Hausdorff distance, ∂S\partial S is the surface of SS, and Vol⁡(S)\mathrm{Vol}(S) denotes points sampled in its interior. We uniformly sample 20,000 points per component to compute this metric. For reconstruction metric, we measure mean surface Chamfer distance between original shape and the union of convex hull, we also sample 20,000 points to calculate this metrics.

## Appendix B Baseline Comparisons Details

#### BSP-Net [10](#bib.bib22)

We use the official PyTorch codebase and the released checkpoint trained on ShapeNet. In addition, we train the network on the Objaverse subset used by our model. Following the official training protocol, we train the auto-encoding network (voxel input) for 8M steps at voxel resolutions 16 and 32, and for 16M steps at resolution 64 during Phase 0. We then train for another 16M steps at resolution 64 for Phase 1. We use the default network architecture and optimizer settings.

#### Cvx-Net [14](#bib.bib23)

We use the official TensorFlow implementation. Since no pretrained checkpoint is available, we train the network separately on ShapeNet and on our Objaverse subset. The model takes 20 depth images as input. Following their original protocol, for each shape, we sample random camera positions uniformly on a sphere of radius 1.5 centered at the origin and render depth maps at a resolution of 224×224224\times 224. We train the network for 1M steps.

#### VHACD [34](#bib.bib11)

We run VHACD using the implementation in the PyBullet[11](#bib.bib24) package. All shapes are processed with a 1M-voxel approximation.
Like our approach, the algorithm allows the user to select a threshold to control the granularity of the decomposition; finer decomposition granularity generally improves quality metrics at the expense of generating more components.
For fair comparison, we follow a similar approach to [58](#bib.bib9) in selecting the threshold value and manually search for a suitable value that roughly results in the same granularity, i.e. the same number of resulting hulls.
For Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines ‣ 4.2 Baseline Comparisons ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields") and Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Ablation Study ‣ 4.3 Analysis and Ablation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields"), we use a fixed threshold of 0.01.

#### CoACD [58](#bib.bib9)

We use their official implementation in our comparisons.
Similar to VHACD, the algorithm requires specifying a threshold to control the granularity of the decomposition; finer decomposition granularity generally improves quality metrics at the expense of generating more components.
For fair comparison, we follow their evaluation protocol in selecting the threshold value and manually search for a suitable value that roughly results in the same granularity, i.e. the same number of resulting hulls.
For Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines ‣ 4.2 Baseline Comparisons ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields") and Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Ablation Study ‣ 4.3 Analysis and Ablation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning Convex Decomposition via Feature Fields"), we use a fixed threshold of 0.10.

args.key_excerpts: This work proposes a new formulation to the long-standing problem of convex decomposition through learning feature fields, enabling the first feed-forward model for open-world convex decomposition., Our key insight is to adopt a *feature learning* approach. Rather than directly optimizing or learning a discrete set of primitives, we instead operate on continuous features defined along the shape, constructing a set of features such that clustering them yields a good convex decomposition., We formulate convex decomposition as a contrastive learning problem and introduce our novel, self-supervised, geometric loss that enables scalable learning of convex decomposition on open-world data., Quantitative results show that across all datasets, our method consistently outperforms both classical and learning-based baselines in terms of concavity and reconstruction error at any given component count., Our convex approximation yields a 5x faster simulation step v.s. using the original meshes (8ms vs 40ms).
args.summary:
This research paper from NVIDIA Labs introduces a new method for convex decomposition of 3D shapes by learning feature fields, enabling the first feed-forward model for open-world convex decomposition. The key insight is reformulating convex decomposition as a contrastive feature learning problem, where continuous features are learned on the shape surface such that clustering them yields good convex decompositions.

**Methodology:**
- The approach is inspired by the classic geometric definition of convexity: a shape is convex if the line segment between any two points lies entirely within the shape.
- The authors define a self-supervised contrastive loss based on "convex pairs" (point pairs whose connecting line stays inside the shape) and "non-convex pairs" (where the line exits the shape).
- Features are learned using a triplane-encoded architecture with a PVCNN encoder and transformer backbone.
- A recursive binary clustering strategy is used at inference time, controlled by a user-specified concavity threshold for granularity control.

**Training:** Trained on ~340K filtered shapes from the Objaverse dataset on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs over one week. Feature dimensionality is 448, triplane resolution is 512×512.

**Results:**
- Outperforms both classical (V-HACD, CoACD) and learning-based (BSP-Net, Cvx-Net) baselines across all three evaluation datasets (V-HACD dataset, PartObjaverse-Tiny, ShapeNet).
- On the V-HACD dataset: 11.9 components, 0.0973 concavity, 0.0180 reconstruction error vs. next best (CoACD: 14.47 components, 0.1095 concavity, 0.0321 reconstruction).
- Generalizes to meshes, CAD models, 3D scans, and Gaussian splats.
- Enables 5x faster collision detection simulation (8ms vs 40ms).
- Inference takes ~18s total (5s feature generation + 13s recursive decomposition).

**Limitations:** Does not generalize to scene-scale or highly-incomplete geometry; struggles with complex thin structures like fan frames.

# Convex Decomposition

> **Tutorial for convex decomposition for physical simulation and toolkits for doing that**

### What is convex decomposition?[​](#what-is-convex-decomposition "Direct link to What is convex decomposition?")

Convex decomposition involves breaking down complex, non-convex shape into multiple simpler, convex shapes. Here is an example from CoACD[1](#fn-1) showing the original geometry and its corresponding convex decomposition, with each color represent a separate convex mesh.

### Why we care about convex decomposition when using simulator?[​](#why-we-care-about-convex-decomposition-when-using-simulator "Direct link to Why we care about convex decomposition when using simulator?")

In simulation, collision detection determines when objects intersect or come into contact. This is particularly important in physical simulations where interactions between objects need to be realistically modeled, such as the contact between object and gripper in robot manipulation and the contact between leg and ground in locomotion of a robot dog.

Collision detection algorithms typically involve two phases: the broad phase and the narrow phase. The broad phase identifies pairs of objects that might be colliding, while the narrow phase accurately calculates whether a collision has occurred and provides additional information like contact points and collision normals. In physics engines, collision detection can take from 10% to 50% of the total computation time, depending on the complexity of the object geometry.

Using convex meshes to represent geometry can accelerate the narrow phase of collision detection, by simplifying the collision detection process, resulting in faster collision detection algorithms compared to the algorithm handling non-convex meshes. Thus, it can enhance the overall performance of physical simulation. Moreover, many simulators automatically **convert your imported mesh into a convex hull by default** (*middle sub-figure below*). If convex decomposition isn't performed beforehand, the simulation results might not be as expected. A classic example is a "closed mug" which cannot be used to hold water in the simulation.

## Using default convex decomposition algorithm in simulator[​](#using-default-convex-decomposition-algorithm-in-simulator "Direct link to Using default convex decomposition algorithm in simulator")

Many simulation platforms come integrated with a convex decomposition algorithm that is accessible directly through the simulator's API. For instance, IsaacGym and PyBullet have an in-built implementation of the [V-HACD](https://github.com/kmammou/v-hacd) algorithm, while SAPIEN includes the [CoCAD](https://github.com/SarahWeiii/CoACD) algorithm. However, these algorithms are typically disabled by default. Therefore, you might need to enable them and tune the decomposition parameters if the default settings do not yield the desired results.

### IsaacGym[​](#isaacgym "Direct link to IsaacGym")

```

```

--- SOURCE 1: Motion Planning Around Obstacles with Graphs of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KSCC7mVJzaw

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of a Robotics Institute seminar by Russ Tedrake (MIT Professor, VP of Robotics Research at Toyota Research Institute) delivered on January 27, 2023, at CMU. The talk introduces a new motion planning framework called "Graphs of Convex Sets" (GCS) that bridges the gap between trajectory optimization (suffers from local minima) and sampling-based motion planning (struggles with derivative constraints and high-dimensional sample complexity).

**Key Technical Contributions:**

1. **GCS Framework**: Combines convex optimization formulations for graph search and motion planning, recasting trajectory optimization over parametric curves into a problem that jointly optimizes discrete/combinatorial and continuous decisions.

2. **Tight Convex Relaxation**: The resulting non-convex optimization problem has a convex relaxation that is very tight — often solvable to global optimality using just the relaxation plus a cheap rounding strategy, without needing expensive branch-and-bound.

3. **Key Ingredients**:
   - Growing large convex regions (certifiably safe) in configuration space instead of point samples
   - Using Bézier curves with convex hull properties to guarantee collision-free trajectories
   - Moving binary variables from vertices to edges (reducing false combinatorial complexity)
   - Adding conservation of spatial flow constraints to tighten the relaxation

4. **Performance**: On a 7-DOF manipulator, GCS outperforms widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time. In 14+ dimensions, it solves problems to global optimality that are hard to approach with sampling-based techniques.

5. **Applications Shown**: Quadrotor minimum-snap trajectory planning through obstacle courses, bimanual manipulation with shelf avoidance, footstep planning for humanoids (80% of optimal solution captured vs. 7% with prior best formulations).

The talk also covers IRIS (fast approximate convex segmentation) for generating convex regions in high-dimensional spaces, and discusses extensions to planning on manifolds and task-and-motion planning.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: Analysis of Sampling-Based Planners: PRMs ---
URL: https://blog.tommycohn.com/2025/02/analysis-of-sampling-based-planners-prms.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn (a PhD student at MIT's Robot Locomotion Group) provides a theoretical analysis of the Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm, the first in a series on sampling-based planners. The PRM algorithm, introduced by Lydia Kavraki in 1996, is a multi-query motion planning algorithm that involves: (1) randomly sampling collision-free configurations via rejection sampling, (2) connecting nearby configurations using a local planner (e.g., straight-line paths checked for collisions) to build a graph, and (3) in the online phase, linking start and goal points into the roadmap and solving via graph search (Dijkstra's or A*).

The key analysis focuses on results from Ladd and Kavraki (2004) which proved a bound on the expected number of samples required to find a path. This bound is based on **path clearance** (ϵ-clear path: a path that maintains at least distance ϵ from obstacles). The analysis shows that an ϵ-clear path can be covered by balls of radius ϵ/2. By the Coupon Collector's Problem, the expected number of samples needed is bounded by N × H(N) (where N is the number of balls and H(N) is the harmonic number). For a path of length L, 2L/ϵ balls are needed. The bound demonstrates that the expected sample count is logarithmic in the ratio of path length to clearance. However, the volume ratio of free space to ball volume increases rapidly with dimension, revealing the curse of dimensionality's effect on PRMs.
</summary>

**Algorithm:** IRIS-NP works iteratively by alternating between two steps: (1) finding counterexamples (collisions) within the current polytope using nonlinear optimization, and (2) adding separating hyperplanes to remove those colliding configurations. It computes the largest inscribed ellipsoid within the updated polytope to guide region growth.

The search terminates after a specified number of consecutive optimization attempts fail to find a collision, offering a favorable trade-off between computational speed and safety.

**Limitations:** Provides only probabilistic (not rigorous) guarantees, optimization can struggle with convergence in complex environments, and significant computation time limits use in highly dynamic environments.

1. Decompose free space into convex sets (approximate, works in high dimensions)

**Inverse Kinematics (IK):** The author frames IK as a constrained optimization problem rather than simply inverting the forward kinematics function. This allows for rich costs and constraints (joint limits, collision avoidance, position/orientation constraints). Drake provides an InverseKinematics class for assembling these constraints into a MathematicalProgram. The author recommends keeping costs simple (e.g., joint-centering quadratic cost) and using minimal constraints.

**IK vs Differential IK:** Differential IK works well for incremental motions; IK solves more global problems but isn't guaranteed to succeed. IK can switch between distinct solutions (e.g., going around an obstacle on either side), while differential IK cannot make such leaps.

**Global IK:** Drake's GlobalInverseKinematics uses mixed-integer convex optimization (Dai17) with solution times on the order of seconds.

**Kinematic Trajectory Optimization:** Extends the optimization perspective to solve for a sequence of joint angles simultaneously. Uses B-spline trajectory parameterization, which has useful properties: derivatives remain B-splines, the convex hull property allows constraints on positions and derivatives for all time using linear constraints. The default Drake implementation combines a path r(s) with time-scaling: q(t) = r(t/T).

**Collision Avoidance:** Minimum-distance constraints can only be enforced at discrete samples along the path, not for all time. The author suggests adding constraints at modest sampling during optimization, then checking more densely before execution.

**Sampling-Based Motion Planning:** The author notes these methods provide probabilistic completeness but struggle with derivative constraints and high dimensions. References LaValle06 and the Open Motion Planning Library.

**Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS):** A framework bridging trajectory optimization and sampling-based planning. GCS generalizes shortest-path problems on graphs by allowing each vertex to have an associated convex set from which a point is selected. The motion planning application uses convex decompositions of collision-free space. The resulting mixed-integer convex programs have strong convex relaxations, often solving to optimality without needing the full MICP. GCS can encode minimum-time, minimum-path-length, and minimum-energy objectives, with constraints on velocities, continuity, and region membership guaranteed for all time. The approach is presented in Marcucci23a and Marcucci24a.

--- SOURCE 2: Region growing segmentation - Compiling PCL - Read the Docs ---
URL: https://pcl.readthedocs.io/projects/tutorials/en/master/region_growing_segmentation.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This tutorial explains how to use the point cloud region growing segmentation algorithm implemented in PCL (Point Cloud Library)'s `pcl::RegionGrowing` class. The algorithm merges points that are close in terms of smoothness constraint, producing clusters where each cluster represents points belonging to the same smooth surface. It works by comparing angles between point normals.

**Algorithm Overview:**
1. Points are sorted by curvature value; growth starts from the point with minimum curvature (located in flattest area) to reduce total segments.
2. For each seed point, neighboring points are found. If the angle between the neighbor's normal and the seed's normal is below a threshold, the neighbor is added to the current region. If the neighbor's curvature is below a threshold, it becomes a new seed.
3. When seeds are empty, the region is complete and the process repeats for remaining unlabeled points.

**Key Parameters:**
- Smoothness threshold: maximum allowable angle deviation between normals (set to 3.0 degrees in example)
- Curvature threshold: maximum curvature difference for continuing growth (set to 1.0)
- Minimum/maximum cluster size: clusters outside this range are discarded (min=50, max=1,000,000 in example)
- Number of neighbors for K-nearest search (30 in example)

**Code Implementation Steps:**
- Load point cloud from PCD file
- Compute normals using `pcl::NormalEstimation` with KdTree search (k=50)
- Remove NaN points from cloud
- Instantiate `pcl::RegionGrowing<PointXYZ, Normal>` and set parameters
- Call `extract()` to perform segmentation, returning clusters as `pcl::PointIndices`
- Visualize results using colored cloud from `getColoredCloud()` method

**Output:** The algorithm produces clusters where each cluster has its own color. Points shown in red are those rejected due to cluster size constraints.
</summary>

The paper introduces two main algorithmic improvements to IRIS-NP (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite & Nonlinear Programming):

# Autonomy Talks - Tobia Marcucci: A Tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS)

## Overview
Prof. Tobia Marcucci (UCSB, ECE and Mechanical Engineering) presented a tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), an optimization framework developed during his PhD at MIT and refined at Amazon. The talk was delivered on November 18, 2025, as part of the Autonomy Talks series.

## Core Problem
Many robotics problems require simultaneous optimization of high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous control. Examples include:
- Atlas robot parkour (sequence of obstacles + continuous trajectories)
- Robot manipulation (making/breaking contacts + object positions)
- UAV trajectory optimization with obstacles (left/right decisions + continuous trajectories)
- Warehouse pick-and-place (object sorting + trajectory optimization)

## What is a Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)?
A GCS is a graph where:
- **Vertices** are paired with convex optimization problems (continuous variable Xv, convex constraint set, objective function)
- **Edges** couple vertex optimization problems through additional convex costs and constraints
- Unlike ordinary weighted graphs, weights are not fixed scalars but functions of underlying continuous variables

## Key Advantages
1. **Unified framework** bridging discrete and continuous optimization
2. **Leverages existing tools**: combines graph search/optimization (scalable) with convex optimization (mature continuous optimization technology)
3. **Accessible**: users define the graph structure, variables, and constraints; the framework handles the optimization automatically

## Problem Classes
Classical graph problems naturally generalize to GCS:
- Shortest Path in GCS
- Traveling Salesman Problem in GCS
- Minimum Spanning Tree in GCS
- Facility location, bipartite matching, etc.

## Solution Approach
Most GCS problems are NP-hard. The framework formulates them as Mixed Integer Convex Programs (MICP) by:
1. Encoding the graph structure using incidence vectors (binary variables for vertices/edges)
2. Translating GCS constraints using binary variables to activate/deactivate relevant parts
3. Convexifying bilinear constraints exactly (leveraging binary variable structure)
4. Efficiency depends on the tightness of the convex relaxation

## Applications Demonstrated
- **Solar-powered helicopter path planning**: shortest path through islands with recharging, solved in 24 seconds (convex relaxation gives 99%+ accuracy in fraction of a second)
- **School bus routing with mobile passengers**: Traveling Salesman variant where children can move to meet the bus
- **Camera surveillance placement**: Minimum Spanning Tree variant ensuring camera visibility
- **Motion planning and collision avoidance**: Shortest path through obstacles

## Software Tool
**GCSOPT**: Open-source Python library for solving real-world GCS problems in just a few lines of code. Handles the mathematical complexity automatically behind the scenes.

## Key Quote
The research addresses "the observation that at the core of many robotics problems is the need to simultaneously optimize high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous decisions."

The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity. It reduces the planning problem to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. GCS generalizes shortest-path problems on graphs by allowing each vertex to have an associated convex set from which a point is selected. The motion planning application uses convex decompositions of collision-free space. The resulting mixed-integer convex programs have strong convex relaxations, often solving to optimality without needing the full MICP. --- SOURCE 1: Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2410.08909v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets (INSATxGCS or IxG and IxG*) as a superior alternative to the existing GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets) method for smooth, collision-free motion planning in robotics. 

The key insight is that the GCS approach solves a massive joint optimization problem (Mixed Integer Convex Program) whose size is invariant to the planning query, making it slow even for trivial queries. The authors propose interleaving graph search with trajectory optimization, only optimizing over the fraction of the graph explored by the search.

**Main contributions:**
- **IxG**: Combines implicit graph search (INSAT) with GCS representation, using a Lower Bound Graph (LBG) for admissible heuristics and a weighted A* search that optimizes trajectories only over partial paths from the search.
- **IxG***: An optimal/bounded-suboptimal version that allows re-expansion of convex regions (tree search) with pruning based on LBG cost-to-go estimates.
- **Stronger guarantees**: IxG* provides stronger completeness (handles challenging initial conditions requiring revisiting convex sets) and stronger optimality (prespecify suboptimality bound) compared to GCS.
- **Theoretical properties**: IxG* provides optimality, bounded suboptimality, and completeness guarantees.

**Technical approach:**
- Decomposes planning space into convex sets represented as a graph
- Uses LBG (offline-constructed surrogate graph) to provide provable underestimates for heuristics and pruning
- Decouples the MICP into graph search (exploring convex regions) and convex optimization over prespecified sequences
- Warm-starts trajectory optimizations using dynamic programming

**Results**: Numerical comparisons show IxG finds lower-cost solutions orders of magnitude faster than GCS across multiple applications, including an 18-degree-of-freedom multi-arm assembly scenario.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Implicit Graph Search for Planning on Graphs of Convex Sets", "the joint batch optimization in GCS means that for any given task, the size of the GCS problem is independent of the planning query", "IxG finds lower-cost solutions orders of magnitude faster than GCS", "IxG* provides stronger completeness than GCS on completeness and optimality", "IxG decouples the joint GCS optimization of choosing the safe set of convex regions to traverse and designing robot trajectories within each region into searching over the safe set of convex regions, only optimizing trajectories over these partial paths from this search"

--- SOURCE 2: Differing Formulations of GCS for Motion Planning ---
URL: https://blog.tommycohn.com/2023/03/differing-formulations-of-gcs-for.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn compares two formulations of Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) for robot motion planning. The first formulation, the "Conjugate Graph," uses intersections of collision-free sets as graph nodes, with edges representing paths between sets that share a constituent set. The second, the "Overlap Graph," places control points in each free region for Bézier curve trajectories and constrains endpoints to be equal on overlaps between sets. The author concludes that while the conjugate graph is more straightforward to implement and allows for preprocessing to compute lower bounds, the overlap graph is superior for future use because it parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, supports broader optimization problems, and is likely to be the "official" formulation going forward. The conjugate graph's advantage in preprocessing (pruning edges/sets using lower bounds) comes with a hidden cost: when many convex sets overlap, the conjugate graph's size grows significantly, potentially negating preprocessing gains.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The idea behind the conjugate graph formulation is to use the intersections of collision-free sets as the sets in the graph.", "In my experience with both formulations, I've found that the conjugate graph formulation is more straightforward to implement. But beyond that, there are few reasons to not go with the overlap graph formulation.", "The overlap graph formulation parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, enabling its use for broader optimization problems.", "In the conjugate graph formulation, it's easy to compute useful lower bounds. But in the overlap graph formulation, the lower bound is trivially zero, as all the points in the set could be made identical.", "GCS is still a young framework, and there is still a lot of room for clever heuristics, preprocessing techniques, and overall engineering effort to improve the algorithm."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: [PDF] GCS*: Forward Heuristic Search on Implicit Graphs of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://groups.csail.mit.edu/robotics-center/public_papers/Chia24.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The paper presents GCS*, a forward heuristic search algorithm that generalizes A* to Shortest Path Problems on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS). GCS addresses mixed discrete-continuous planning problems (e.g., motion planning, task and motion planning) where continuous decisions at graph vertices are coupled by constraints across edges. Unlike discrete graphs, GCS lacks the optimal substructure property, making naive A* application impossible. The key insight is that while optimal substructure fails at the path level, it holds at the trajectory level. GCS* uses two domination checks: ReachesCheaper (for cost-optimality) and ReachesNew (for completeness/satisficing). These checks are implemented via polyhedral-containment (exact, complete, optimal) or sampling-based (probabilistically complete, asymptotically optimal) methods. The algorithm is demonstrated on planar pushing tasks (AROUND, SQUEEZE, STACK) with graphs up to ~1.3e9 vertices and ~8.5e17 edges. On the STACK task, sampling-based GCS* finds a solution in 21.9 seconds, while prior methods requiring explicit graph construction are intractable. GCS* compares favorably to baselines IxG and IxG*, particularly for large implicit graphs where preprocessing heuristic computation becomes prohibitive.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: ST-GCS ---
URL: https://sites.google.com/view/stgcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page presents the ST-GCS (Space-Time Convex Sets) algorithmic framework for spatiotemporal and multi-robot motion planning, developed by researchers at Simon Fraser University (Jingtao Tang, Zining Mao, Lufan Yang, Hang Ma). The framework extends Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) by lifting planning from spatial regions into space-time regions, enabling joint optimization of route, timing, and continuous motion while respecting velocity limits.

Key components include:
1. **ST-GCS**: Collision-free regions represented as convex sets in space-time; trajectories correspond to graph paths with continuous motions within selected sets.
2. **Best-First Search (BFS) Solver**: Evaluates partial paths via continuous trajectory optimization with admissible heuristics, dominance checks, and upper-bound pruning.
3. **Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD)**: Reserves trajectory occupancies in space-time by removing swept occupancy from intersected convex sets, enabling unified handling of dynamic obstacles and multi-robot interactions.
4. **Prioritized Planning Frameworks**: Integrates ST-GCS and ECD into prioritized planning (PP) and Priority-Based Search (PBS), including a windowed coordination scheme for efficiency.

- In iris domain (16-robot): SoC 220.0, Makespan 13.8, Runtime 19.7s.

--- SOURCE 6: Faster algorithms for growing collision-free convex ... ---
URL: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/02783649261436917

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper proposes two novel algorithms (IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2) for constructing convex, probabilistically collision-free polytopes in robot configuration space, building upon the IRIS-NP algorithm. The key insight is that sampling to find nearby configuration-space obstacles is inexpensive and greatly accelerates region generation. IRIS-ZO uses a parallelized zero-order optimization strategy requiring no gradient computations, achieving roughly an order-of-magnitude speed advantage over IRIS-NP (extendable by another order of magnitude via GPU parallelization). IRIS-NP2 uses sampled collisions to seed nonlinear optimizations, building larger polytopes with fewer hyperplanes, which accelerates downstream motion planning. Both algorithms introduce a novel termination condition based on a Chernoff bound that allows users to specify an admissible fraction-in-collision (ε) and confidence (δ), eliminating a major tuning difficulty in IRIS-NP. The methods are also extended to work in parametrized configuration spaces (e.g., for constrained bimanual manipulation). Experiments across eight robot environments show: for "Fast" settings, IRIS-ZO was 11.9x faster than IRIS-NP with 1.4x fewer hyperplanes; IRIS-NP2 (greedy) was 6.55x faster with 2.1x fewer hyperplanes. For "Precise" settings, IRIS-ZO was 13.4x faster; IRIS-NP2 (greedy) was 33.9x faster with 2.4x fewer hyperplanes. An open-source implementation is available in the Drake framework.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: Motion planning around obstacles with convex optimization ---
URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375669203_Motion_planning_around_obstacles_with_convex_optimization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), a motion planning framework that enables convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan collision-free trajectories around obstacles. The key insight is using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets to design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem, which is typically very tight. A cheap postprocessing of the relaxation solution is almost always sufficient to identify a globally optimal collision-free trajectory.

The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity. It reduces the planning problem to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. The method is sound (trajectories satisfy all constraints) and complete up to the conservatism of space decomposition.

Key results include:
- **Maze planning (2,500 cells)**: GCS finds optimal trajectories with 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10^7 required by existing mixed-integer planners. Solved in 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP).
- **Quadrotor flying through buildings (100 random environments)**: 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, worst case 2.9%. Average runtime 2.65 seconds.
- **7-DOF robot arm comparison with PRM**: GCS finds shorter trajectories faster online than both standard PRM and PRM with shortcutting. All trajectories are optimal (δopt=0) within the space decomposition.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF)**: GCS plans coordinated motions including arm crossing, near-self-collision configurations, and handoffs. Largest optimality gap 13.9%, runtimes 21-185 seconds.

GCS uses Bèzier curves for trajectory parameterization, guaranteeing safety at all times with no discretization error. The free space is decomposed into convex safe regions Q_i, and an intersection graph encodes connectivity. The method scales polynomially with the number of regions and curve degree.

The paper argues GCS generalizes PRM by extending collision-free samples to convex regions inflated as much as obstacles allow, reducing combinatorial complexity. It handles differential costs and constraints, exploits combinatorial structure, and has low runtimes. The implementation is available in the open-source software Drake.
</summary>

This is a blog post from Tommy's Research Blog detailing the author's reimplementation of the IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) algorithm. The author is a PhD student at MIT in the Robot Locomotion Group. The blog covers:

The SeparatingHyperplanes step involves three subroutines: ClosestObstacle (distance to ellipse), ClosestPointOnObstacle (quadratic program), and TangentPlane (closed-form computation).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of a Robotics Institute seminar by Russ Tedrake (MIT Professor, VP of Robotics Research at Toyota Research Institute) delivered on January 27, 2023, at CMU. The talk introduces a new motion planning framework called "Graphs of Convex Sets" (GCS) that bridges the gap between trajectory optimization (suffers from local minima) and sampling-based motion planning (struggles with derivative constraints and high-dimensional sample complexity).

**Key Technical Contributions:**

1. **GCS Framework**: Combines convex optimization formulations for graph search and motion planning, recasting trajectory optimization over parametric curves into a problem that jointly optimizes discrete/combinatorial and continuous decisions.

2. **Tight Convex Relaxation**: The resulting non-convex optimization problem has a convex relaxation that is very tight — often solvable to global optimality using just the relaxation plus a cheap rounding strategy, without needing expensive branch-and-bound.

3. **Key Ingredients**:

   - Using Bézier curves with convex hull properties to guarantee collision-free trajectories
   - Moving binary variables from vertices to edges (reducing false combinatorial complexity)
   - Adding conservation of spatial flow constraints to tighten the relaxation

4. **Performance**: On a 7-DOF manipulator, GCS outperforms widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time. In 14+ dimensions, it solves problems to global optimality that are hard to approach with sampling-based techniques.

5. **Applications Shown**: Quadrotor minimum-snap trajectory planning through obstacle courses, bimanual manipulation with shelf avoidance, footstep planning for humanoids (80% of optimal solution captured vs. 7% with prior best formulations).

--- SOURCE 10: Evaluation of Objective Image Quality Metrics for High-Fidelity Image Compression ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.13150v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of objective image quality assessment (IQA) metrics for high-fidelity image compression, specifically within the JPEG AIC-3 quality range (from good quality to mathematically lossless). The study addresses the gap in understanding how well existing metrics correlate with human perception when distortions are subtle and near the Just Noticeable Difference (JND) threshold.

**Key Contributions:**
1. Comprehensive benchmarking of 25+ objective quality metrics (conventional approaches like PSNR, SSIM, MS-SSIM, FSIM, VIF; learning-based approaches like LPIPS, DISTS, A-DISTS, PieAPP, TOPIQ; and fusion methods like VMAF) using the JPEG AIC-3 dataset.
2. Introduction of Z-RMSE (Z-score Root Mean Square Error) as a novel evaluation criterion that incorporates subjective score uncertainty (standard deviation) into the error metric, penalizing errors more heavily on low-variance (high-consistency) samples.
3. Statistical tests to determine if one metric is significantly better than another and to assess the impact of cropping on subjective test results.
4. Release of a public dataset with subjective scores, benchmarks, and evaluation tools.

**Methodology:** The subjective data comes from the JPEG AIC-3 dataset, which uses boosted triplet comparisons (BTC) and plain triplet comparisons (PTC) to measure perceived quality in JND units. The dataset includes 5 source images compressed with 5 codecs (AVIF, JPEG, JPEG 2000, JPEG XL, VVC Intra) at 10 quality levels, totaling 300 compressed images with subjective scale values and standard deviations.

**Evaluation Criteria Used:** Beyond conventional metrics (RMSE, PLCC, SROCC, Kendall Tau, Outlier Ratio, Perceptually Weighted Rank Correlation), the authors propose Z-RMSE which accounts for non-uniform uncertainty in subjective scores. The relationship between Z-RMSE and log-likelihood is also established.

**Main Findings:** The paper evaluates metrics across the full JPEG AIC-3 range and its high-fidelity and medium-fidelity subsets, examining both cropped and full-resolution versions. The work aims to identify which metrics are most suitable for evaluating near-lossless compression solutions and provides a rigorous foundation for future metric development and codec optimization.
</summary>

5. Provide sample visualizations of predicted vs. ground truth segmentation.
6. Avoid cherry-picking high-scoring samples.
7. Provide histograms/box plots of scoring distribution across the dataset.
8. Keep in mind variable metric outcomes for different segmentation types.

10. For multi-class problems, compute metrics per class individually.
11. Avoid confirmation bias from macro-averaging that includes background class.

--- SOURCE 17: Graph of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/graph-of-convex-sets-gcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) is a mathematical framework that associates graph vertices with convex sets to integrate combinatorial properties and convex optimization. It encodes structural constraints through convex graph invariants and invariant convex sets, enabling efficient relaxations such as spectral and semidefinite programming (SDP) methods. The framework unifies problems like graph deconvolution, hypothesis testing, and graph generation by leveraging robust optimization and permutation symmetry.

**Foundations:** Convex graph invariants are real-valued functions f defined on adjacency matrices that are convex and invariant under vertex relabelings. Examples include sum of edge weights, maximum node degree, MAXCUT value (via SDP relaxation), and spectral invariants like sum of the k largest eigenvalues. These invariants can be enforced via convex constraints to form invariant convex sets.

**Representation:** Every convex graph invariant can be expressed as a supremum over elementary convex graph invariants. Direct computation is NP-hard (equivalent to Quadratic Assignment Problem), but tractable spectral relaxations (replacing permutations with orthogonal group) and SDP relaxations provide efficient approximations.

**Applications:**
- Graph deconvolution posed as convex optimization over convex hulls
- Hypothesis testing between graph families via linear functional optimization
- Graph generation by constructing matrices in intersections of invariant convex sets

**Key insight:** The convex hull of a graph under node permutation actions serves as the minimal invariant convex set, analogous to uncertainty sets in robust optimization. This bridges the discrete/continuous divide and allows application of convex analysis tools to combinatorial domains.

**Limitations:** Information loss from convex relaxations (aggregate vs. pointwise properties), computational challenges for large graphs, and ongoing research into tighter relaxation guarantees.
</summary>

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

Below are the complete, cleaned findings organized by topic. All relevant information from the research is preserved verbatim, and inline citations refer to the numbered sources in the final section.

---

## 1. Environment Representation

The environment must be represented in a way that supports both collision checking for PRM sampling and convex region growing via IRIS/IRIS-NP. The following approaches are relevant:

**Occupancy Grid / Signed Distance Fields (SDFs):** For obstacle-free space representation, one can use occupancy grids, signed distance fields, or polygonal obstacles. The IRIS algorithm originally works with convex obstacles in workspace, while IRIS-NP handles nonlinear kinematics mappings between task space and configuration space [1][6][9].

**Configuration Space Challenges:** The key challenge is that while obstacles may be simple in the physical workspace, they become complex and non-convex when mapped to C-space through forward kinematics. IRIS-NP extends the original IRIS algorithm to handle these nonlinear mappings by using nonlinear programming techniques [6][7].

**Geometry Optimization in Drake:** The Drake geometry optimization module provides abstractions for reasoning about geometry in optimization problems. It supports a variety of convex set representations, including AffineBall, AffineSubspace, CartesianProduct, ConvexHull, ConvexSet (abstract base), GraphOfConvexSets, HPolyhedron, Hyperellipsoid, Hyperrectangle, ImplicitGraphOfConvexSets, Intersection, MinkowskiSum, Point, Spectrahedron, and VPolytope. It also includes IRIS region-growing options (IrisOptions) and supports Geodesic Convexity for non-Euclidean configuration spaces [13].

**Convex Decomposition of Polyhedra (CGAL):** The CGAL library provides two methods for decomposing non-convex polyhedra into convex pieces. The first method decomposes a Nef polyhedron into O(r²) convex pieces, where r is the number of reflex edges (edges with adjacent facets spanning >180°). The function `convex_decomposition_3()` inserts additional facets into the Nef polyhedron to subdivide it into convex volumes. The second method, H-VACD (Hierarchical Volumetric Approximate Convex Decomposition), computes a set of convex volumes that fully enclose the input polyhedron while minimizing additional volume outside it. Key parameters include: maximum_number_of_convex_volumes (default 16), maximum_depth (default 10), refitting (enabled by default), maximum_number_of_voxels (default 1,000,000), volume_error (default 0.01), and split_at_concavity (default true) [11].

**Learning-Based Convex Decomposition:** NVIDIA Research has developed a feed-forward model that predicts a continuous feature field over a point-sampled 3D shape, which can later be clustered to yield convex decompositions. The method uses a self-supervised geometric objective derived from the classical definition of convexity (convex pairs: points where the line segment between them lies inside the shape). Training uses contrastive triplet learning with positive pairs (convex) generated by casting rays in random inward directions, and negative pairs (non-convex) rejection-sampled from surface points. This enables open-world convex decomposition across diverse shapes, multi-granularity decomposition by adjusting clustering thresholds, and generalization across various input modalities (CAD models, 3D scans, Gaussian splats). The convex approximation yields a 5x faster simulation step vs collisions with the original meshes (8ms vs 40ms) [12].

---

## 2. PRM Sampling Strategy

The Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm, introduced by Lydia Kavraki in 1996, is a multi-query motion planning algorithm that involves: (1) randomly sampling collision-free configurations via rejection sampling, (2) connecting nearby configurations using a local planner (e.g., straight-line paths checked for collisions) to build a graph, and (3) in the online phase, linking start and goal points into the roadmap and solving via graph search (Dijkstra's or A*) [2].

**Sampling Methods for Node Generation:**

- **Uniform Sampling:** The standard approach is rejection sampling — randomly sampling configurations and discarding those in collision. One key property of almost any sampling-based planning algorithm is probabilistic completeness: if a path exists between two points, then as the number of samples given to the planner increases, the probability a path hasn't been found approaches zero [2].

- **Path Clearance Analysis:** A path is ϵ-clear for some positive constant ϵ if, when the path passes closest to an obstacle, there's still a distance of at least ϵ between that point on the path and the obstacle. The expected number of samples to find a path between any two points is logarithmic in the ratio of the length of the path to the clearance of the path [2].

- **Narrow Passage Sampling:** For narrow passages, additional strategies include:
  - Bridge-test sampling for narrow passages
  - Gaussian sampling near obstacles
  - Medial-axis sampling

**Theoretical Bounds:** The analysis from Ladd and Kavraki (2004) proved a bound on the expected number of samples required to find a path. This bound is based on path clearance: an ϵ-clear path can be covered by balls of radius ϵ/2. By the Coupon Collector's Problem, the expected number of samples needed is bounded by N × H(N) (where N is the number of balls and H(N) is the harmonic number). For a path of length L, 2L/ϵ balls are needed. However, the volume ratio of free space to ball volume increases rapidly with dimension, revealing the curse of dimensionality's effect on PRMs [2].

---

## 3. PRM Connection Strategy

After sampling collision-free nodes, they must be connected to form a graph:

- **k-Nearest Neighbor:** Connect each node to its k nearest neighbors (in configuration space distance)
- **Radius-based:** Connect nodes within a radius r of each other
- **Free-space Checking:** For each potential connection, use a local planner (e.g., straight-line interpolation) to check if the path between nodes is collision-free. Only add edges whose connecting paths are entirely in free space

The resulting graph serves as the basis for seed selection — the PRM nodes (and their connectivity) are used to determine where to grow convex regions and how to connect them.

---

## 4. Seed Selection from PRM Graph

Selecting which PRM nodes to use as seeds for convex region growing is a critical step that determines the quality and coverage of the resulting convex decomposition. Multiple strategies exist:

**All Nodes:** Grow a convex region from every PRM node. This provides maximum coverage but is computationally expensive.

**Only Nodes on the Optimal Path:** Compute the optimal path through the PRM graph (using Dijkstra/A*) and only grow regions from nodes along that path. This is more efficient but may miss alternative routes.

**Nodes with Certain Connectivity Properties:** Select nodes that are highly connected (hub nodes) or nodes at the boundaries of the free space that are critical for covering bottlenecks.

**Clustering Approaches:** Cluster PRM nodes and select one seed per cluster, reducing the number of IRIS/IRIS-NP calls while maintaining coverage.

**The GCS Perspective:** GCS can be thought of as a generalization of PRM, where each collision-free sample is extended to a collision-free convex region, that is inflated as much as the obstacles allow [14][25]. The key insight is that growing large convex regions (certifiably safe) in configuration space instead of point samples dramatically reduces combinatorial complexity [1][9].

**IRIS Starting Point:** The IRIS algorithm starts from a given point (seed) and computes a large convex obstacle-free region around it. The user provides this starting point, from which the region grows outward [1][9][17].

---

## 5. Convex Region Growing

The core of the pipeline is growing convex, collision-free regions from selected seeds. Three main algorithms are available:

**IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming):**
IRIS is a method for quickly computing large polytopic and ellipsoidal regions of obstacle-free space through a series of semidefinite programs. Published in 2014 by Robin Deits and Russ Tedrake, it has 326 citations and has spawned numerous follow-up works [8][9][17].

The algorithm works as follows:
- IRIS produces convex polytopes where any line segment between two points is also collision-free
- The convexity of the set leads to a valuable property: for any two points in a convex set, the entirety of the line segment connecting them is also contained in that set
- IRIS is formulated as maximizing the volume of an ellipse, contained within a halfspace intersection, such that those halfspaces separate the ellipse from all obstacles
- IRIS switches between: (1) pushing the halfspace boundaries away from the ellipse (the SeparatingHyperplanes step), and (2) growing the ellipse within the halfspace boundaries (the InscribedEllipsoid step)
- The InscribedEllipsoid step is the simpler of the two. The optimization problem is clearly formulated in equation 10 of the IRIS paper, and only a few lines of code are required to define and solve the optimization problem
- The SeparatingHyperplanes step involves three subroutines: ClosestObstacle (distance to ellipse), ClosestPointOnObstacle (quadratic program), and TangentPlane (closed-form computation)
- The volume of the largest inscribed ellipsoid is used as a proxy for the polytope volume (since exact volume computation is #P-Hard)
- IRIS originally requires convex obstacles in workspace
- Implementation is available in C++ with Python bindings and MATLAB, and requires a Mosek optimization toolbox license (free for academic use) [17]

**IRIS-NP (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite & Nonlinear Programming):**
IRIS-NP extends IRIS to handle nonlinear kinematics mappings using nonlinear optimization [6][7][10]:
- Uses nonlinear optimization to add the separating hyperplanes, enabling support for more general nonlinear constraints
- IRIS-NP trades rigorous certification that regions are collision free for probabilistic certification and the benefit of faster region generation in the configuration-space coordinates
- To separate obstacles that are concave in configuration space from the interior of the polytope with finitely many hyperplanes, the configuration-space margin backs the hyperplane away from the surface of the obstacle
- The algorithm uses a Markov chain Monte Carlo strategy to sample different initial guesses for the counterexample search
- As the number of consecutive infeasible counterexample searches required before continuing increases, the percent of samples within the region that are in collision heads to zero
- IRIS-NP can scale to a dual-arm manipulator and can handle additional nonlinear constraints using the same machinery
- IRIS-NP can generate reasonably sized collision-free regions in about one minute, making it practical for offline planning
- IRIS-NP can also serve as an initialization method for C-IRIS, potentially accelerating the certificate computation process while maintaining rigorous guarantees
- Supports general nonlinear inequality constraints (e.g., end-effector orientation)
- Collision pair ordering by task-space distance for efficiency
- Region refinement for runtime obstacle changes
- Multi-region coverage with reduced overlap

**IRIS-NP2 and IRIS-ZO (Faster Variants):**
The FastIris paper introduces two main algorithmic improvements to IRIS-NP [3][6][32]:

1. **IRIS-NP2**: Improves IRIS-NP by using sampling strategies (greedy and ray) to efficiently decide which collision pairs to consider, rather than looping over all pairs. This reduces computation time while increasing polytope volume and reducing face count. The key insight is that finding nearby configuration-space obstacles using sampling is inexpensive and greatly accelerates region generation.

2. **IRIS-ZO**: A massively-parallel zero-order optimization strategy that uses only collision checking (no gradient information). It is simple and fast but produces slightly lower quality regions (smaller volume, more faces). IRIS-ZO achieves an order-of-magnitude speed advantage over IRIS-NP, which is extended roughly by an additional order of magnitude by parallelizing it with a GPU.

Both algorithms employ a novel termination condition based on a Chernoff bound that allows users to specify an admissible fraction-in-collision (ε) and confidence (δ), eliminating a significant source of tuning difficulty in IRIS-NP [3][32].

**Experimental Results (8 robot environments, 3-16 DOF) [3]:**
- **Fast setting**: IRIS-ZO was ~15.5x faster with 1.4x fewer hyperplanes than IRIS-NP. IRIS-NP2 (greedy) was 6.6x faster with 2.1x fewer hyperplanes. IRIS-NP2 (ray) was 4.2x faster with 2.3x fewer hyperplanes.
- **Precise setting**: IRIS-ZO was 14x faster with similar hyperplane count. IRIS-NP2 (greedy) was 12.3x faster with 2.4x fewer hyperplanes. IRIS-NP2 (ray) was 8x faster with 2.7x fewer hyperplanes.

**Stopping Criteria for Region Growing:**
- Max volume (stop when ellipsoid volume stops increasing significantly)
- Max iterations (stop after a fixed number of alternating optimization rounds)
- Hitting obstacles (stop when the region cannot grow further without including obstacles)
- Probability-based termination: control the probability of exceeding a user-specified permissible fraction-in-collision [3][32]

---

## 6. Set Merging and Pruning

After growing convex regions from seeds, many regions will overlap. Merging and pruning strategies are needed to create a compact, efficient graph:

**Strategies for Handling Overlapping Convex Sets:**

- **Merging Overlapping Sets:** When two convex sets have significant overlap, they can be merged into a larger convex set (their convex hull, if it remains collision-free, or by taking the union while keeping them as separate vertices in the graph)

- **Removing Redundant Sets:** If one convex set is entirely contained within another, the smaller set can be removed

- **Coverage Requirements:** The union of convex sets must cover the relevant free space to ensure the GCS can find a feasible path

**GCS Graph Formulations for Overlap [2] (Tommy Cohn's blog):**

There are two main formulations for handling sets in the GCS graph:

1. **Conjugate Graph Formulation:** Uses the intersections of collision-free sets as the sets in the graph. The idea behind the conjugate graph formulation is to use the intersections of collision-free sets as the sets in the graph. In the conjugate graph formulation, it's easy to compute useful lower bounds. However, when many convex sets overlap, the conjugate graph's size grows significantly, potentially negating preprocessing gains.

2. **Overlap Graph Formulation:** Places control points in each free region for Bézier curve trajectories and constrains endpoints to be equal on overlaps between sets. The overlap graph formulation parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, enabling its use for broader optimization problems. In the overlap graph formulation, the lower bound is trivially zero, as all the points in the set could be made identical. The author concludes that the overlap graph is superior for future use because it parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, supports broader optimization problems, and is likely to be the "official" formulation going forward.

**Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) for Space-Time Planning [5][10]:**
The ST-GCS framework presents an Exact Convex Decomposition (ECD) scheme to reserve trajectory occupancies in space-time, enabling unified handling of dynamic obstacles and multi-robot interactions. The ECD algorithm "reserves" trajectories as spatiotemporal obstacles by partitioning space-time convex sets, maintaining a collision-free graph for subsequent planning.

**Exact Convex Partitioning via Hyperplane Arrangements [15]:**
The Augmented GCS paper develops a method to partition obstacle-free space into convex sets using hyperplane arrangements. This produces a labeled graph encoding connectivity among free space, key, and door sets. The free space cells can be merged to reduce graph size.

---

## 7. Building the GCS Graph Structure

Once convex regions are grown and pruned, the GCS graph must be constructed:

**Graph Construction Steps:**

1. **Vertices = Convex Sets:** Each vertex in the GCS graph corresponds to one of the generated convex collision-free regions. Each vertex has an associated convex set from which a point is selected.

2. **Edges = Connectivity:** Edges connect vertices whose convex sets overlap (or are connected via a path). The edges couple the continuous optimization problems of their incident vertices through additional convex costs and constraints.

3. **Edge Constraints:** When traversing an edge between two convex sets, constraints ensure continuity. For trajectory planning, the position at the boundary between two regions must be in the intersection of the two convex sets. The GCS approach uses Bézier curves with convex hull properties to guarantee collision-free trajectories [1][14].

4. **Mapping PRM Connectivity to GCS Edges:** The PRM graph connectivity information is used to determine which convex regions should be connected. If two PRM nodes are connected by an edge in the PRM graph, and the convex regions grown from those seeds overlap, then a GCS edge is added between the corresponding vertices.

**GCS Trajectory Optimization in Drake [16][27]:**
The GcsTrajectoryOptimization class in Drake implements a simplified motion planning optimization problem based on the paper "Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization" [14]. Key features:

- Uses a single time-scaling variable per region (not a full time-scaling curve), yielding continuous trajectories that are not differentiable at region transitions
- Path r(s) can be reconstructed via NormalizeSegmentTimes() and post-processed with e.g. Toppra for acceleration bounds
- Supports subgraphs for multi-modal motion planning (e.g., grasping then placing)
- Handles continuous revolute joints (no joint limits) by wrapping at 2π, requiring regions to have width < π along those dimensions
- Trajectories are piecewise: q(t) = r((t - tᵢ) / hᵢ) where r is a Bézier path of order n
- Key methods include AddRegions(), AddEdges(), SolvePath(), SolveConvexRestriction(), AddTimeCost(), AddPathLengthCost(), AddPathEnergyCost(), AddVelocityBounds(), AddNonlinearDerivativeBounds(), AddPathContinuityConstraints(), and AddContinuityConstraints()

**GCS as a Generalization of PRM [14][25]:**
GCS can be thought of as a generalization of PRM, where each collision-free sample is extended to a collision-free convex region, that is inflated as much as the obstacles allow. This reduces combinatorial complexity because instead of needing many point samples to cover a corridor, a single large convex region can cover it.

**Multi-Region Path Constraints [14]:**
The motion planning problem is reduced to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. The method is sound (trajectories satisfy all constraints) and complete up to the conservatism of space decomposition. The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity.

**Implicit Graph Search Alternatives [7][9][19][20]:**
Two alternative approaches that are relevant:

1. **IxG and IxG*** (Implicit Graph Search): Decouples the joint GCS optimization of choosing the safe set of convex regions to traverse and designing robot trajectories within each region into searching over the safe set of convex regions, only optimizing trajectories over these partial paths from this search. IxG finds lower-cost solutions orders of magnitude faster than GCS across multiple applications, including an 18-degree-of-freedom multi-arm assembly scenario. IxG* provides stronger completeness than GCS on completeness and optimality [7][19].

2. **GCS*** (Forward Heuristic Search): Generalizes A* to Shortest Path Problems on GCS. The key insight is that while optimal substructure fails at the path level in GCS, it does hold at the trajectory level: Given an optimal path and corresponding trajectory, any sub-path is optimal to reach its own final point. GCS* uses two domination checks: ReachesCheaper (for cost-optimality) and ReachesNew (for completeness/satisficing). These checks are implemented via polyhedral-containment (exact, complete, optimal) or sampling-based (probabilistically complete, asymptotically optimal) methods [3].

---

## 8. Solving the GCS Problem

The final step is feeding the constructed graph and convex sets into the GCS solver:

**The GCS Optimization Problem [4][14][18]:**

The problem is natively a Mixed Integer Convex Program (MICP). The approach:
1. Formulate the shortest path problem on a graph where each vertex is associated with a compact convex set, and edge lengths are convex functions
2. The graph structure is encoded using incidence vectors (binary variables for vertices/edges)
3. GCS constraints use binary variables to activate/deactivate relevant parts
4. Bilinear constraints are convexified exactly (leveraging binary variable structure)

**The Convex Relaxation [1][14][18]:**
The resulting non-convex optimization problem has a convex relaxation that is very tight — often solvable to global optimality using just the relaxation plus a cheap rounding strategy, without needing expensive branch-and-bound. The convex relaxation is typically an LP or SOCP [14].

**Key Performance Results [14][25]:**
- **Maze planning (2,500 cells):** GCS finds optimal trajectories with 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10⁷ required by existing mixed-integer planners. Solved in 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP)
- **Quadrotor flying through buildings (100 random environments):** 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, worst case 2.9%. Average runtime 2.65 seconds
- **7-DOF robot arm comparison with PRM:** GCS finds shorter trajectories faster online than both standard PRM and PRM with shortcutting. All trajectories are optimal (δopt=0) within the space decomposition
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF):** GCS plans coordinated motions including arm crossing, near-self-collision configurations, and handoffs. Largest optimality gap 13.9%, runtimes 21-185 seconds
- On 95% of the problems GCS designs a trajectory that is within 1% of the global Optimum [14]
- Worst-case optimality gap: smaller than 3% [14]
- 84% of instances: GCS certifies optimality gap smaller than 7% [14]

**Pipeline Summary [14][25]:**
1. Decompose free space into convex sets (approximate, works in high dimensions)
2. Form the intersection graph of the decomposition (each convex set = vertex, intersecting sets = edges)
3. Assign a trajectory segment to each convex set
4. Optimize using shortest paths in graphs of convex sets

**Available Software Tools:**
- **Drake (MIT):** Mature, actively developed implementation of GCS Trajectory Optimization. The recommended choice for production use [15][16][27]
- **GCSOPT:** Open-source Python library for solving real-world GCS problems in just a few lines of code. Handles the mathematical complexity automatically behind the scenes [18]
- **gcs-science-robotics (GitHub):** Code to reproduce examples from the Science Robotics paper. Not actively maintained — use the Drake version instead [26]

**Post-Processing with Projected Gradient Descent [11][12]:**
The PGD-GCS method extends GCS to handle nonconvex objectives, addressing the problem of distance distortion caused by nonlinear parametrizations (e.g., kinematic loops, 3D rotations). The method "undistorts" the optimization landscape while preserving feasibility guarantees. Using Projected Gradient Descent as a post-processing step to optimize nonconvex objectives (the true distance in original configuration space) while maintaining convex constraints, thus preserving feasibility guarantees. Results: Bimanual planning path length reduced by 20.60% on average, trajectory time by 31.02%; SO(3) planning relative error decreased by 42.5% on average; 7-DOF iiwa paths improved by 3.89% in length and 4.74% in trajectory time on average [11][12].

---

## Key Challenges Addressed

### Computational Burden: Scaling IRIS/IRIS-NP

IRIS/IRIS-NP can be expensive for many seeds. Scaling strategies include:

- **IRIS-NP2 and IRIS-ZO [3][6][32]:** The FastIris methods achieve order-of-magnitude speedups. IRIS-NP2 uses sampling strategies (greedy and ray) to efficiently decide which collision pairs to consider. IRIS-ZO is a massively-parallel zero-order optimization strategy that uses only collision checking (no gradient information). IRIS-ZO achieves an order-of-magnitude speed advantage over IRIS-NP, which is extended roughly by an additional order of magnitude by parallelizing it with a GPU.

- **Seed Selection Reduction:** Only grow regions from a subset of PRM nodes (e.g., clustered nodes, nodes on the optimal path)

- **Implicit Graph Search [7][19]:** IxG and GCS* avoid explicitly constructing the full GCS graph. Instead, they interleave graph search with trajectory optimization, only optimizing over the fraction of the graph explored by the search. The joint batch optimization in GCS means that for any given task, the size of the GCS problem is independent of the planning query, making it slow even for trivial queries. Motivated by the observation that the trajectory solution lies only on a fraction of the set of convex sets, implicit graph search methods achieve faster planning while maintaining completeness and optimality guarantees.

### Coverage Gaps

Ensuring the generated convex sets cover enough free space for the GCS to find a feasible path:

- **Multiple Seeds:** Use enough seeds to cover the free space. The IRIS algorithm grows regions from starting points, and the union of these regions should cover the connectivity of the free space
- **GCS Completeness:** GCS is complete and globally optimal within the convex decomposition [4][14]. It guarantees collision-free motion along piecewise polynomial trajectories and completeness/global optimality within a convex decomposition
- **Overlap Between Regions:** Ensure regions overlap to provide continuous connectivity. The intersection graph of the decomposition encodes connectivity
- **Approximate Convex Decomposition of Polyhedra [11]:** The H-VACD method computes a set of convex volumes that fully enclose the input polyhedron while minimizing additional volume outside it. Contrary to the decomposition of the polyhedron into convex parts, the convex volumes cover the polyhedron, but also include additional volume outside of it

### Narrow Passages

How the pipeline handles thin corridors that PRM struggles with and where convex sets are hard to grow:

- **GCS Advantage in Narrow Corridors [5][10]:** ST-GCS offers a fundamentally different, deterministic approach by systematically covering the entire collision-free space-time region with convex sets, inherently capturing spatiotemporal bottlenecks and avoiding the pitfalls of random sampling. Results demonstrate how restricting the collision-free region to space-time convex sets grants ST-GCS a unique advantage, especially in 'narrow corridors' or crowded settings [5]

- **Bézier Curve Guarantees [1][14]:** Using Bézier curves with convex hull properties guarantees collision-free trajectories. The convex hull property of Bézier curves allows constraints on positions and derivatives for all time using linear constraints [15]

- **IRIS Growth in Narrow Passages:** IRIS/IRIS-NP will naturally grow regions that fill the free space available. In narrow passages, the resulting convex regions will be elongated and thin, matching the corridor shape

- **Sampling-Based Connection:** The PRM connection strategy ensures that even if individual convex regions are small in narrow passages, the graph connectivity captures the passage

### Non-Convex Obstacles

Handling complex obstacle geometries:

- **Nonlinear Programming [6][7]:** IRIS-NP uses nonlinear optimization to add the separating hyperplanes, enabling support for more general nonlinear constraints. IRIS-NP handles nonlinear kinematics mappings between task space and configuration space, allowing it to work with non-convex obstacles in workspace that become complex in C-space

- **Probabilistic Certification [6][7]:** IRIS-NP trades rigorous certification that regions are collision free for probabilistic certification and the benefit of faster region generation in the configuration-space coordinates. This avoids the need to explicitly compute the (non-convex) C-space obstacle representation

- **Parametrized Configuration Spaces [3][32]:** Both IRIS-ZO and IRIS-NP2 are extended to work in parametrized configuration spaces (e.g., for constrained bimanual manipulation)

### Dimensionality Scaling

How this scales to 3D, 6D, or higher-dimensional configuration spaces:

- **High-Dimensional Performance [1][14]:** On a seven-degree-of-freedom manipulator, GCS can outperform widely-used sampling-based planners by finding higher-quality trajectories in less time, and in 14 dimensions (or more) it can solve problems to global optimality which are hard to approach with sampling-based techniques. GCS has a polynomial time algorithm for dimensions that for any dimension greater than four. The convex relaxation is statistically almost always everything we've tried it on is tight [1]

- **IRIS-NP Scalability [6][7]:** IRIS-NP can scale to a dual-arm manipulator (14-DOF) and can handle additional nonlinear constraints using the same machinery. IRIS-NP can generate reasonably sized collision-free regions in about one minute, making it practical for offline planning

- **Curse of Dimensionality [2]:** The volume ratio of free space to ball volume increases rapidly with dimension, revealing the curse of dimensionality's effect on PRMs. However, GCS mitigates this by replacing point samples with large convex regions

- **Geodesic Convexity [13]:** A robot that has revolute joints without any limits has an inherently non-Euclidean configuration space, but one can still consider 'geodesically-convex' sets, akin to convex sets in Euclidean space. Drake supports this concept

### Quality Metrics

How to evaluate the quality of the generated GCS graph:

- **Path Optimality Gap (δopt) [14][25]:** The gap between the trajectory cost found by GCS and the true global optimum. On 95% of the environments GCS designs a trajectory with optimality gap δopt ≤ 1%, and even in the worst case, we only have δopt = 2.9%. For dual-arm manipulation, largest optimality gap was 13.9%

- **Solve Time:** Average runtime for GCS. For quadrotor through buildings: 2.65 seconds average. For dual-arm manipulation: 21-185 seconds. For maze: 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP)

- **Coverage Ratio:** The fraction of the relevant free space that is covered by the union of convex sets. This can be estimated by Monte Carlo sampling (sample points in free space and check if they fall in any convex region)

- **Number of Binary Variables:** GCS reduces the number of binary variables dramatically. For maze planning (2,500 cells): 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10⁷ required by existing mixed-integer planners [14]

- **Region Quality Metrics [3]:** Number of hyperplanes (fewer = better for downstream computation), polytope volume (larger = better), and collision probability (controlled by the termination condition)

- **Path Length / Trajectory Duration Improvement [11][12]:** For PGD-GCS refinement, paths are on average 20.60% shorter in ℝ¹⁴ configuration space after applying the post-processing step, and trajectory time improves by 31.02%

- **Comparison with Baselines [14]:** GCS trajectories have a lower cost in all the tasks in the benchmark. GCS is also as fast or even faster than the sampling-based competitors

---
