# Dynamic constraints in implicit form

There is another, seemingly subtle but potentially important, opportunity that can be exploited in a few of these transcriptions, if our main interest is in optimizing systems with significant multibody dynamics. In some cases, we can actually write the dynamics constraints directly in their implicit form. We've [introduced this idea already](lyapunov.html#implicit) in the context of Lyapunov analysis. In many cases, it is nicer or more efficient to obtain the equations of motion in an implicit form, ${\bf g}(\bx,\bu,\dot\bx) = 0$, and to avoid ever having to solve for the explicit form $\dot\bx = {\bf f}(\bx,\bu).$ This can become even more important when we consider systems for which the explicit form doesn't have a unique solution -- we will see examples of this when we study trajectory optimization through contact because the Coulomb model for friction actually results in a differential inclusion instead of a differential equation.

The collocation methods, which operate on the dynamic constraints at collocation points directly in their continuous form, can use the implicit form directly. It is possible to write a time-stepping (discrete-time approximation) for direct transcription using implicit integrators -- again providing constraints in implicit form. The implicit form is harder to exploit in the shooting methods.

There should really be better versions of direct transcription and the collocation methods that are specialized for second-order systems. We should only have $\bq$ as a decision variable, and be able to impose the dynamics only on the second derivatives (the first derivatives are consistent by construction). This is one of the main talking points in DMOC, even though the emphasis is on the discrete mechanics.

# Solution techniques

The different transcriptions presented above represent different ways to map the (potentially continuous-time) optimal control problem into a finite set of decision variables, objectives, and constraints. But even once that choice is made, there are numerous approaches to solving this optimization problem. Any general approach to [nonlinear programming](optimization.html#nonlinear) can be applied here; in the python examples we've included so far, the problems are handed directly to the sequential-quadratic programming (SQP) solver SNOPT, or to the interior-point solver IPOPT.

There is also quite a bit of exploitable problem-specific structure in these trajectory optimization problems due to the sequential nature of the problem. As a result, there are some ideas that are fairly specific to the trajectory optimization formulation of optimal control, and customized solvers can often (and sometimes dramatically) outperform general purpose solvers.

This trajectory-optimization structure is easiest to discuss, and implement, in unconstrained formulations, so we will start there.

# Efficiently computing gradients

Providing gradients of the objectives and constraints to the solver is not strictly required -- most solvers will obtain them from finite differences if they are not provided -- but I feel strongly that for smooth problems the solvers are faster and more robust when exact gradients are provided (systems that make and break contact might be a different storySuh22b). Providing the gradients for the direct transcription methods is very straight-forward -- we simply provide the gradients for each constraint individually. But in the direct shooting approach, where we have removed the $\bx$ decision variables from the program but still write objectives and constraints in terms of $\bx$, it would become very inefficient to compute the gradients of each objective/constraint independently. We need to leverage the chain rule.

To be concise (and slightly more general), let us define $\bx[n+1]=f\_d(\bx[n],\bu[n])$ as the discrete-time approximation of the continuous dynamics; for example, the forward Euler integration scheme used above would give $f\_d(\bx[n],\bu[n]) = \bx[n]+f(\bx[n],\bu[n])dt.$ Then we have \[\pd{J}{\bu\_k} = \pd{\ell\_f(\bx[N])}{\bu\_k} + \sum\_{n=0}^{N-1} \left(\pd{\ell(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bx[n]} \pd{\bx[n]}{\bu\_k} + \pd{\ell(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bu\_k} \right), \] where the gradient of the state with respect to the inputs can be computed during the "forward simulation", \[ \pd{\bx[n+1]}{\bu\_k} = \pd{f\_d(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bx[n]} \pd{\bx[n]}{\bu\_k} + \pd{f\_d(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bu\_k}. \] These simulation gradients can also be used in the chain rule to provide the gradients of any constraints. Note that there are a lot of terms to keep around here, on the order of (state dim) $\times$ (control dim) $\times$ (number of time steps). Ouch. Note also that many of these terms are zero; for instance with the Euler integration scheme above $\pd{\bu[n]}{\bu\_k} = 0$ if $k\ne n$. (If this looks like I'm mixing two notations here, recall that I'm using $\bu\_k$ to represent the decision variable and $\bu[n]$ to represent the input used in the $n$th step of the simulation.)

 

# The special case of direct shooting without state constraints

By solving for $\bx(\cdot)$ ourselves, we've removed a large number of constraints from the optimization. If no additional state constraints are present, and the only gradients we need to compute are the gradients of the objective, then a surprisingly efficient algorithm emerges. I'll give the steps here without derivation, but will derive it in the Pontryagin section below:

1. Simulate forward: $$\bx[n+1] = f\_d(\bx[n],\bu\_n),$$ from $\bx[0] = \bx\_0$.
2. Calculate backwards: $$\lambda[n-1] = \pd{\ell(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bx[n]}^T + \pd{f(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bx[n]}^T \lambda[n],$$ from $\lambda[N-1]=\pd{\ell\_f(\bx[N])}{\bx[N]}$.
3. Extract the gradients: $$\pd{J}{\bu[n]} = \pd{\ell(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bu[n]} + \lambda[n]^T \pd{f(\bx[n],\bu[n])}{\bu[n]},$$ with $\pd{J}{\bu\_k} = \sum\_n \pd{J}{\bu[n]}\pd{\bu[n]}{\bu\_k}$.

Here $\lambda[n]$ is a vector the same size as $\bx[n]$ which has an interpretation as $\lambda[n]=\pd{J}{\bx[n+1]}^T$. The equation governing $\lambda$ is known as the *adjoint equation*, and it represents a dramatic efficiency improvement over calculating the huge number of simulation gradients described above. In case you are interested, yes the adjoint equation is exactly the *backpropagation algorithm* that is famous in the neural networks literature, or more generally a bespoke version of reverse-mode [automatic differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation). (The previous section would correspond to forward-mode automatic differentiation.)

 

# Penalty methods and the Augmented Lagrangian

In fact, in recent years we have seen a surge in popularity in robotics for doing trajectory optimization using (often special-purpose) solvers for unconstrained trajectory optimization, where the constrained problems are transformed into unconstrained problem via penalty methods.

Manually adding penalty terms to the cost function with user-specified cost weighting can be nasty business. Often this generates a significant amount of effort in "cost function tuning"; setting the weights too large can cause the problems to become numerically ill-conditioned, but setting them too small can allow unwanted constraint violations. The [*augmented Lagrangian*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augmented_Lagrangian_method) approach offers a principled solution to this problem, by automatically scheduling the weights in order to achieve "essentially exact" satisfaction of the constraints with finite penalties Bertsekas82, Nocedal06.

Methods based on the augmented Lagrangian are particularly popular for trajectory optimization these days Lin91+Toussaint14.

 

# Zero-order optimization

Cross-entropy method (CEM) Kobilarov12 and Model-predictive path-integral control (MPPI) Williams17.

In the last few years, we've seen trajectory optimization playing a major role in "model-based reinforcement learning", especially when the model is represented using a deep neural network (e.g. Li18+Li18a). Despite the fact that neural network toolboxes can provide efficient gradients, the gradient-free trajectory optimization methods described here normally the tool of choice. There are a few possible explanations for this. The trajectory optimization problem has local minima, and the zero-order optimizers do provide some aspect of "global optimization" (at least they tend to explore multiple possible minima before converging). Neural network models fit with limited data may even have more local minima than if one used the original physics model -- the standard regression loss could be small even if the neural representation of the function is locally bumpy/non-smooth. But I think the biggest reason for the popularity of the zero-order methods is that they are trivially parallelizable, and very nicely compatible with the existing GPU neural-network workflows. When rolling out 10,000 samples in parallel costs approximately the same as rolling out 1, then this certainly makes the zero-order methods more appealing.

 

# Getting good solutions... in practice.

As you begin to play with these algorithms on your own problems, you might feel like you're on an emotional roller-coaster. You will have moments of incredible happiness -- the solver may find very impressive solutions to highly nontrivial problems. But you will also have moments of frustration, where the solver returns an awful solution, or simply refuses to return a solution (saying "infeasible"). The frustrating thing is, you cannot distinguish between a problem that is actually infeasible, vs. the case where the solver was simply stuck in a local minima.

So the next phase of your journey is to start trying to "help" the solver along. There are two common approaches.

The first is tuning your cost function -- some people spend a lot of time adding new elements to the objective or adjusting the relative weight of the different components of the objective. This is a slippery slope, and I tend to try to avoid it (possibly to a fault; other groups tend to put out more compelling videos!).

The second approach is to give a better initial guess to your solver to put it in the vicinity of the "right" local minimal. I find this approach more satisfying, because for most problems I think there really is a "correct" formulation for the objective and constraints, and we should just aim to find the optimal solution. Once again, we do see a difference here between the direct shooting algorithms and the direct transcription / collocation algorithms. For shooting, we can only provide the solver with an initial guess for $\bu(\cdot)$, whereas the other methods allow us to also specify an initial guess for $\bx(\cdot)$ directly. I find that this can help substantially, even with very simple initializations. In the direct collocation examples for the swing-up problem of the Acrobot and cart-pole, simply providing the initial guess for $\bx(\cdot)$ as a straight line trajectory between the start and the goal was enough to help the solver find a good solution; in fact it was necessary.

I'm old enough now, though, that I've tired of playing games with finicky solvers that require hand-holding. In recent work, my group has been working on more robust "global" solutions to the motion planning problem, based on an idea call Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) Marcucci21. The initial transcriptions of motion planning into GCS were focused on kinematic trajectory optimization (as needed in robotic manipulation) Marcucci23a, but we are growing the capability towards dynamic (underactuated) trajectory optimization. [You can read more about here](https://manipulation.mit.edu/trajectories.html#gcs).

# Local Trajectory Feedback Design

Once we have obtained a locally optimal trajectory from trajectory optimization, we have found an open-loop trajectory that (at least locally) minimizes our optimal control cost. Up to numerical tolerances, this pair $\bu\_0(t), \bx\_0(t)$ represents a feasible solution trajectory of the system. But we haven't done anything, yet, to ensure that this trajectory is locally stable.

In fact, there are a few notable approximations that we've already made to get to this point: the integration accuracy of our trajectory optimization tends to be much less than the accuracy used during forward simulation (we tend to take bigger time steps during optimization to avoid adding too many decision variables), and the default convergence tolerance from the optimization toolboxes tend to satisfy the dynamic constraints only to around $10^{-6}$. As a result, if you were to simulate the optimized control trajectory directly *even from the exact initial conditions* used in / obtained from trajectory optimization, you might find that the state trajectory diverges from your planned trajectory.

There are a number of things we can do about this. It is possible to evaluate the local stability of the trajectory during the trajectory optimization, and add a cost or constraint that rewards open-loop stability (e.g. Mombaur05+Johnson16). This can be very effective (though it does tend to be expensive). But open-loop stability is a quite restrictive notion. A potentially more generally useful approach is to design a feedback controller to regulate the system back to the planned trajectory.

# Finite-horizon LQR

We have already developed one approach for [trajectory stabilization in the LQR chapter](lqr.html#finite_horizon_nonlinear). This is one of my favorite approaches to trajectory feedback, because it provides a (numerically) closed-form solution for the controller, $\bK(t),$ and even comes with a time-varying quadratic cost-to-go function, $S(t),$ that can be used for Lyapunov analysis.

The basic procedure is to create a time-varying linearization along the trajectory in the error coordinates: $\bar\bx(t) = \bx(t) - \bx\_0(t)$, $\bar\bu(t) = \bu(t)-\bu\_0(t)$, and $\dot{\bar{\bx}}(t) = {\bf A}(t)\bar\bx(t) + {\bf B}(t)\bar\bu(t).$ This linearization uses all of the same gradients of the dynamics that we have been using in our trajectory optimization algorithms. Once we have the time-varying linearization, then we can apply finite-horizon LQR (see the [LQR chapter](lqr.html#finite_horizon_nonlinear) for the details).

A major virtue of this approach is that we can proceed immediately to verifying the performance of the closed-loop system under the LQR policy. Specifically, we can apply the finite-time reachability analysis to obtain "funnels" that certify a desired notion of invariance -- guaranteeing that trajectories which start near the planned trajectory will stay near the planned trajectory. Please see the [finite-time reachability analysis](lyapunov.html#finite-time) section for those details. We will put all of these ideas together in the perching case-study below.

 

# Model-Predictive Control

The maturity, robustness, and speed of solving trajectory optimization using convex optimization leads to a beautiful idea: if we can optimize trajectories quickly enough, then we can use our trajectory optimization as a feedback policy. The recipe is simple: (1) measure the current state, (2) optimize a trajectory from the current state, (3) execute the first action from the optimized trajectory, (4) let the dynamics evolve for one step and repeat. This recipe is known as *model-predictive control* (MPC).

Despite the very computational nature of this controller (there is no closed-form representation of this policy; it is represented only implicitly as the solution of the optimization), there is a bounty of theoretical and algorithmic results on MPC Garcia89+Camacho13. The theoretical and practical aspects of Linear MPC are so well understood today that it is considered the de-facto generalization of LQR for controlling a linear system subject to (linear) constraints. And there are a few core ideas that practitioners should really understand.

# Receding-horizon MPC

One core idea is the concept of *receding-horizon* MPC. Since our trajectory optimization problems are formulated over a finite-horizon, we can think each optimization as reasoning about the next $N$ time steps. If our true objective is to optimize the performance over a horizon longer than $N$ (e.g. over the infinite horizon), then it is standard to continue solving for an $N$ step horizon on each evaluation of the controller. In this sense, the total horizon under consideration continues to move forward in time (e.g. to recede).

 

# Recursive feasibility

Some care must be taken in receding-horizon formulations because on each new step we are introducing new costs and constraints into the problem (the ones that would have been associated with time $N+1$ on the previous solve) -- it would be very bad to march forward in time solving convex optimization problems only to suddenly encounter a situation where the solver returns "infeasible!". One can design MPC formulations that guarantee *recursive feasibility* -- e.g. guarantee that if a feasible solution is found at time $n$, then the solver will also find a feasible solution at time $n+1$.

Perhaps the simplest mechanism for guaranteeing recursive feasibility in an optimization for stabilizing a fixed point, $(\bx^\*, \bu^\*)$, is to add a final-value constraint to the receding horizon, $\bx[N] = \bx^\*$. This idea is simple but important. Considering the trajectories/constraints in absolute time, then on step $k$ of the algorithm, we are optimizing for $\bx[k], ... , \bx[k+N],$ and $\bu[k], ..., \bu[k+N-1]$; let us say that we have found a feasible solution for this problem. The danger in receding-horizon control is that when we shift to the next step ($k+1$) we introduce constraints on the system at $\bx[k+N+1]$ for the first time. But if our feasible solution in step $k$ had $\bx[k+N] = \bx^\*$, then we know that setting $\bx[k+N+1] = \bx^\*, \bu[k+N] = \bu^\*$ is guaranteed to provide a feasible solution to the new optimization problem in step $k+1$. With feasibility guaranteed, the solver is free to search for a lower-cost solution (which may be available now because we've shifted the final-value constraint further into the future). It is also possible to formulate MPC problems that guarantee recursive feasibility even in the presence of modeling errors and disturbances (c.f. Bemporad99).

 

# MPC and Lyapunov functions

Even though the MPC policy is only defined implicitly as the result of an optimization problem, it is still possible to make Lyapunov stability arguments. If, in the receding-horizon MPC setting, in addition to recursive feasibility (of the *constraints*) we have the property that the *cost* added at step $k+N+1$ is less than or equal to the cost removed corresponding to step $k$. Then the optimal cost, $J(\bx,k)$, of the trajectory optimization is a Lyapunov function: $$\forall \bx, k, \quad J^\*({\bf f}(\bx, \bu^\*), k+1) \le J^\*(\bx, k).$$ Once again, a particularly simple way to achieve this is to have a final-value constraint at the $N$th step of every optimization, which gets me to an equilibrium configuration with zero cost. But, again, there are ways to extend this Lyapunov argument even in the presence of modeling errors and disturbances (c.f. Bemporad99).

Unlike the nice explicit time-varying quadratic Lyapunov functions that we get from finite-horizon LQR, this Lyapunov function in general does not admit a compact representation (this is the object of study in [explicit MPC](#explicit_mpc)), and is more difficult to use with e.g. sums-of-squares optimization.

# Case Study: A glider that can land on a perch like a bird

From 2008 til 2014, my group conducted a series of increasingly sophisticated investigations Cory08+Roberts09+Cory10a+Moore11a+Moore12+Moore14b which asked the question: can a fixed-wing UAV land on a perch like a bird?

 ![](figures/perch-sequence.jpg) 

Basic setup for the glider landing on a perch.

 

At the outset, this was a daunting task. When birds land on a perch, they pitch up and expose their wings to an "angle-of-attack" that far exceeds the typical flight envelope. Airplanes traditionally work hard to avoid this regime because it leads to aerodynamic "stall" -- a sudden loss of lift after the airflow separates from the wing. But this loss of lift is also accompanied by a significant increase in drag, and birds exploit this when they rapidly decelerate to land on a perch. Post-stall aerodynamics are a challenge for control because (1) the aerodynamics are time-varying (characterized by periodic vortex shedding) and nonlinear, (2) it is much harder to build accurate models of this flight regime, at least in a wind tunnel, and (3) stall implies a loss of attached flow on the wing and therefore on the control surfaces, so a potentially large reduction in control authority.

We picked the project initially thinking that it would be a nice example for model-free control (like reinforcement learning -- since the models were unknown). In the end, however, it turned out to be the project that really taught me about the power of model-based trajectory optimization and linear optimal control. By conducting dynamic system identification experiments in a motion capture environment, we were able to fit both surprisingly simple models (based on flat-plate theory) to the dynamicsCory08, and also more accurate models using "neural-network-like" terms to capture the residuals between the model and the data Moore14b. This made model-based control viable, but the dynamics were still complex -- while trajectory optimization should work, I was quite dubious about the potential for regulating to those trajectories with only linear feedback.

I was wrong. Over and over again, I watched time-varying linear quadratic regulators take highly nontrivial corrective actions -- for instance, dipping down early in the trajectory to gain kinetic energy or tipping up to dump energy out of the system -- in order to land on the perch at the final time. Although the quality of the linear approximation of the dynamics did degrade the farther that we got from the nominal trajectory, the validity of the controller dropped off much less quickly (even as the vector field changed, the direction that the controller needed to push did not). This was also the thinking that got me initially so interested in understanding the regions of attraction of linear control on nonlinear systems.

# Trajectory Optimization - Underactuated Robotics

This webpage is part of **Russ Tedrake's Underactuated Robotics course at MIT** (Spring 2024). It covers **trajectory optimization** as a practical computational approach to optimal control for high-dimensional systems, focusing on finding optimal control solutions from a single initial condition rather than over the entire state space.

## Key Topics Covered:

### Problem Formulation
- Trajectory optimization minimizes a finite-horizon cost function $\ell_f(\bx(t_f)) + \int \ell(\bx(t),\bu(t))dt$ subject to dynamics $\dot{\bx} = f(\bx,\bu)$ and initial condition $\bx_0$.
- Additional constraints (collision avoidance, input limits) can be included.

### Convex Formulations for Linear Systems
- **Direct Transcription**: Adds both $\bx[\cdot]$ and $\bu[\cdot]$ as decision variables, with dynamics as explicit linear constraints. Produces convex QPs/LPs for linear systems.
- **Direct Shooting**: Uses only $\bu[\cdot]$ as decision variables, solving for $\bx$ via forward simulation. Still convex for linear/quadratic objectives.
- **Trade-offs**: Direct transcription has better numerical conditioning, easier state constraint handling, and parallelizability; direct shooting has fewer variables.

### Nonconvex Trajectory Optimization
- Nonlinear dynamics make the problem nonconvex.
- **Direct Collocation**: Represents trajectories as piecewise polynomials (cubic splines for $\bx$, linear for $\bu$), with derivative constraints at collocation points (midpoints). Accurate to third order.
- **Pseudo-spectral Methods**: Use global polynomial basis functions (Lagrange polynomials) with collocation at Gauss-Lobatto or Gauss-Radau points.
- Gradients can be computed efficiently via the **adjoint equation** (reverse-mode automatic differentiation / backpropagation).

### Local Trajectory Feedback
- Finite-horizon LQR can be used to stabilize trajectories via time-varying linearization.
- **Model-Predictive Control (MPC)**: Receding-horizon formulation where trajectory optimization is solved online as a feedback policy. Concepts of recursive feasibility and Lyapunov stability are discussed.

### Case Study: Perching Glider
- A decade-long project (2008-2014) on fixed-wing UAV perching like a bird, using post-stall aerodynamics.
- Simple flat-plate foam gliders with a single elevator actuator were used successfully.
- Time-varying LQR proved highly effective for trajectory stabilization despite nonlinear dynamics.

### Practical Advice
- Initial guesses matter significantly, especially for $\bx(\cdot)$ in direct transcription/collocation.
- Augmented Lagrangian methods offer principled handling of constraints.
- Zero-order methods (CEM, MPPI) are popular for model-based RL with neural network models.
- **Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS)** provides more robust global solutions for motion planning.

Research Topic 1: Technical Feasibility of PRM + Convex Decomposition Pipeline for Generating GCS Safety Regions

Background: The Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) algorithm (from Tobia Marcucci, et al., MIT) is a motion planning and trajectory optimization framework that solves a shortest path problem over a graph where each vertex is associated with a convex set. Currently, the convex sets (safety regions) in GCS are typically generated through a combination of manual seeding and automated tools like IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) or IRIS-NP, which are run offline with human guidance.

Query: Investigate the technical feasibility of the following pipeline:
1. Use a Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm (or improved variants like PRM*, SPARS, SPARTA, or lazy PRM) to generate a static connectivity graph of the free space in a robotics/planning environment.
2. Apply convex decomposition and optimization algorithms (such as IRIS, IRIS-NP, CIDR (Convex Iterative Decomposition of Regions), or other convex region growing methods) on the nodes and/or edges of the PRM graph to automatically construct convex safety regions.
3. Feed these automatically generated convex sets into the GCS algorithm for path solving.

Specific questions to answer:
- What are the theoretical connections between PRM sampling/connectivity and convex region decomposition? Is there existing literature combining sampling-based planners with convex optimization?
- How can PRM milestones (nodes) serve as seeds for convex region growing algorithms like IRIS? What are the geometric properties that make a PRM node a good or bad seed?
- How should the PRM graph's edges inform convex decomposition? E.g., should convex sets be grown along edges, around nodes, or between connected nodes?
- What are the key challenges: overlapping convex sets, coverage completeness, computational complexity of the decomposition, and handling narrow passages in the environment?
- What PRM variants are best suited for this pipeline (e.g., PRM* for asymptotic optimality, SPARS for sparsity, or bridge-test PRM for narrow passages)?
- How does the quality (size, number, overlap) of the generated convex sets affect GCS solver performance?

Provide a thorough technical analysis of feasibility, including reference to relevant algorithms and their properties.

--- SOURCE 1: Motion planning around obstacles with convex optimization ---
URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375669203_Motion_planning_around_obstacles_with_convex_optimization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), a motion planning framework that enables convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan collision-free trajectories around obstacles. The key insight is using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets to design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem, which is typically very tight. A cheap postprocessing of the relaxation solution is almost always sufficient to identify a globally optimal collision-free trajectory.

The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity. It reduces the planning problem to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. The method is sound (trajectories satisfy all constraints) and complete up to the conservatism of space decomposition.

Key results include:
- **Maze planning (2,500 cells)**: GCS finds optimal trajectories with 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10^7 required by existing mixed-integer planners. Solved in 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP).
- **Quadrotor flying through buildings (100 random environments)**: 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, worst case 2.9%. Average runtime 2.65 seconds.
- **7-DOF robot arm comparison with PRM**: GCS finds shorter trajectories faster online than both standard PRM and PRM with shortcutting. All trajectories are optimal (δopt=0) within the space decomposition.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF)**: GCS plans coordinated motions including arm crossing, near-self-collision configurations, and handoffs. Largest optimality gap 13.9%, runtimes 21-185 seconds.

GCS uses Bèzier curves for trajectory parameterization, guaranteeing safety at all times with no discretization error. The free space is decomposed into convex safe regions Q_i, and an intersection graph encodes connectivity. The method scales polynomially with the number of regions and curve degree.

The paper argues GCS generalizes PRM by extending collision-free samples to convex regions inflated as much as obstacles allow, reducing combinatorial complexity. It handles differential costs and constraints, exploits combinatorial structure, and has low runtimes. The implementation is available in the open-source software Drake.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Here, we present a framework that enables convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan trajectories around obstacles. Specifically, we focus on collision-free motion planning with costs and constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory.", "Using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem. We show that this relaxation is typically very tight, to the point that a cheap postprocessing of its solution is almost always sufficient to identify a collision-free trajectory that is globally optimal (within the parameterized class of curves).", "Through numerical and hardware experiments, we demonstrate that our planner, which we name GCS, can find better trajectories in less time than widely used sampling-based algorithms and can reliably design trajectories in high-dimensional complex environments.", "On 95% of the environments GCS designs a trajectory with optimality gap δopt ≤ 1%, and, even in the worst case, we only have δopt = 2.9%.", "GCS can be thought of as a generalization of PRM, where each collision-free sample is extended to a collision-free convex region, that is inflated as much as the obstacles allow."

--- SOURCE 2: Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) Optimization ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/graphs-of-convex-sets-gcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) is a mixed discrete-continuous optimization framework that integrates graph search with convex optimization, primarily used for path planning and control in robotics. In GCS, graph structure represents combinatorial choices, and each selected vertex or edge carries a convex optimization problem. The framework generalizes classical problems like shortest path, TSP, spanning tree, and assignment by coupling discrete decisions with continuous convex program solvers.

**Foundational Model:** A general GCS problem selects an admissible subgraph along with continuous variables on selected vertices. Edge costs need not be static and can encode distances, control-theoretic stage costs, or continuity constraints. The shortest-path problem in GCS is NP-hard.

**Exact Formulations:** The standard exact formulation uses mixed-integer convex programs (MICP) via perspective/homogenization operators. Convex relaxations (dropping integrality) are often very tight but not exact in general. Tools like GCSOPT automatically transform ILP models into MICPs.

**Search Algorithms:** Several efficient algorithms have been developed: A*-GCS (uses heuristics on representative points, provable lower bounds), GCS* (forward heuristic search, complete and cost-optimal), IxG/IxG* (interleaves graph search with convex optimization), and multi-query SPP (offline SDP for lower bounds, online in milliseconds).

**Temporal Logic Integration:** GCS has been integrated with LTL and STL for symbolic task planning with continuous motion. For LTL, product graphs combine transition systems with finite automata; for STL, timed automata are used. Reported benchmarks include a 30-DoF humanoid solved in ~7.72 seconds and a 5-key/5-door problem in 5.82 seconds.

**Space-Time Planning:** ST-GCS adds time as an optimization dimension, enabling multi-robot planning in dynamic environments. Applications include autonomous driving (with Bézier curves and polynomial time-scaling) and game-theoretic highway driving scenarios.

**Limitations:** GCS problems remain NP-hard in general. Relaxation quality is problem-dependent. Model fidelity may be traded for convexity (e.g., small-slip assumptions in driving). Augmented formulations for TSP remain exponential. Software ecosystem includes GCSOPT, Drake, MOSEK, CVXPY, and CLARABEL.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) are a mixed discrete-continuous optimization framework in which graph structure represents combinatorial choices and each selected vertex or edge carries a convex optimization problem.", "A defining feature of GCS is that edge costs and feasibility need not be static. An edge may encode a true distance, a control-theoretic stage cost, a continuity constraint between trajectory segments, or feasibility through an infinite cost outside a convex coupling set.", "The standard exact formulation of shortest paths in GCS is a mixed-integer convex program built from perspective or homogenization operators.", "A central empirical fact in the literature is that the convex relaxation obtained by dropping integrality is often very tight, but it is not exact in general.", "The method guarantees soundness for co-safe and full LTL, probabilistic completeness under the stated relaxation-and-rounding assumptions, polynomial complexity in the number of control points and the configuration dimension for the GCS solve itself, and it scales to problems including a 30-DoF humanoid; one reported benchmark solves a '5 keys, 5 doors' problem in 5.82 seconds, and the 30-DoF humanoid example in about 7.72 seconds."

URL: https://slides.com/russtedrake/periscope-gcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents research on "Graphs of Convex Sets" (GCS), a framework for solving motion planning and optimization problems that combine discrete graph structures with continuous convex optimization. Key contributions include:

- **Two key ingredients**: (1) The linear programming formulation of shortest path problems on discrete graphs, and (2) Convex formulations of continuous motion planning (without obstacle navigation), such as kinematic trajectory optimization for robot arms.
- **GCS formulation**: For each vertex i in a graph V, there is a compact convex set X_i ⊂ ℝ^d where a point x_i ∈ X_i is chosen. Edge lengths are given by convex functions ℓ(x_i, x_j). The motion planning problem uses ℓ_{i,j}(x_i, x_j) = |x_i - x_j|₂.
- **Key results**: The convex relaxation is tight (solves to global optimality). Previous formulations were intractable, requiring 6.25 × 10^6 binaries. The approach transcribes to a mixed-integer convex program with a very tight relaxation, solving orders of magnitude faster than previous work. Solving only the convex optimization (+rounding) is almost always sufficient to obtain the globally optimal solution.
- **Applications**: Guaranteed collision-free motion planning along piecewise polynomial trajectories with completeness/global optimality within convex decomposition. Also applicable to traveling salesman problems with neighborhoods (orders of magnitude faster) and task and motion planning.
- **Additional context**: The page references two related papers: "Shortest Paths in Graphs of Convex Sets" (Marcucci, Umenberger, Parrilo, Tedrake) and "Motion Planning around Obstacles with Convex Optimization" (Marcucci, Petersen, von Wrangel, Tedrake), both available on arXiv.
- **Presented by**: Russ Tedrake, a roboticist at MIT and TRI.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the DSpace@MIT repository entry for Tobia Marcucci's doctoral thesis titled "Graphs of Convex Sets with Applications to Optimal Control and Motion Planning," submitted in May 2024 to MIT's Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science. The thesis introduces a new class of problems at the intersection of combinatorial and convex optimization, called Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS). In this framework, each vertex in a graph is paired with a convex program, and each edge couples two programs through additional convex costs and constraints. The key contribution is an efficient, unified method for solving any GCS problem by formulating it as a Mixed-Integer Convex Program (MICP) that can be solved to global optimality using branch-and-bound solvers or approximately via rounding. The work focuses on the Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, with applications to optimal control of dynamical systems and collision-free motion planning. The techniques are implemented in two open-source software packages: Drake (a mature robotics software) and gcspy (a lightweight Python package). The thesis is 3.9 MB in PDF format, available under "In Copyright - Educational Use Permitted" terms, with the persistent link hdl.handle.net/1721.1/156598.
</summary>

# Superfast Configuration-Space Convex Set Computation on GPUs for Online Motion Planning

This paper presents a GPU-accelerated approach for constructing probabilistically collision-free convex sets in robot configuration space for online motion planning in changing environments.

## Key Contributions

1. **EI-ZO Algorithm**: The authors propose "Edge Inflation Zero-Order" (EI-ZO), which inflates collision-free line segments into sequences of convex sets (SCS) using massive GPU parallelism. Unlike prior methods that inflate points, EI-ZO guarantees the resulting polytope contains the original collision-free line segment.

2. **Motion Planning Pipeline**: The pipeline combines:
   - Dynamic Roadmaps (DRMs) for rapid path finding
   - EI-ZO for inflating piecewise-linear paths into convex sets
   - Decomposition-based motion planning (DBMP) for trajectory optimization
   - Iterative collision recovery mechanism

3. **GPU Implementation**: The authors provide a CUDA-based implementation (CSDecomp library) that minimizes CPU-GPU data transfer, using thread-level parallelization for sampling, collision checking, and optimization.

## Results

- **17.1× faster** than nonlinear trajectory optimization baseline
- **27.9% increase in reliability** (72% → 100% success rate on simulation benchmark)
- Validated on simulation benchmark (2D and 7D) and KUKA iiwa 7 robot with perception

## Background

The work addresses a key bottleneck in DBMPs: constructing convex decompositions of the collision-free configuration space. Prior methods were slow, scaled poorly, and only worked in static environments. The authors extend IRIS-ZO to handle line segments rather than points, making set construction fast enough for real-time use in changing environments.

## Methodology

EI-ZO iteratively samples configurations within the current polytope, finds collisions, and places separating hyperplanes tangent to sub-level sets of the distance function to the line segment. The algorithm uses a probabilistic termination condition guaranteeing that at most an ε-fraction of the polytope volume is in collision with probability 1-δ.

The pipeline also includes a collision recovery mechanism that refines sets when the optimized trajectory contains collisions, and supports inflating multiple paths for better coverage.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Improving Sparse Roadmap Spanners - Rutgers CS ---
URL: https://www.cs.rutgers.edu/~kb572/pubs/spars2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Dobson and Bekris (Rutgers University) presents SPARS2, an extension of the SPARS algorithm for building sparse roadmap spanners in motion planning. SPARS2 provides probabilistic completeness and asymptotic near-optimality while dramatically reducing memory requirements during construction compared to prior methods. The key innovation is that SPARS2 does not require building a dense underlying roadmap (PRM∗) in parallel with the spanner, unlike its predecessor SPARS. Instead, it uses localized sampling and auxiliary information to determine when to add nodes for coverage, connectivity, interfaces, or shortcuts. The algorithm maintains the property that the probability of adding new nodes converges to zero as iterations increase, enabling a natural stopping criterion. The paper provides theoretical analysis proving probabilistic completeness, connected interfaces, and asymptotic near-optimality with additive cost. Experimental results in SE(2) and SE(3) environments (using OMPL's "2D Maze" and "Bugtrap") show SPARS2 uses approximately two orders of magnitude less memory during offline construction than SPARS or PRM∗, while returning competitive quality paths that often exceed theoretical guarantees. SPARS2 produces slightly denser final spanners than SPARS but still orders of magnitude smaller than PRM∗, leading to very efficient online query resolution. Key parameters include stretch factor t, visibility distance ∆, and sampling parameters δ and k.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: [PDF] Sparse Roadmap Spanners for Asymptotically Near-Optimal Motion ... ---
URL: https://www.cs.rutgers.edu/~kb572/pubs/DobsonBekris_Spanner.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Andrew Dobson and Kostas E. Bekris (Rutgers University) presents SPARS and SPARS2, algorithms for constructing sparse roadmap spanners for asymptotically near-optimal motion planning. The key problem addressed is that asymptotically optimal planners like PRM* produce dense roadmaps that include all sampled configurations, making them impractical for resource-constrained robots due to memory and online query efficiency.

**Key Contributions:**
- SPARS builds a sparse roadmap spanner with three theoretical guarantees: (a) probabilistic completeness, (b) asymptotic near-optimality with additive cost (paths of length: t·c* + 4·Δ), and (c) asymptotic sparsity (probability of adding new nodes converges to zero as iterations increase).
- SPARS2 removes the dependency on maintaining a dense graph (like PRM*) during construction, significantly reducing memory requirements while preserving the same theoretical properties.
- Four criteria determine when a sample is added to the spanner: coverage (guards), connectivity (bridges), interface nodes, and shortcut nodes (for path quality).

**Methodology:**
- SPARS builds a dense PRM* graph in parallel with the spanner to compute shortest C-space paths between interfaces.
- SPARS2 uses conservative approximations via local sampling (k samples in δ-neighborhood) and bookkeeping information stored on spanner nodes, avoiding the dense graph entirely.
- The approach provides a natural stopping criterion (similar to Visibility-based PRM) based on consecutive failed samples.

**Experimental Results:**
- Simulations in OMPL with rigid body motion planning (SE(2) and SE(3)) show SPARS2 uses significantly less memory during construction than SPARS.
- Resulting graphs are orders of magnitude smaller than asymptotically optimal roadmaps for the same construction time.
- Path quality from spanners is competitive with PRM* and significantly better than theoretical bounds.
- Rate of node addition decreases over time, supporting the finite-size data structure claim.
- SPARS returns a slightly smaller final spanner than SPARS2 (since SPARS has access to the dense graph).

**Key Parameters:**
- M: termination criterion threshold
- t: stretch factor of the spanner
- δ and Δ: distance thresholds (Δ = visibility range, δ = local neighborhood radius, typically δ << Δ)
- k: parameter for SPARS2's local sampling

This is the first work to argue about the existence of finite data structures with near-optimality guarantees for continuous path planning.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The method provides the following properties: (a) probabilistic completeness, (b) asymptotic near-optimality and (c) the probability of adding nodes to the spanner converges to zero as iterations increase. The last point suggests that finite-size data structures with asymptotic near-optimality in continuous spaces may indeed exist.", "To the best of the author's knowledge, no previous line of work argues about the existence of finite data structures with some form of near-optimality guarantee for continuous path planning.", "The resulting graph is orders of magnitude smaller than the asymptotically optimal roadmap for the same construction time.", "Interestingly, paths returned by the spanners are very competitive to those computed by PRM* for the same amount of construction time and significantly better than the theoretical guarantees.", "The rate of nodes added to the spanner does decrease over time."

--- SOURCE 4: Probabilistic roadmap ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_roadmap

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The probabilistic roadmap (PRM) is a motion planning algorithm in robotics used to find a collision-free path between a robot's starting configuration and a goal configuration. The algorithm works by randomly sampling points from the robot's configuration space, testing if they are in free space, and connecting nearby configurations using a local planner. PRM consists of two phases: a construction phase where a roadmap (graph) is built by sampling random configurations and connecting them to neighbors, and a query phase where start and goal configurations are connected to the graph and a path is found using Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm. PRM is provably probabilistically complete—as the number of sampled points increases, the probability of finding a path (if one exists) approaches one. The invention of PRM is credited to Lydia E. Kavraki (1996). Many variants exist that modify sampling and connection strategies for faster performance.
</summary>

Kavraki.

--- SOURCE 5: Sparsification of motion-planning roadmaps by edge ... ---
URL: https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/2014/11/0278364914556517.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper presents RSEC (Roadmap Sparsification by Edge Contraction), an algorithm for reducing the size of motion-planning roadmaps while minimizing path quality degradation. Roadmaps constructed by algorithms like PRM* for asymptotically-optimal motion planning are often extremely dense, leading to prohibitive storage requirements and long query processing times.

The RSEC algorithm adapts edge-contraction techniques from computer graphics surface simplification to roadmap simplification. The primitive operation contracts a roadmap edge (u,v) to a new vertex p, connecting p to all neighboring vertices of the original edge's endpoints. The algorithm maintains a bounded-drift invariant, ensuring that vertices in the sparsified graph do not move more than a distance d from their ancestors.

Key technical components include:
- A degradation factor utility function that bounds the increase in path length due to edge contractions
- A priority queue ordering edges by minimizing the sum of squares of degradation factors
- Edge re-insertion to achieve higher compression rates

Experimental results on four scenarios (Easy, Cubicles, Bug trap, Alpha puzzle) using the OMPL library show:
- Compression of over 97% of edges and vertices with only 4% average path length degradation
- Compression factors up to 48x in some scenarios
- Negligible connectivity degradation
- Superior performance compared to SPANNER (a graph-spanner approach), achieving higher compression rates with better path quality

The authors note RSEC is an offline algorithm and suggest future directions including hybrid approaches combining RSEC with SPANNER, extending to online settings, and handling systems with complex dynamics.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
We compress more than 97% of the edges and vertices of a given roadmap at the cost of degradation of average shortest path length by at most 4%.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Differing Formulations of GCS for Motion Planning ---
URL: https://blog.tommycohn.com/2023/03/differing-formulations-of-gcs-for.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn compares two formulations of Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) for robot motion planning. The first formulation, the "Conjugate Graph," uses intersections of collision-free sets as graph nodes, with edges representing paths between sets that share a constituent set. The second, the "Overlap Graph," places control points in each free region for Bézier curve trajectories and constrains endpoints to be equal on overlaps between sets. The author concludes that while the conjugate graph is more straightforward to implement and allows for preprocessing to compute lower bounds, the overlap graph is superior for future use because it parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, supports broader optimization problems, and is likely to be the "official" formulation going forward. The conjugate graph's advantage in preprocessing (pruning edges/sets using lower bounds) comes with a hidden cost: when many convex sets overlap, the conjugate graph's size grows significantly, potentially negating preprocessing gains.
</summary>

But beyond that, there are few reasons to not go with the overlap graph formulation.", "The overlap graph formulation parameterizes a wider class of trajectories, enabling its use for broader optimization problems.", "In the conjugate graph formulation, it's easy to compute useful lower bounds. But in the overlap graph formulation, the lower bound is trivially zero, as all the points in the set could be made identical.", "GCS is still a young framework, and there is still a lot of room for clever heuristics, preprocessing techniques, and overall engineering effort to improve the algorithm."

--- SOURCE 7: [PDF] A* for Bounding Shortest Paths in the Graphs of Convex Sets ---
URL: https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICAPS/article/download/36127/38281/40200

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper (ICAPS 2025) presents A* for Graphs of Convex Sets (A*-GCS), a novel algorithm that fuses convex programming with heuristic information to find optimality guarantees for the Shortest Path Problem in the Graph of Convex Sets (SPP-GCS). SPP-GCS generalizes the classic shortest path problem by associating each vertex with a convex set, where the edge cost depends on the points selected from each set. The problem is NP-hard in general.

The key innovation is reversing the typical approach: first, A* is run using representative points (e.g., centroids) from each convex set to obtain a feasible solution, then a convex program is solved on subsets of vertices informed by A* to find a relaxed solution for lower bounds. A*-GCS initiates a best-first search from a cut-set S (containing the origin but not the destination) and iteratively expands it. It operates in two phases: Phase 1 (destination not in neighborhood of S) and Phase 2 (destination is in the neighborhood).

Theoretical results establish that A*-GCS terminates in at most |V|-1 iterations and produces valid lower bounds. Numerical results on 2D mazes, axis-aligned bar instances, and large 3D village maps (up to 11,258 vertices, 321,603 edges) demonstrate that A*-GCS reduces convex program sizes by over 45% on average and achieves significant computation time savings (up to 61-65% reduction) compared to solving the full convex relaxation baseline, while maintaining comparable optimality gaps. When the heuristic weight is increased, cut-set sizes and run times decrease further.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Planning Shorter Paths in Graphs of Convex Sets by Undistorting Parametrized Configuration Spaces ---
URL: https://arxiv.org/html/2411.18913v1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents a method to extend Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) trajectory optimization to handle nonconvex objectives while maintaining feasibility guarantees. GCS is a technique that represents configuration space as a union of convex sets and optimizes over discrete paths through these sets while simultaneously optimizing continuous trajectories within them. The key problem addressed is that nonlinear parametrizations of configuration space (used to handle cases like kinematic loops, 3D rotations, and rational kinematics) distort distances, causing convex objectives to yield suboptimal paths in the original space.

The authors propose using Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) as a post-processing step to optimize nonconvex objectives that represent the true (undistorted) cost in the original configuration space. Since constraints remain convex, projection back to feasibility is always possible through a quadratic program. The method is tested on three domains:

1. **Constrained Bimanual Motion Planning**: Two robot arms moving with a fixed transform between end effectors. The method reduces path length by 20.60% on average in the ℝ14 configuration space, reduces trajectory time by 31.02%, and balances the distance traveled between both arms (imbalance metric shifts toward zero).

2. **Planning over SO(3) with Euler Angles**: The method reduces relative error in path length by 42.5% on average compared to standard Euler angle GCS planning, with little additional runtime (0.62 seconds solver time).

3. **Rational Parametrizations of Robot Kinematics**: For a 7-DOF robot, path lengths shorten by 3.89% and trajectory times by 4.74% on average. Improvements are more significant when joints travel near their limits.

The method also enables optimization of general nonconvex objectives like curvature, which can produce trajectories with larger radii of curvature that are traversable more quickly after time-optimal path parametrization (TOPP).

Key implementation details include: backtracking line search for optimal step sizes, gradient precompilation using JAX, affine projections to reduce costly QP solves, and convergence criteria based on moving average of cost. The trade-off is additional computation time (e.g., 0.055 seconds for bimanual, 4.08 seconds for SO(3) including setup overhead), but the authors argue this is worthwhile for applications requiring high-quality trajectories with guarantees.
</summary>

Since we keep constraints convex, a small convex program can always project infeasible solutions back to feasibility.", "In constrained bimanual motion planning, our post-processing step produces paths that are more balanced between the arms, 20% shorter on average, and 31.02% faster after being time-parametrized.", "For Euler angles, the paths are 40% shorter on average."

--- SOURCE 9: Tobia Marcucci: A Tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) - YouTube ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N-qSSUX83Rk

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Autonomy Talks - Tobia Marcucci: A Tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS)

## Overview
Prof. Tobia Marcucci (UCSB, ECE and Mechanical Engineering) presented a tutorial on Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), an optimization framework developed during his PhD at MIT and refined at Amazon. The talk was delivered on November 18, 2025, as part of the Autonomy Talks series.

## Core Problem
Many robotics problems require simultaneous optimization of high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous control. Examples include:
- Atlas robot parkour (sequence of obstacles + continuous trajectories)
- Robot manipulation (making/breaking contacts + object positions)
- UAV trajectory optimization with obstacles (left/right decisions + continuous trajectories)
- Warehouse pick-and-place (object sorting + trajectory optimization)

## What is a Graph of Convex Sets (GCS)?
A GCS is a graph where:
- **Vertices** are paired with convex optimization problems (continuous variable Xv, convex constraint set, objective function)
- **Edges** couple vertex optimization problems through additional convex costs and constraints
- Unlike ordinary weighted graphs, weights are not fixed scalars but functions of underlying continuous variables

## Key Advantages
1. **Unified framework** bridging discrete and continuous optimization
2. **Leverages existing tools**: combines graph search/optimization (scalable) with convex optimization (mature continuous optimization technology)
3. **Accessible**: users define the graph structure, variables, and constraints; the framework handles the optimization automatically

## Problem Classes
Classical graph problems naturally generalize to GCS:
- Shortest Path in GCS
- Traveling Salesman Problem in GCS
- Minimum Spanning Tree in GCS
- Facility location, bipartite matching, etc.

## Solution Approach
Most GCS problems are NP-hard. The framework formulates them as Mixed Integer Convex Programs (MICP) by:
1. Encoding the graph structure using incidence vectors (binary variables for vertices/edges)
2. Translating GCS constraints using binary variables to activate/deactivate relevant parts
3. Convexifying bilinear constraints exactly (leveraging binary variable structure)
4. Efficiency depends on the tightness of the convex relaxation

## Applications Demonstrated
- **Solar-powered helicopter path planning**: shortest path through islands with recharging, solved in 24 seconds (convex relaxation gives 99%+ accuracy in fraction of a second)
- **School bus routing with mobile passengers**: Traveling Salesman variant where children can move to meet the bus
- **Camera surveillance placement**: Minimum Spanning Tree variant ensuring camera visibility
- **Motion planning and collision avoidance**: Shortest path through obstacles

## Software Tool
**GCSOPT**: Open-source Python library for solving real-world GCS problems in just a few lines of code. Handles the mathematical complexity automatically behind the scenes.

## Key Quote
The research addresses "the observation that at the core of many robotics problems is the need to simultaneously optimize high-level discrete decisions and low-level continuous decisions."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 13: [PDF] Sampling-Based Methods for Motion Planning with Constraints ---
URL: https://www.cs.rice.edu/~mmoll/publications/kingston2018sampling-based-methods-for-motion-planning.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a survey paper from the Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems (2018) by Kingston, Moll, and Kavraki from Rice University, reviewing sampling-based methods for motion planning with constraints. The paper addresses the challenge of planning motions for high-DOF robots (e.g., humanoids, mobile manipulators) that must satisfy task constraints (e.g., keeping a cup level, writing on a board, turning a valve).

Key concepts:
- **Constraint manifold X**: An implicit lower-dimensional space within configuration space Q defined by constraint function F(q)=0, where k equality constraints reduce effective DOF.
- **Sampling-based planning**: Methods like PRM and RRT that randomly sample configurations and build graphs/trees, providing probabilistic completeness guarantees.

The paper organizes constraint-handling methods along a spectrum of complexity:

1. **Relaxation**: Relaxes the constraint to ||F(q)||<ε, giving the manifold non-zero volume. Simple but inefficient; pushes constraint handling to the controller.
2. **Projection**: Uses iterative optimization (Jacobian pseudo-inverse gradient descent) to project sampled configurations onto the constraint manifold. Widely used in methods like CBiRRT2 and Task Constrained RRT.
3. **Tangent Space**: Computes the nullspace of the constraint Jacobian at a known satisfying configuration to generate new samples and local motions.

5. **Reparameterization**: Computes a new parameterization for direct sampling of constraint-satisfying configurations.
6. **Implicit Space Representation**: Uses alternative sampling strategies not dependent on uniform sampling.

--- SOURCE 14: Analysis of Sampling-Based Planners: PRMs ---
URL: https://blog.tommycohn.com/2025/02/analysis-of-sampling-based-planners-prms.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Tommy Cohn (a PhD student at MIT's Robot Locomotion Group) provides a theoretical analysis of the Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm, the first in a series on sampling-based planners. The PRM algorithm, introduced by Lydia Kavraki in 1996, is a multi-query motion planning algorithm that involves: (1) randomly sampling collision-free configurations via rejection sampling, (2) connecting nearby configurations using a local planner (e.g., straight-line paths checked for collisions) to build a graph, and (3) in the online phase, linking start and goal points into the roadmap and solving via graph search (Dijkstra's or A*).

The key analysis focuses on results from Ladd and Kavraki (2004) which proved a bound on the expected number of samples required to find a path. This bound is based on **path clearance** (ϵ-clear path: a path that maintains at least distance ϵ from obstacles). The analysis shows that an ϵ-clear path can be covered by balls of radius ϵ/2. By the Coupon Collector's Problem, the expected number of samples needed is bounded by N × H(N) (where N is the number of balls and H(N) is the harmonic number). For a path of length L, 2L/ϵ balls are needed. The bound demonstrates that the expected sample count is logarithmic in the ratio of path length to clearance. However, the volume ratio of free space to ball volume increases rapidly with dimension, revealing the curse of dimensionality's effect on PRMs.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article (Mathematics, 2025) presenting exact and heuristic algorithms for convex polygon decomposition. The problem involves partitioning a non-convex polygon into the smallest possible number of convex subpolygons, which is a key preprocessing step in applications such as robotic motion planning, 2D packing, pattern recognition, and manufacturing.

**Authors:** Johana Milena Martínez Contreras, Germán Fernando Pantoja Benavides, Astrid Xiomara Rodríguez, John Willmer Escobar, and David Álvarez-Martínez (affiliations: Universidad de Los Andes, Colombia; Tecnologico de Monterrey, Mexico; Universidad del Valle, Colombia).

**Key Contributions:**
1. An exact convex decomposition method inspired by Keil's dynamic-programming approach (Algorithm 1), which recursively subdivides the polygon into triangles and subpolygons, evaluating candidate merges to obtain minimal convex components (complexity O(n³)).
2. A heuristic algorithm that approximates decomposition by identifying and linking notches (concave vertices), selecting vertices with high visible neighbors, and exploring three-vertex configurations.
3. A visibility-preserving bridge transformation that converts polygons with holes into equivalent simple instances, enabling decomposition of more complex topologies.
4. A convex-union post-processing phase applied to both exact and heuristic outputs to further reduce the number of convex pieces.
5. A new publicly available dataset of polygons with holes, addressing the lack of standardized benchmark instances in the literature.
6. The exact model produces optimal decompositions for small and medium instances, while the heuristic achieves near-optimal solutions with significantly reduced computation times.

**Literature Review:** The paper reviews convex decomposition applications in topographic modeling, pattern recognition, packing/nesting problems, machine learning, and multi-robot terrain coverage. Key prior methods discussed include Keil's exact dynamic programming approach, Fernández et al.'s vector-dependency procedure, and Lien and Amato's approximate convex decomposition framework for polygons with holes.

**Methodology Details:**
- Visibility is defined as the ability to connect two points with a straight segment entirely inside the polygon without intersecting edges.
- Reference vertices include all concave (reflex) vertices plus the initial and final vertices of the polygon's boundary traversal.
- The exact algorithm uses dynamic programming, solving small subproblems once and storing information to avoid repetitive iterations.
- The heuristic processes vertices in counterclockwise order (simplifying implementation), drawing partially on Fernández et al.'s method.
- For polygons with holes, a bridge construction converts holed polygons into equivalent simple polygons while preserving structural relations.

**Algorithm 1 (Exact Convex Decomposition):** Input is vertex coordinates; output is coordinates of convex parts. Steps include computing angles, determining notches (concave vertices), finding visibility of vertices, ordering subpolygons, determining base triangles, and using dynamic programming to find minimum convex decomposition.

**Algorithm 2 (Visibility Between Points):** Determines which points are mutually visible using the v1v2 function, which evaluates the position of one point with respect to lines formed by another point, considering collinearity and intersection checks.

Research Topic 1: Technical Feasibility of PRM + Convex Decomposition Pipeline for Generating GCS Safety Regions

Background: The Graph of Convex Sets (GCS) algorithm (from Tobia Marcucci, et al., MIT) is a motion planning and trajectory optimization framework that solves a shortest path problem over a graph where each vertex is associated with a convex set. Currently, the convex sets (safety regions) in GCS are typically generated through a combination of manual seeding and automated tools like IRIS (Iterative Regional Inflation by Semidefinite programming) or IRIS-NP, which are run offline with human guidance.

Query: Investigate the technical feasibility of the following pipeline:
1. Use a Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) algorithm (or improved variants like PRM*, SPARS, SPARTA, or lazy PRM) to generate a static connectivity graph of the free space in a robotics/planning environment.
2. Apply convex decomposition and optimization algorithms (such as IRIS, IRIS-NP, CIDR (Convex Iterative Decomposition of Regions), or other convex region growing methods) on the nodes and/or edges of the PRM graph to automatically construct convex safety regions.
3. Feed these automatically generated convex sets into the GCS algorithm for path solving.

Specific questions to answer:
- What are the theoretical connections between PRM sampling/connectivity and convex region decomposition? Is there existing literature combining sampling-based planners with convex optimization?
- How can PRM milestones (nodes) serve as seeds for convex region growing algorithms like IRIS? What are the geometric properties that make a PRM node a good or bad seed?
- How should the PRM graph's edges inform convex decomposition? E.g., should convex sets be grown along edges, around nodes, or between connected nodes?
- What are the key challenges: overlapping convex sets, coverage completeness, computational complexity of the decomposition, and handling narrow passages in the environment?
- What PRM variants are best suited for this pipeline (e.g., PRM* for asymptotic optimality, SPARS for sparsity, or bridge-test PRM for narrow passages)?
- How does the quality (size, number, overlap) of the generated convex sets affect GCS solver performance?

Provide a thorough technical analysis of feasibility, including reference to relevant algorithms and their properties.

--- SOURCE 1: Motion planning around obstacles with convex optimization ---
URL: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/375669203_Motion_planning_around_obstacles_with_convex_optimization

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper presents GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), a motion planning framework that enables convex optimization to efficiently and reliably plan collision-free trajectories around obstacles. The key insight is using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets to design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem, which is typically very tight. A cheap postprocessing of the relaxation solution is almost always sufficient to identify a globally optimal collision-free trajectory.

The framework handles costs and constraints on trajectory shape, duration, and velocity. It reduces the planning problem to a Shortest-Path Problem in GCS, solving a convex relaxation (typically an LP or SOCP) followed by a randomized rounding algorithm. The method is sound (trajectories satisfy all constraints) and complete up to the conservatism of space decomposition.

Key results include:
- **Maze planning (2,500 cells)**: GCS finds optimal trajectories with 5,000 binary variables vs. the 10^7 required by existing mixed-integer planners. Solved in 0.98 seconds (SOCP) and 9.1 seconds (LP).
- **Quadrotor flying through buildings (100 random environments)**: 95% of trajectories have optimality gap ≤1%, worst case 2.9%. Average runtime 2.65 seconds.
- **7-DOF robot arm comparison with PRM**: GCS finds shorter trajectories faster online than both standard PRM and PRM with shortcutting. All trajectories are optimal (δopt=0) within the space decomposition.
- **Dual-arm manipulation (14 DOF)**: GCS plans coordinated motions including arm crossing, near-self-collision configurations, and handoffs. Largest optimality gap 13.9%, runtimes 21-185 seconds.

GCS uses Bèzier curves for trajectory parameterization, guaranteeing safety at all times with no discretization error. The free space is decomposed into convex safe regions Q_i, and an intersection graph encodes connectivity. The method scales polynomially with the number of regions and curve degree.

The paper argues GCS generalizes PRM by extending collision-free samples to convex regions inflated as much as obstacles allow, reducing combinatorial complexity. It handles differential costs and constraints, exploits combinatorial structure, and has low runtimes. The implementation is available in the open-source software Drake.
</summary>

Specifically, we focus on collision-free motion planning with costs and constraints on the shape, the duration, and the velocity of the trajectory.", "Using recent techniques for finding shortest paths in Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS), we design a practical convex relaxation of the planning problem. We show that this relaxation is typically very tight, to the point that a cheap postprocessing of its solution is almost always sufficient to identify a collision-free trajectory that is globally optimal (within the parameterized class of curves).", "Through numerical and hardware experiments, we demonstrate that our planner, which we name GCS, can find better trajectories in less time than widely used sampling-based algorithms and can reliably design trajectories in high-dimensional complex environments.", "On 95% of the environments GCS designs a trajectory with optimality gap δopt ≤ 1%, and, even in the worst case, we only have δopt = 2.9%.", "GCS can be thought of as a generalization of PRM, where each collision-free sample is extended to a collision-free convex region, that is inflated as much as the obstacles allow."

--- SOURCE 2: Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) Optimization ---
URL: https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/graphs-of-convex-sets-gcs

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) is a mixed discrete-continuous optimization framework that integrates graph search with convex optimization, primarily used for path planning and control in robotics. In GCS, graph structure represents combinatorial choices, and each selected vertex or edge carries a convex optimization problem. The framework generalizes classical problems like shortest path, TSP, spanning tree, and assignment by coupling discrete decisions with continuous convex program solvers.

**Foundational Model:** A general GCS problem selects an admissible subgraph along with continuous variables on selected vertices. Edge costs need not be static and can encode distances, control-theoretic stage costs, or continuity constraints. The shortest-path problem in GCS is NP-hard.

**Exact Formulations:** The standard exact formulation uses mixed-integer convex programs (MICP) via perspective/homogenization operators. Convex relaxations (dropping integrality) are often very tight but not exact in general. Tools like GCSOPT automatically transform ILP models into MICPs.

**Search Algorithms:** Several efficient algorithms have been developed: A*-GCS (uses heuristics on representative points, provable lower bounds), GCS* (forward heuristic search, complete and cost-optimal), IxG/IxG* (interleaves graph search with convex optimization), and multi-query SPP (offline SDP for lower bounds, online in milliseconds).

**Temporal Logic Integration:** GCS has been integrated with LTL and STL for symbolic task planning with continuous motion. For LTL, product graphs combine transition systems with finite automata; for STL, timed automata are used. Reported benchmarks include a 30-DoF humanoid solved in ~7.72 seconds and a 5-key/5-door problem in 5.82 seconds.

**Space-Time Planning:** ST-GCS adds time as an optimization dimension, enabling multi-robot planning in dynamic environments. Applications include autonomous driving (with Bézier curves and polynomial time-scaling) and game-theoretic highway driving scenarios.

**Limitations:** GCS problems remain NP-hard in general. Relaxation quality is problem-dependent. Model fidelity may be traded for convexity (e.g., small-slip assumptions in driving). Augmented formulations for TSP remain exponential. Software ecosystem includes GCSOPT, Drake, MOSEK, CVXPY, and CLARABEL.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents research on "Graphs of Convex Sets" (GCS), a framework for solving motion planning and optimization problems that combine discrete graph structures with continuous convex optimization. Key contributions include:

- **Two key ingredients**: (1) The linear programming formulation of shortest path problems on discrete graphs, and (2) Convex formulations of continuous motion planning (without obstacle navigation), such as kinematic trajectory optimization for robot arms.
- **GCS formulation**: For each vertex i in a graph V, there is a compact convex set X_i ⊂ ℝ^d where a point x_i ∈ X_i is chosen. Edge lengths are given by convex functions ℓ(x_i, x_j). The motion planning problem uses ℓ_{i,j}(x_i, x_j) = |x_i - x_j|₂.
- **Key results**: The convex relaxation is tight (solves to global optimality). Previous formulations were intractable, requiring 6.25 × 10^6 binaries. The approach transcribes to a mixed-integer convex program with a very tight relaxation, solving orders of magnitude faster than previous work. Solving only the convex optimization (+rounding) is almost always sufficient to obtain the globally optimal solution.

<summary>
# Superfast Configuration-Space Convex Set Computation on GPUs for Online Motion Planning

This paper presents a GPU-accelerated approach for constructing probabilistically collision-free convex sets in robot configuration space for online motion planning in changing environments.

## Key Contributions

1. **EI-ZO Algorithm**: The authors propose "Edge Inflation Zero-Order" (EI-ZO), which inflates collision-free line segments into sequences of convex sets (SCS) using massive GPU parallelism. Unlike prior methods that inflate points, EI-ZO guarantees the resulting polytope contains the original collision-free line segment.

2. **Motion Planning Pipeline**: The pipeline combines:
   - Dynamic Roadmaps (DRMs) for rapid path finding
   - EI-ZO for inflating piecewise-linear paths into convex sets
   - Decomposition-based motion planning (DBMP) for trajectory optimization
   - Iterative collision recovery mechanism

3. **GPU Implementation**: The authors provide a CUDA-based implementation (CSDecomp library) that minimizes CPU-GPU data transfer, using thread-level parallelization for sampling, collision checking, and optimization.

## Results

- **17.1× faster** than nonlinear trajectory optimization baseline
- **27.9% increase in reliability** (72% → 100% success rate on simulation benchmark)
- Validated on simulation benchmark (2D and 7D) and KUKA iiwa 7 robot with perception

## Background

The work addresses a key bottleneck in DBMPs: constructing convex decompositions of the collision-free configuration space. Prior methods were slow, scaled poorly, and only worked in static environments. The authors extend IRIS-ZO to handle line segments rather than points, making set construction fast enough for real-time use in changing environments.

## Methodology

EI-ZO iteratively samples configurations within the current polytope, finds collisions, and places separating hyperplanes tangent to sub-level sets of the distance function to the line segment. The algorithm uses a probabilistic termination condition guaranteeing that at most an ε-fraction of the polytope volume is in collision with probability 1-δ.

The pipeline also includes a collision recovery mechanism that refines sets when the optimized trajectory contains collisions, and supports inflating multiple paths for better coverage.
</summary>

2. A heuristic algorithm that approximates decomposition by identifying and linking notches (concave vertices), selecting vertices with high visible neighbors, and exploring three-vertex configurations.
3. A visibility-preserving bridge transformation that converts polygons with holes into equivalent simple instances, enabling decomposition of more complex topologies.
4. A convex-union post-processing phase applied to both exact and heuristic outputs to further reduce the number of convex pieces.

URL: https://www.cs.rutgers.edu/~kb572/pubs/spars2.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This paper by Dobson and Bekris (Rutgers University) presents SPARS2, an extension of the SPARS algorithm for building sparse roadmap spanners in motion planning. SPARS2 provides probabilistic completeness and asymptotic near-optimality while dramatically reducing memory requirements during construction compared to prior methods. The key innovation is that SPARS2 does not require building a dense underlying roadmap (PRM∗) in parallel with the spanner, unlike its predecessor SPARS. Instead, it uses localized sampling and auxiliary information to determine when to add nodes for coverage, connectivity, interfaces, or shortcuts. The algorithm maintains the property that the probability of adding new nodes converges to zero as iterations increase, enabling a natural stopping criterion. Experimental results in SE(2) and SE(3) environments (using OMPL's "2D Maze" and "Bugtrap") show SPARS2 uses approximately two orders of magnitude less memory during offline construction than SPARS or PRM∗, while returning competitive quality paths that often exceed theoretical guarantees.
